lessons.title: What Computer Architecture and Organization Are
lessons.content:
Imagine you open the back of an old desktop computer at a repair shop in Dhaka's IDB Bhaban. You see a green board, a chip with a fan on top, some long sticks of RAM, and a lot of tiny lines running between them. You type a message on Facebook, and somehow these silent pieces of metal and silicon turn your key presses into letters on the screen, send them across the world, and show a reply. How? That question, 'how does the machine actually do it inside?', is what this whole course is about.

What it is in one line: Computer Architecture and Organization is the study of how a computer is designed and built so that it can run programs. It explains what the processor understands, how it is put together from smaller parts, how it talks to memory and to input and output devices, and how designers make it fast, cheap and low on power.

The problem it solves: Software people write programs in languages like C, Python or Dart. Hardware people build circuits from transistors and logic gates. These two worlds speak completely different languages. A transistor knows nothing about a 'for loop', and a Python programmer does not want to think about voltages. Somebody has to design the bridge between them: a clear agreement about what the hardware will do when the software asks for something, and a smart way to build hardware that keeps that promise quickly. That bridge is computer architecture.

Before this idea was clear: The earliest electronic computers of the 1940s, like ENIAC, were 'programmed' by plugging cables and setting switches by hand. Changing the program could take days. Every new machine also had its own completely different set of commands, so a program written for one machine was useless on the next one. In 1964 IBM launched the System/360 family and made a big decision: several machines with very different speeds and prices would all understand the same set of instructions. A customer could buy a small model, write programs, and later move to a bigger model without rewriting anything. That was the moment people clearly separated 'what the machine promises' from 'how a particular machine is built'. Those two halves are exactly the two words in our course title.

Architecture, the promise: Computer architecture is the part of the design that a programmer (or a compiler) can see. It answers questions like: What instructions exist, such as ADD, LOAD, STORE, JUMP? How many registers are there and how big is each one? How are numbers stored, for example 32-bit two's complement integers? How does an instruction say where its data is? What happens when something goes wrong, like dividing by zero? The official name for this list of promises is the Instruction Set Architecture, or ISA. x86-64 (used in most Intel and AMD laptops) and ARM (used in almost all smartphones) are two famous ISAs.

Organization, the building: Computer organization is how a specific chip actually keeps those promises. It answers questions like: How many adders are inside the ALU? Is there a cache, and how big? Is the processor pipelined, and how many stages? How wide is the bus to memory? Is multiplication done in one clock tick or ten? A programmer usually cannot see these details directly; she only notices that one chip runs her program faster than another. Two processors can have the same architecture but very different organization.

A restaurant analogy: Think of a restaurant in Old Dhaka famous for kacchi biryani. The menu is the architecture: it tells customers exactly what they can order and what they will get. 'One plate kacchi, one borhani' is like an instruction. The kitchen is the organization: how many cooks, how many big handis, whether one cook does everything or there is an assembly line where one person cuts, one cooks, one serves. Two branches of the same restaurant can share the same menu (same architecture) but have very different kitchens (different organization). A small branch in Mirpur has one cook; the main branch has ten cooks working in parallel. The customer gets the same biryani from both, only faster at one.

Where the analogy breaks: In a restaurant, a customer can often peek into the kitchen and sometimes even ask for changes. In a computer, the line between architecture and organization is strict: software must work correctly no matter how the inside is organized. Also, a real processor follows instructions with total obedience and zero creativity; a cook might 'improve' your order, a CPU never will. The analogy helps you remember the split, but the real rules are much stricter.

A real example of the split: Intel's Core i3 and Core i9 processors of the same generation both run the x86-64 instruction set. The same Windows and the same Chrome browser run on both. That is the shared architecture. But the i9 has more cores, a larger cache and often a higher clock speed. That is different organization. Similarly, a cheap Android phone and an expensive one both use the ARM architecture, so the same app from the Play Store works on both, yet one feels much faster because of how its chip is organized inside.

Levels of abstraction: Computer scientists handle complexity by stacking layers, where each layer only needs to understand the one directly below it. From top to bottom the stack looks like this: Application (your bKash app) -> High-level language (Kotlin, C) -> Compiler and operating system -> ISA (the architecture) -> Microarchitecture (the organization: datapath, control, pipeline, cache) -> Logic gates and flip-flops -> Transistors -> Physics of electrons. Each arrow means 'is built on top of'. The ISA sits right in the middle like a waist: everything above it is software, everything below it is hardware. This is why the ISA is often called the hardware/software interface.

Why the layers help: Because of this layering, a Bangladeshi app developer can write one Flutter app without knowing which exact chip is inside each customer's phone. The compiler turns the code into ARM instructions, and every ARM chip promises to run those instructions correctly. In the other direction, a chip designer at ARM or Apple can invent a faster cache without breaking any existing app, because the promise at the ISA level stays the same. Layers let thousands of people work on different parts without stepping on each other.

The main parts you will meet: Almost every computer has five classic parts. Input devices bring data in (keyboard, touch screen, microphone). Output devices send results out (display, speaker). Memory stores both programs and data. The datapath is the part of the processor that actually moves and transforms data: registers, the ALU and the connections between them. The control unit is the part that reads each instruction and tells the datapath what to do, step by step. Datapath plus control together form the processor, also called the CPU. Here is a simple picture: Input -> [ CPU = Control + Datapath ] <-> Memory, and CPU -> Output. You will study each of these boxes in depth in later lessons.

What happens when you run a program, in short: When you tap an app icon, the operating system copies the program's instructions from storage (like the phone's flash memory) into main memory (RAM). The CPU then repeats a simple loop again and again: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode it to understand what it asks, execute it using the ALU or memory, and store the result. A modern phone CPU does this loop billions of times every second. Everything you see on the screen comes out of this one boring loop running at amazing speed. Lessons 12 to 18 open this loop up completely.

Why you should study this course: First, you will write faster programs. A program that walks through an array row by row can run several times faster than the same program walking column by column, purely because of how the cache works. Without this course, that looks like magic. Second, many later courses depend on it: Operating Systems talks about virtual memory and interrupts, Compiler Design produces instructions for an ISA, Embedded Systems works directly with hardware, and Microprocessors uses a real chip. Third, careers like chip design, embedded firmware, game engine programming, high performance computing and even backend performance tuning need this understanding.

What designers care about: Designing a computer is a game of trade-offs. Speed (how quickly a program finishes), cost (how much silicon area and money), power (how much battery it drains and how hot it gets), and reliability (does it give correct answers even when something goes slightly wrong). You can almost never improve one without paying in another. A bigger cache makes programs faster but costs more area and power. A higher clock speed makes each step shorter but makes the chip hotter. Good architects choose the balance that suits the device: a phone wants low power, a data-center server wants raw throughput, a washing machine controller wants very low cost.

When to think at the architecture level: When you are choosing a processor for a product, porting software to a new chip, writing a compiler, or deciding whether a program can run on both a laptop and a phone, you think about the ISA, because that is what decides compatibility. When to think at the organization level: when you are tuning performance, measuring why something is slow, comparing two chips with the same ISA, or designing hardware itself.

When this course is not the right tool: If your only goal is to build a simple website form, you do not need to know about pipeline hazards to finish the job. Most day-to-day programming hides the hardware well. But the moment you hit a performance wall, see strange memory bugs, work on phones, games, IoT devices or servers handling millions of requests, the knowledge from this course becomes the difference between guessing and understanding.

Real-life example 1, buying a laptop in Bangladesh: Suppose you go to a computer shop in Multiplan Center with a budget of 70,000 taka. The seller shows you two laptops. Both run Windows, so both use the x86-64 architecture. One says '4 cores, 3.0 GHz, 6 MB cache', the other says '8 cores, 2.5 GHz, 12 MB cache'. Which is faster? A person who has not studied this course just picks the bigger GHz. After this course you will know that GHz is only one part of performance; the number of instructions done per clock, the cache size and the number of cores matter too, and the answer depends on what you will run. Lesson 3 gives you the exact formula.

Real-life example 2, apps on a cheap and an expensive phone: Your cousin has a 12,000 taka Android phone and your uncle has a 1,20,000 taka phone. Both install the same bKash app from the Play Store, and it works on both. Why does one app work on both phones? Because both chips follow the ARM architecture, so the app's instructions mean the same thing on both. Why does it open faster on your uncle's phone? Because his chip has a better organization: wider pipelines, bigger caches, faster memory, more cores. Same promise, better kitchen.

Common mistakes students make: Many students mix up architecture and organization and use the words as if they mean the same thing. Remember: architecture is what the programmer sees (instructions, registers, data types, addressing); organization is how it is built (cache, pipeline, bus width, control design). Another mistake is thinking 'more GHz always means faster'; it does not. A third is thinking the CPU understands C or Python directly; it does not, it only understands machine instructions of its ISA, and a compiler or interpreter does the translation. Finally, some think 'architecture' means only the physical shape of the computer; in this course it means the instruction set level design.

What exams usually ask: Define computer architecture and computer organization with an example. Differentiate between them in a table. Explain the levels of abstraction. Draw the block diagram of a computer with its five main parts. Explain why a family of computers with the same ISA is useful. Be ready to give the example of two processors with the same ISA but different organization.

The road map of this course: We start with the basic stored-program model and how to measure performance. Then we look at how numbers live in hardware and how the ALU does arithmetic, including floating point. Next comes the instruction set: formats, addressing modes, RISC versus CISC. Then we build the processor: datapath, hardwired and microprogrammed control, multi-cycle execution, and pipelining with its hazards and branch prediction. After that comes the memory system: hierarchy, cache, main memory and virtual memory. Finally input/output and parallel processors. Each lesson builds on the ones before it.

Quick recap: Architecture is the promise the hardware makes to software, written down as the ISA. Organization is the way a particular chip is built to keep that promise. Layers of abstraction let software and hardware improve independently, with the ISA in the middle. Every design is a trade-off among speed, cost, power and reliability. Keep the biryani restaurant in mind: same menu, different kitchens. Next lesson, we meet the simple but powerful idea that started it all, the stored-program computer.
key_points: Computer architecture is the programmer-visible design of a computer, mainly its Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).
Computer organization is how a particular processor is built to implement that ISA: cache, pipeline, bus width, control design.
Two chips can share one architecture but differ in organization, like Core i3 and Core i9 both running x86-64.
The ISA is the hardware/software interface: software above it, hardware below it.
Layers of abstraction (app, language, OS, ISA, microarchitecture, gates, transistors) let each part change independently.
A computer has five classic parts: input, output, memory, datapath and control; datapath plus control is the CPU.
Design is a trade-off among speed, cost, power and reliability; higher GHz alone does not mean faster.
IBM System/360 (1964) popularised one ISA across a whole family of machines with different speeds.
lessons.tip: Every time a new term appears in this course, ask yourself one question: is this something the programmer can see (architecture) or only how it is built inside (organization)? Sorting terms this way builds a clean mental map.
lessons.task: Open Settings > About phone on your phone (or the system information page on a computer) and write down the processor name, number of cores, clock speed and RAM. Then look the processor up and find which ISA it uses (ARM or x86-64). Make two columns on paper: things that are architecture and things that are organization.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of computer architecture rather than organization?
options: The list of instructions the processor understands
How many adders are inside the ALU
quiz.explain: The instruction set is visible to programmers and compilers, so it is architecture. Cache size, pipeline depth and adder count are organization details.

quiz.q: A Core i3 and a Core i9 of the same generation run the same Windows programs. Why?
options: They have the same clock speed
They have the same number of cores
They have the same cache size
quiz.explain: Compatibility comes from the shared architecture, the x86-64 ISA. Their organization (cores, cache, speed) is different.

quiz.q: In the levels of abstraction, what sits between software and hardware?
quiz.explain: The ISA is the hardware/software interface: compilers and operating systems sit above it, microarchitecture and logic sit below it.

quiz.q: Which pair together make up the processor (CPU)?
quiz.explain: The datapath moves and transforms data, and the control unit tells it what to do. Together they are the CPU.

quiz.q: Why is 'higher GHz always means faster' a wrong idea?
options: GHz measures memory size, not speed
Performance also depends on instructions per clock, cache, cores and the program
Clock speed has no effect at all on performance
quiz.explain: Clock speed is one factor. How much work is done per clock, the memory system and parallelism also decide how fast a program finishes.

lessons.title: The Stored-Program Computer: von Neumann and Harvard
lessons.content:
Imagine a calculator that can only add. If you want it to multiply, you must open it up and rewire it. Now imagine a different machine: you simply type a new list of steps into its memory, and it starts doing a completely new job. No screwdriver, no new wires. That second machine is a stored-program computer, and almost every computer you have ever touched, from your phone to the bKash server, works this way. In this lesson we see where this idea came from, how it works inside, and what its weak spot is.

What it is: A stored-program computer is a computer that keeps its program, the list of instructions, inside the same kind of memory where it keeps data. The processor reads the instructions from memory one by one and carries them out. Because the program is just numbers in memory, changing the program is as easy as writing new numbers.

The problem before: The first big electronic computer, ENIAC, was finished in 1945 in the USA. It was very fast for its time, but to give it a new problem, operators had to plug cables between panels and set thousands of switches. Setting up a new program could take days, while the calculation itself might take only minutes. The machine was flexible in theory, but changing its job was painfully slow, and every mistake meant hunting for a wrong cable.

The solution: In 1945 John von Neumann wrote a report, the 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC', describing a design where instructions are stored in memory as numbers, just like data. Other people working on ENIAC, such as J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, had similar ideas, so historians say the credit is shared, but the design became famous under von Neumann's name. Early machines that actually ran stored programs include the Manchester 'Baby' (1948) and EDSAC in Cambridge (1949). From then on, loading a new program meant loading new numbers, not rewiring.

The von Neumann model, the five parts: The classic design has a memory that holds both instructions and data, an arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) that does calculations, a control unit that reads instructions and directs everything, and input and output devices. The ALU plus a few registers is the datapath; datapath plus control is the CPU. A one-line picture: Input -> CPU (Control + ALU + Registers) <-> Memory (instructions + data) -> Output. The double arrow between CPU and memory is the most important line in the whole picture.

Key idea 1, one memory for everything: In the von Neumann model there is one memory and one path (bus) between it and the CPU. An instruction such as 'ADD the number at address 100 to register R1' lives at some address, say 20. The number it uses lives at address 100. Both are just patterns of bits in the same memory. The memory itself does not know which is which.

Key idea 2, sequential execution: Instructions are normally executed one after another in the order they sit in memory. A special register called the program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. After each instruction the PC moves forward. Only a jump or branch instruction changes the PC to a different address, which is how loops and if-else decisions happen.

Key idea 3, addressable memory: Memory is a long row of numbered cells, like post office boxes. Each cell has an address (0, 1, 2, ...) and holds a fixed number of bits. The CPU asks for 'the contents of address 100', and memory answers. It does not search by content; it goes straight to the number.

How it works, step by step: Let us run a tiny program. Memory address 0 holds 'LOAD R1, [100]', address 1 holds 'ADD R1, [101]', address 2 holds 'STORE R1, [102]', address 3 holds 'HALT'. Address 100 holds 7 and address 101 holds 5. Step 1: PC = 0, the CPU fetches the instruction at 0, decodes it as LOAD, reads 7 from address 100 into R1, PC becomes 1. Step 2: fetch at 1, decode ADD, read 5 from 101, ALU computes 7 + 5 = 12, R1 = 12, PC becomes 2. Step 3: fetch at 2, STORE writes 12 into address 102, PC becomes 3. Step 4: HALT stops. Notice: every step needed the memory at least once for the instruction, and some steps needed it a second time for data.

An analogy: Think of a cook in a small home kitchen in Chattogram. On the same shelf she keeps both the recipe notebook and the jars of ingredients. She reads one line of the recipe, puts the notebook back, takes the jar it mentions, uses it, puts it back, then reads the next line. Recipe lines are instructions; jars are data; the shelf is memory; the cook is the CPU; her two hands and the narrow door to the shelf are the bus. Where it breaks: a real CPU never 'understands' the recipe, it just follows bit patterns, and real memory holds billions of cells, not a few jars.

The big advantage, flexibility: Because programs are data, a program can load other programs. This is what makes an operating system possible: it reads an app from storage into memory and then jumps to it. A compiler is also possible: it is a program whose output is another program. Even downloading an app update from the Play Store is just copying new instruction numbers into storage. None of this would work if programs were wires.

The weak spot, the von Neumann bottleneck: There is only one path between CPU and memory, and both instructions and data must travel on it. The CPU can calculate far faster than memory can deliver. So the CPU often sits idle, waiting. This limit is called the von Neumann bottleneck, a phrase made popular by John Backus in 1977. In our example, four instructions needed seven memory trips. Today a CPU can do an addition in well under a nanosecond, while getting data from main memory takes many tens of nanoseconds, so the gap is real.

A safety weak spot too: Since instructions and data look the same, a bug can make a program write data over its own instructions, or an attacker can trick a program into treating attacker-supplied data as code. Classic buffer overflow attacks worked like this. Modern systems add protection, such as marking memory pages as 'no execute', which you will meet again in virtual memory.

The Harvard architecture: The Harvard Mark I (1944) used separate storage for instructions and data. The name stuck: a Harvard architecture has two separate memories and two separate buses, one for instructions and one for data. Picture: Instruction memory <-> CPU <-> Data memory. Now the CPU can fetch the next instruction and read data at the same moment, so the bottleneck is reduced. The cost: two memories, two sets of wires, and a fixed split of space. If your program is big but your data is small, the extra data memory is wasted.

Where Harvard is used: Many small microcontrollers, such as the AVR chips in Arduino boards and many digital signal processors, use a Harvard design. Their program lives in flash memory and their variables live in a separate small RAM. This suits devices like a rice cooker controller or a traffic light controller, where the program is fixed and speed per cycle matters.

Modified Harvard, what your laptop really uses: Modern PCs and phones mix both ideas. Main memory (RAM) is one unified memory, von Neumann style, so programs are still data and the OS can load apps. But inside the CPU, the closest level of cache is split into an instruction cache and a data cache, Harvard style, so an instruction fetch and a data access can happen in the same cycle. This is called a modified Harvard architecture. You get flexibility from the outside and speed on the inside.

Comparison in words: von Neumann has one memory and one bus, simpler and cheaper, flexible, but suffers the bottleneck. Harvard has two memories and two buses, faster per cycle and safer against code being overwritten, but costs more and splits space rigidly. Modified Harvard keeps a unified main memory with split caches, which is why it is the common choice for general computers.

When to choose which: For a general-purpose computer that must load any program a user downloads, a unified von Neumann main memory is the right choice. For a small fixed-function device that must be cheap and predictable, pure Harvard is often better. For a high-performance processor, modified Harvard gives the best of both. When not to use pure Harvard: when programs need to be loaded and changed often, because writing into instruction memory becomes awkward.

Real-life example 1, a bKash transaction: When you send money, the bKash server's CPU runs program code that was loaded into its RAM when the service started. The same RAM holds your account balance as data. Each step, such as checking the PIN or subtracting the amount, means fetching instructions and data over the memory system. Engineers keep these servers fast by using large caches so the CPU rarely waits on the bottleneck.

Real-life example 2, an Arduino project at a school science fair: A student in Rajshahi builds a soil moisture alarm with an Arduino Uno. Its ATmega328P chip keeps the program in 32 KB of flash and variables in 2 KB of SRAM, two separate memories, Harvard style. When she uploads new code from her laptop, a special loader writes the flash; the running program cannot casually rewrite itself. That is the Harvard trade-off in action: safe and simple, less flexible.

Common mistakes: Students often say von Neumann invented the computer; he described the stored-program design, and others contributed. Another mistake is thinking Harvard means 'two CPUs'; it means two memories and two paths for one CPU. Some think modern PCs are purely von Neumann or purely Harvard; at the cache level they are split, at main memory they are unified. Finally, people confuse the bottleneck with slow disks; the bottleneck is about the CPU-memory path.

What exams ask: Explain the stored-program concept. Draw the von Neumann block diagram and label each part. What is the von Neumann bottleneck and how is it reduced (caches, wider buses, split caches, prefetching)? Compare von Neumann and Harvard architectures in a table. What is modified Harvard architecture and why do modern CPUs use it?

Recap: A stored-program computer keeps instructions and data in memory as numbers, so changing the program means loading new numbers. The von Neumann model has one memory and one bus, which is flexible but creates the bottleneck. Harvard separates instruction and data memory for speed. Modern processors use modified Harvard: unified RAM with split caches. Next lesson we learn how to measure whether one computer is really faster than another.
key_points: A stored-program computer keeps instructions and data in the same kind of memory, as numbers.
ENIAC was reprogrammed by rewiring; the 1945 EDVAC report described storing programs in memory.
The von Neumann model: memory, ALU, control unit, input and output, with one bus between CPU and memory.
The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; jumps change the PC.
The von Neumann bottleneck: the single CPU-memory path limits speed because the CPU waits for memory.
Harvard architecture uses separate instruction and data memories and buses, common in microcontrollers like AVR.
Modern CPUs use modified Harvard: unified main memory with split instruction and data caches.
Programs being data makes operating systems and compilers possible, but also enables code-injection bugs.
lessons.tip: Draw the von Neumann and Harvard diagrams side by side from memory three times this week. If you can draw and label them in under a minute, you understand the difference well enough for any exam.
lessons.task: Take a page and draw 8 boxes numbered 0 to 7 as memory. Write the 4-instruction program from this lesson in boxes 0-3 and the numbers 7 and 5 in boxes 5 and 6 (change addresses accordingly). Then play CPU with a pencil as the PC: count how many times you touch memory. Change the numbers and run it again.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of the stored-program concept?
options: Programs are set by plugging cables
Instructions are stored in memory as numbers, like data
Each program needs its own CPU
Data is stored on paper tape only
quiz.explain: Storing instructions in memory as numbers lets a computer change its program by loading new numbers instead of rewiring.

quiz.q: What causes the von Neumann bottleneck?
options: The single shared path between CPU and memory for both instructions and data
Having separate instruction and data memories
quiz.explain: Instructions and data both travel over one CPU-memory path, and memory is slower than the CPU, so the CPU waits.

quiz.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction?
quiz.explain: The program counter (PC) points to the next instruction; it moves forward after each instruction or changes on a jump.

quiz.q: A Harvard architecture mainly differs from von Neumann by having:
options: Separate memories and buses for instructions and data
quiz.explain: Harvard splits instruction and data storage so both can be accessed at the same time.

quiz.q: What do most modern laptop and phone processors use?
options: Pure Harvard with no shared RAM
Modified Harvard: unified main memory with split L1 instruction and data caches
Pure von Neumann with no caches
quiz.explain: They keep one unified RAM for flexibility and split the first-level cache for speed.

lessons.title: Measuring Performance: Clock, CPI, CPU Time and Amdahl's Law
lessons.content:
Two friends in Khulna argue about whose laptop is faster. One says 'mine is 3.5 GHz', the other says 'mine has 8 cores'. They run the same game and the result surprises both of them. Who was right? Neither, because they were each looking at only one number. Performance is not a single label on a box; it comes from a small formula with three parts. Once you know that formula, you can reason about almost any speed claim. That is the goal of this lesson.

What performance means: For a single user, performance usually means response time, also called execution time: how long from starting a task to finishing it. Shorter is better. For a server that handles many users, such as a bank's website, people also care about throughput: how many tasks finish per second. A faster processor usually improves both. Adding more processors to a server improves throughput but may not make any single request finish sooner.

Comparing two machines: We define performance as 1 divided by execution time. If machine A runs a program in 10 seconds and machine B runs it in 15 seconds, then performance of A divided by performance of B equals 15 / 10 = 1.5. We say 'A is 1.5 times faster than B'. Always compare times on the same program; comparing a game on one machine with a spreadsheet on another tells you nothing.

The problem with simple numbers: Before people used careful formulas, buyers compared clock speed alone, or a single number called MIPS. Manufacturers loved these numbers because they were easy to make look big. But a chip can have a high clock speed and still do little work per tick, so the numbers misled people. The solution was to break execution time into parts that each tell an honest story.

The clock: Inside every processor a clock signal ticks like a very fast metronome. Each tick is a clock cycle. The clock rate is ticks per second, measured in hertz. 1 GHz means one billion cycles per second. The cycle time is the length of one tick: cycle time = 1 / clock rate. At 2 GHz, the cycle time is 1 / (2 x 10^9) = 0.5 nanoseconds. Everything inside the processor happens in step with these ticks.

CPI, cycles per instruction: Different instructions take different numbers of cycles. An add might take 1 cycle, a multiply 3, a memory load might take more. CPI is the average number of clock cycles per instruction for a program. If a program runs 100 instructions and they take 250 cycles in total, CPI = 250 / 100 = 2.5. CPI depends on the processor's organization (pipelining, caches) and on the mix of instructions the program uses.

The CPU time equation: Here is the most important formula of the course: CPU time = Instruction count x CPI x Cycle time. Equivalently, CPU time = (Instruction count x CPI) / Clock rate. Read it as a chain: Instructions -> cycles -> seconds. Instruction count says how many instructions the program executes. CPI says how many cycles each takes on average. Cycle time says how many seconds each cycle lasts.

Worked example 1: A program executes 2 billion instructions on a 2 GHz processor with CPI 1.5. CPU time = 2 x 10^9 x 1.5 / (2 x 10^9) = 1.5 seconds. Now suppose a new compiler cuts the instruction count to 1.6 billion but raises CPI to 1.7 because it uses heavier instructions. New time = 1.6 x 10^9 x 1.7 / (2 x 10^9) = 1.36 seconds. The new compiler wins, even though CPI got worse. That is why you must look at all three parts together.

Who controls each part: The algorithm and the programming language affect instruction count. The compiler affects instruction count and CPI. The ISA affects all three: a richer ISA may need fewer instructions but each may take more cycles. The organization (pipelining, cache) mainly affects CPI. The circuit technology and organization affect clock rate. A diagram in words: Algorithm, Language, Compiler -> Instruction count; ISA, Organization -> CPI; Technology, Organization -> Clock rate.

CPI with an instruction mix: Suppose a program has 50 percent ALU instructions with CPI 1, 30 percent loads and stores with CPI 2, and 20 percent branches with CPI 3. Average CPI = 0.5 x 1 + 0.3 x 2 + 0.2 x 3 = 0.5 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.7. This weighted average is how architects predict the effect of a change. If a better cache drops load/store CPI to 1.5, new CPI = 0.5 + 0.45 + 0.6 = 1.55, so the program becomes 1.7 / 1.55, about 1.1 times faster.

Worked example 2, GHz is not everything: Machine P runs at 4 GHz with CPI 2.0. Machine Q runs at 3 GHz with CPI 1.2. Same program, 1 billion instructions. P: 10^9 x 2.0 / (4 x 10^9) = 0.5 seconds. Q: 10^9 x 1.2 / (3 x 10^9) = 0.4 seconds. The slower-clocked Q is 1.25 times faster. This is exactly the trap the two friends in Khulna fell into.

Why MIPS misleads: MIPS means million instructions per second: MIPS = Instruction count / (Execution time x 10^6) = Clock rate / (CPI x 10^6). It sounds fair, but it ignores how much work each instruction does. A machine with simple instructions may need many more of them for the same job, so it shows a big MIPS number while finishing later. MIPS also changes from program to program on the same machine. Use it only to compare machines with the same ISA running the same program, and even then execution time is safer.

Benchmarks: Since performance depends on the program, we measure with real programs called benchmarks. The SPEC CPU suite is a well-known set of programs such as compilers, compression and scientific codes. Each program's time is compared with a reference machine to get a ratio, and the ratios are combined using the geometric mean, which keeps the comparison consistent no matter which machine is the reference. Phone reviewers use other benchmark apps for the same reason. A good benchmark looks like the work you actually do.

Amdahl's law, the problem: Suppose you make one part of a program super fast. How much faster is the whole program? Not as much as you hope, because the part you did not improve still takes the same time. Gene Amdahl stated this in 1967. It is the most important warning in all of performance work.

Amdahl's law, the formula: If a fraction f of the original time can be sped up by a factor s, the overall speedup = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / s). Example: 40 percent of the time is spent on multiplication, and you make multiplication 4 times faster. Speedup = 1 / (0.6 + 0.4 / 4) = 1 / (0.6 + 0.1) = 1 / 0.7, about 1.43. Even if multiplication became infinitely fast, the limit is 1 / 0.6, about 1.67. The 60 percent you did not touch caps everything.

Amdahl's law with cores: If 90 percent of a program can run in parallel and you use 8 cores, speedup = 1 / (0.1 + 0.9 / 8) = 1 / (0.1 + 0.1125) = 1 / 0.2125, about 4.7, not 8. With unlimited cores the limit is 1 / 0.1 = 10. This is why the friend with 8 cores did not win either: the game had a serial part. The lesson: make the common case fast, and do not expect miracles from speeding up a small part.

The power wall: For decades designers raised clock rates every year. Around 2004 this stopped, with typical desktop clock rates staying around 3 to 4 GHz since. The reason is power. The dynamic power of CMOS chips is roughly proportional to capacitive load x voltage squared x frequency. Raising frequency raised power and heat beyond what a normal fan could remove. Lowering voltage helped for a while but cannot go down forever. So the industry turned to multiple cores per chip instead of faster single cores, which is why your phone says 'octa-core'.

An analogy: Think of a Dhaka to Chattogram bus trip. Instruction count is the distance in kilometres, CPI is how many minutes the bus takes per kilometre (traffic, stops), and cycle time is how long one minute is. You can shorten the trip by taking a shorter road (fewer instructions), by having less traffic per kilometre (lower CPI), or by, in this impossible story, making each minute shorter (faster clock). Where it breaks: a real clock rate is fixed for a design, and instruction count and CPI interact in ways a road trip does not.

Real-life example 1, a video editor in Dhaka: A freelancer exports wedding videos. Measured on a single core, export would take 20 minutes; 80 percent of that is video encoding that can use many cores, 20 percent is serial. She thinks of upgrading from 4 to 16 cores. Using Amdahl: with 4 cores the parallel part takes 16 / 4 = 4 minutes plus 4 serial minutes, so 8 minutes; with 16 cores, 16 / 16 = 1 minute plus 4, so 5 minutes. Going from 4 to 16 cores saves 3 minutes, not 6. Now she can judge if the price is worth it.

Real-life example 2, a school result server: On SSC result day, the education board website gets huge traffic. Here throughput matters more than one person's response time. Adding more servers increases how many students are served per second, even if each page takes the same time to build. Making each request faster (better code, caching) helps both. Knowing which metric matters tells you where to spend money.

Common mistakes: Comparing clock speeds across different processor designs. Forgetting that CPI is an average that depends on the program. Using MIPS to compare different ISAs. Applying Amdahl's law with f as the fraction of code lines instead of the fraction of time. Writing speedup as the time saved instead of old time divided by new time.

What exams ask: Calculate CPU time from instruction count, CPI and clock rate. Find average CPI from an instruction mix. Compare two machines and say which is faster and by how much. Show why MIPS is misleading with an example. Apply Amdahl's law, including the limit when s goes to infinity. Explain the power wall and why multicore came.

Recap: Performance is 1 over execution time. CPU time = Instruction count x CPI x Cycle time, and every part matters. MIPS and GHz alone mislead; benchmarks with real programs are better. Amdahl's law says the part you do not improve limits your speedup. Power limits stopped clock growth and pushed us to multicore. Next lesson we look at how numbers themselves are stored inside the hardware.
key_points: Performance = 1 / execution time; 'A is n times faster than B' means time of B / time of A = n.
Cycle time = 1 / clock rate; 2 GHz gives a 0.5 ns cycle.
CPU time = Instruction count x CPI x Cycle time = Instruction count x CPI / Clock rate.
Average CPI is the weighted sum of each instruction class's CPI times its fraction.
A lower clock rate can still win if CPI or instruction count is lower.
MIPS ignores how much work an instruction does, so it misleads across different ISAs.
Amdahl's law: speedup = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / s); the unimproved part sets the limit.
The power wall (power roughly proportional to C x V^2 x f) stopped clock growth and led to multicore chips.
lessons.tip: For every performance problem, first write the CPU time equation and fill in what you know. Most exam questions are just this one formula used two or three times, plus Amdahl's law.
lessons.task: Time yourself solving 20 easy sums on paper (the parallel part) and then writing your name and date at the top (the serial part). Now imagine 4 friends split the sums. Use Amdahl's law to predict the new total time, then try it with real friends or family and compare.

quiz.q: A program has 4 x 10^9 instructions, CPI 2, on a 2 GHz clock. What is the CPU time?
quiz.explain: CPU time = 4 x 10^9 x 2 / (2 x 10^9) = 4 seconds.

quiz.q: Machine A: 4 GHz, CPI 2. Machine B: 3 GHz, CPI 1.2. Same program. Which is faster?
options: A, because its clock is higher
B, because its time per instruction is lower
quiz.explain: Time per instruction: A = 2 / 4 = 0.5 ns, B = 1.2 / 3 = 0.4 ns. B is faster.

quiz.q: A program is 50% ALU (CPI 1), 30% load/store (CPI 2), 20% branch (CPI 3). Average CPI?
40% of time is sped up 4 times. Overall speedup by Amdahl's law is about:
Why did clock rates stop rising quickly around 2004?
options: Power and heat grew too high
quiz.explain: Dynamic power rises with frequency and voltage squared; chips became too hot, so designers moved to multiple cores.

lessons.title: Data Representation for Hardware: Integers, Fixed Point, IEEE 754 and Endianness
lessons.content:
Your bKash balance shows 1,250.50 taka. Your phone's thermometer app shows minus 2 degrees in a Sreemangal winter morning. A game shows your character at position 3.75 on a map. Inside the processor there are no commas, no minus signs and no decimal points, only wires that are either high or low, 1 or 0. So how does a machine store a negative number, or a fraction, using only bits? And why do programmers sometimes get 0.30000000000000004 when they add 0.1 and 0.2? This lesson answers these questions from the hardware's point of view.

What data representation means: Data representation is the agreed rule that maps a pattern of bits to a value. The same 8 bits 11111111 can mean 255 as an unsigned number, minus 1 as a signed number, or a character in some code. The bits do not carry their meaning; the instruction that uses them decides. An ADD instruction treats them as integers; a floating-point instruction treats them as a float. This is an architecture decision: the ISA says which formats exist and which instructions work on them.

Why hardware designers care: The format decides how big the adder must be, how overflow is detected, how many bits memory must move, and how fast arithmetic can be. A good format makes the common operations cheap. Two's complement, for example, lets one adder circuit do both addition and subtraction for signed and unsigned numbers. That saves silicon on every chip ever made.

Unsigned integers, a quick recap: With n bits you can store 0 to 2^n - 1. Each bit has a weight: from the right, 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. 8 bits give 0 to 255; 16 bits give 0 to 65,535; 32 bits give 0 to about 4.29 billion. Example: 0110 0101 = 64 + 32 + 4 + 1 = 101. Digital Logic Design covered conversions in detail, so here we focus on what the hardware does with these patterns.

The problem with negative numbers: Early machines tried sign-magnitude: the leftmost bit is the sign, the rest is the size. So +5 is 0101 and -5 is 1101 in 4 bits. The trouble: there are two zeros (0000 and 1000), and adding +5 and -5 with a normal adder gives a wrong answer. You would need extra circuits to compare signs and subtract. One's complement (flip all bits for negative) still had two zeros and needed an end-around carry. Both made hardware messier.

The solution, two's complement: To make -x, flip all bits of x and add 1. In 4 bits, +5 = 0101, flip gives 1010, add 1 gives 1011, so -5 = 1011. Now add 0101 + 1011 = 1 0000; drop the carry out of the top and you get 0000. Correct! The leftmost bit has weight -2^(n-1) instead of +2^(n-1). So 1011 = -8 + 2 + 1 = -5. With n bits the range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For 8 bits: -128 to +127. There is only one zero, and the same adder works for signed and unsigned values. That is why practically every modern processor uses it.

Subtraction for free: Since a - b = a + (-b), and -b = flip(b) + 1, the hardware computes subtraction by inverting b and setting the adder's carry-in to 1. One adder, a row of XOR gates and a control bit do both jobs. You will see this circuit inside the ALU in the next lesson.

Sign extension: When an 8-bit signed value is loaded into a 32-bit register, the hardware must keep its value. For positive numbers, fill the new left bits with 0. For negative numbers, fill with 1. Rule: copy the sign bit into all new positions. Example: -3 in 4 bits is 1101; in 8 bits it is 1111 1101. Check: -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = -3. If you wrongly fill with zeros you get 0000 1101 = 13, a different number. ISAs usually have both 'load byte' (sign-extend) and 'load byte unsigned' (zero-extend) because of this.

Overflow: If a result does not fit in n bits, it wraps around. In 8-bit two's complement, 100 + 50 = 150, but 150 is above 127, so the bits read as -106. Hardware detects signed overflow with a simple rule: if two numbers with the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign, overflow happened. Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow. Some languages trap on overflow, others silently wrap, which has caused real software bugs.

Fixed point, fractions the simple way: Suppose we agree that in an 8-bit number the last 4 bits are after the binary point. Then 0101 1000 means 0101.1000 = 4 + 1 + 0.5 = 5.5. The hardware just uses the normal integer adder; the programmer remembers where the point is. Fixed point is fast and cheap and is common in small microcontrollers and digital signal processing. The problem: the range is tiny. With 4 integer bits you cannot store 1,000, and with 4 fraction bits you cannot store 0.01 accurately. Money is often stored as whole poisha (integer) for the same reason: 1,250.50 taka is stored as 125,050 poisha, so there is no rounding error.

Floating point, the idea: Scientists need both tiny numbers (the mass of an electron) and huge ones (distance to a star). Scientific notation solves this in decimal: 6.02 x 10^23. Floating point does the same in binary: value = (-1)^sign x 1.fraction x 2^exponent. The binary point 'floats' according to the exponent, so a fixed number of bits can cover an enormous range.

The history problem and IEEE 754: Before 1985, different computer makers had different floating-point formats with different rounding behaviour, so the same program could give different answers on different machines. The IEEE 754 standard, published in 1985 and revised in 2008 and 2019, fixed the formats and rounding rules. Almost all processors now follow it, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives the same slightly odd answer on a phone in Bogura and a server in California.

IEEE 754 single precision (32 bits): 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 fraction bits. Layout: [S | EEEEEEEE | FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF]. The exponent is stored with a bias of 127: stored value = real exponent + 127. Because normal numbers always start with 1 before the point, that 1 is not stored; it is the 'hidden bit', giving 24 bits of precision for the price of 23. Single precision has about 7 decimal digits of precision and a largest value around 3.4 x 10^38.

Worked example, encode -6.25: Step 1, sign: negative, so S = 1. Step 2, binary: 6 = 110, 0.25 = .01, so 6.25 = 110.01. Step 3, normalise: 110.01 = 1.1001 x 2^2. Step 4, exponent: 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000 0001. Step 5, fraction: the bits after the point, 1001, padded with zeros to 23 bits. Result: 1 10000001 10010000000000000000000, which is C0C80000 in hexadecimal. Decoding reverses the steps.

IEEE 754 double precision (64 bits): 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits with bias 1023, and 52 fraction bits. This gives about 15 to 16 decimal digits of precision and a much larger range. Most languages, including Python's float and Dart's double, use double precision by default.

Special values: Exponent all zeros and fraction zero means zero; since there is a sign bit, there are +0 and -0, which compare equal. Exponent all zeros with a non-zero fraction gives denormal (subnormal) numbers, which fill the gap near zero with less precision. Exponent all ones and fraction zero means plus or minus infinity, for example 1.0 / 0.0. Exponent all ones with a non-zero fraction means NaN, 'not a number', for example 0.0 / 0.0. A NaN is not equal to anything, not even itself.

Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3: In binary, 0.1 is a repeating fraction (0.000110011001100...), just like 1/3 is 0.333... in decimal. It must be cut off after 52 bits, so it is stored slightly off. Adding two slightly-off values gives a result that, printed with enough digits, shows as 0.30000000000000004. This is not a bug in the hardware; it is how a finite binary format works. The lesson: never compare floats with == for money or exact checks.

Endianness: A 32-bit number takes 4 bytes, but memory is addressed byte by byte. In which order are the bytes stored? Take 0x12345678 stored at address 100. Big-endian puts the most significant byte first: 100: 12, 101: 34, 102: 56, 103: 78. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: 100: 78, 101: 56, 102: 34, 103: 12. x86 processors are little-endian. ARM can support both, and in practice phones run it little-endian. Network protocols such as TCP/IP use big-endian, called network byte order. If two systems disagree and nobody converts, a number like 1 can be read as 16,777,216.

An analogy for endianness: Writing a date as 2026-10-10 (year first) or 10-10-2026 (day first). Both are correct if everyone agrees; trouble starts when a Dhaka office sends a file to an office that reads dates the other way. Where it breaks: dates have three parts of different meaning, while endianness is just byte order of one number.

Trade-offs: Integers are exact and fast but have limited range. Fixed point is cheap and exact within a small range, perfect for sensors and money in poisha. Floating point covers a huge range but is approximate and needs a bigger, slower circuit. Double uses twice the memory of single and is slower on some hardware such as many GPUs, but is much more accurate. Choose the smallest format that is accurate enough.

Real-life example 1, a mobile banking app: If the app stored 1,250.50 taka as a float, repeated additions of small amounts could drift by fractions of a poisha. Real financial systems store integer poisha or use decimal types. Thousands of transactions a day make this choice matter.

Real-life example 2, a weather station in Cox's Bazar: A small sensor board reads temperature as a 12-bit value and stores it in fixed point with 4 fraction bits, so 0.0625 degree steps. The cheap microcontroller has no floating-point unit, and fixed point gives enough precision for weather.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 when taking two's complement. Forgetting the bias (127 or 1023) when decoding an exponent. Storing the hidden 1 in the fraction field. Mixing up which byte goes first in little-endian. Thinking overflow means a carry out; for signed numbers, carry out and overflow are different things.

What exams ask: Find the two's complement of a number and its range for n bits. Detect overflow in an addition. Sign-extend a value. Convert a decimal number to IEEE 754 single precision and back. Explain special values. Show the memory layout of a word in big- and little-endian.

Recap: Bits have no meaning until an instruction interprets them. Two's complement gives one zero and lets one adder do signed and unsigned add and subtract. Sign extension copies the sign bit. Fixed point is cheap fractions; IEEE 754 floating point is sign, biased exponent and fraction with a hidden 1. Endianness is byte order in memory. Next lesson we build the ALU that adds these numbers.
key_points: Bits have no fixed meaning; the instruction decides whether they are unsigned, signed, or floating point.
Two's complement: flip the bits and add 1; n bits cover -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1 with only one zero.
Subtraction is done as a + flip(b) + 1, using the same adder.
Sign extension copies the sign bit into new left positions; signed overflow happens when same-sign inputs give an opposite-sign result.
Fixed point keeps the binary point at an agreed position; cheap and exact but small range.
IEEE 754 single: 1 sign, 8 exponent (bias 127), 23 fraction bits with a hidden leading 1; double: 1, 11 (bias 1023), 52.
Special values: +0/-0, denormals, infinity and NaN; 0.1 is not exact in binary.
Little-endian stores the least significant byte first (x86); big-endian stores the most significant first (network byte order).
lessons.tip: Practise IEEE 754 with the same five steps every time: sign, binary, normalise, add bias, write fraction. Then check your answer with any online float converter so your mistakes show up quickly.
lessons.task: On paper, encode 10.5 and -0.75 in IEEE 754 single precision and write the results in hexadecimal. Then open a browser console (or Python on a phone app) and type 0.1 + 0.2 to see the rounding effect yourself.

quiz.q: What is -6 in 8-bit two's complement?
The 4-bit value 1101 (two's complement) is sign-extended to 8 bits. Result?
quiz.explain: Copy the sign bit (1) into the new positions: 1111 1101, still -3.

quiz.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, the stored exponent field is:
options: The real exponent with no change
quiz.explain: Single precision uses a bias of 127, so stored = real + 127.

quiz.q: 0x12345678 is stored at address 100 on a little-endian machine. What byte is at address 100?
quiz.explain: Little-endian stores the least significant byte (78) at the lowest address.

quiz.q: Which statement about 8-bit signed addition is true?
options: Adding two positives can never overflow
Adding numbers of opposite signs can overflow
Adding two positives that gives a negative result means overflow
Any carry out of the top bit means signed overflow
quiz.explain: Signed overflow happens when same-sign inputs produce an opposite-sign result; opposite-sign additions never overflow.

lessons.title: The ALU and Integer Addition: Ripple Carry, Carry Lookahead, Flags and Shifters
lessons.content:
Every time your phone adds two numbers, compares two prices on Daraz, checks whether your PIN matches, or moves a game character one step, a small circuit inside the processor does the work. That circuit is the ALU, the Arithmetic Logic Unit. It is the calculator at the heart of the CPU. In this lesson we open it up: how it chooses which operation to do, why simple addition is surprisingly slow, the clever trick that makes it fast, and the little flag bits that let programs make decisions.

What the ALU is: The ALU is a combinational circuit, meaning its output depends only on its current inputs, with no memory inside. It takes two operands, A and B (for example 32 bits each), and a few control bits that say which operation to perform. It produces a result and some status flags. Picture: A, B, ALU control -> [ ALU ] -> Result, Flags. Typical operations: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, ADD, SUBTRACT, set-on-less-than (compare), and sometimes shifts.

Why it matters: Almost every instruction uses the ALU. Arithmetic instructions obviously do. But a load instruction also uses the ALU to compute the memory address (base register plus offset). A branch uses it to compare two values. So the speed of the ALU, especially the adder, often limits how short the clock cycle can be. Make the adder faster and the whole processor can tick faster.

The problem it solves: A processor needs many operations, but building a completely separate circuit for each and wiring each one to the registers would be wasteful. The ALU puts the common operations into one block that shares inputs and outputs, and a multiplexer (MUX) picks which result goes out. One set of wires in, one set out, and a small code chooses the job.

Building a 1-bit ALU: Start with one bit. Inputs: a, b, carry-in. Inside: an AND gate (a AND b), an OR gate (a OR b), and a full adder (a + b + carry-in, giving sum and carry-out). A MUX with a 2-bit select chooses which of these goes to the output. Example select codes: 00 = AND, 01 = OR, 10 = ADD. If a = 1, b = 1, carry-in = 0 and select = 10, the full adder gives sum 0, carry-out 1. You met full adders in Digital Logic Design; here they become one slice of a bigger machine.

Adding subtraction to the slice: Put a XOR gate on input b controlled by a signal called Binvert. When Binvert = 1, the XOR flips b. Set the first slice's carry-in to 1 at the same time, and the adder computes a + NOT(b) + 1 = a - b, which is two's complement subtraction from the last lesson. One control signal turns the adder into a subtractor. Comparison works the same way: to check if a < b, compute a - b and look at the sign (with care for overflow). This is how instructions like 'set on less than' are built.

The 32-bit ALU: Copy the 1-bit slice 32 times. Connect each slice's carry-out to the next slice's carry-in. All slices share the same select and Binvert signals. Picture: slice0 -> carry -> slice1 -> carry -> slice2 -> ... -> slice31. This is called a ripple-carry adder, because the carry ripples from right to left like a wave.

The ripple carry problem: Slice 31 cannot know its correct sum until slice 30 has finished its carry, which waits for slice 29, and so on. Each full adder adds about two gate delays for the carry. For 32 bits that is roughly 64 gate delays; for 64 bits about 128. Worst case: 0111...1 + 0000...1, where a carry is created at bit 0 and must travel all the way across. Since the clock cycle must be long enough for the worst case, a slow adder slows down every instruction.

An analogy: Think of a long queue of people at a Dhaka bank counter passing a token hand to hand. The last person cannot act until the token has passed through everyone before them. Ripple carry is like that. Carry lookahead is like having a supervisor who looks at the whole queue at once and tells each person directly whether a token will reach them. Where it breaks: the supervisor in real hardware is a set of extra gates that grows quickly with size, so it is not free.

Carry lookahead, the idea: Instead of waiting, compute each carry directly from the inputs. For each bit i define two signals. Generate: Gi = ai AND bi. If both bits are 1, this position makes a carry no matter what comes in. Propagate: Pi = ai OR bi (some books use ai XOR bi). If at least one bit is 1, an incoming carry will pass through. Then carry out of bit i is c(i+1) = Gi + Pi.ci, where + is OR and . is AND.

Carry lookahead, expanding: Substitute step by step. c1 = G0 + P0.c0. c2 = G1 + P1.G0 + P1.P0.c0. c3 = G2 + P2.G1 + P2.P1.G0 + P2.P1.P0.c0. c4 = G3 + P3.G2 + P3.P2.G1 + P3.P2.P1.G0 + P3.P2.P1.P0.c0. Every carry is now a two-level sum-of-products of G, P and c0, all available right at the start. So all four carries come out after only a few gate delays, at the same time, instead of one after another.

Worked example: Add A = 0111 and B = 0011 (7 + 3) with c0 = 0. Bits from 0: a = 1,1,1,0 and b = 1,1,0,0. G = 1,1,0,0. P (OR) = 1,1,1,0. c1 = G0 = 1. c2 = G1 + P1.G0 = 1. c3 = G2 + P2.G1 + ... = 0 + 1.1 = 1. c4 = G3 + P3.(...) = 0 + 0 = 0. Sums: s_i = a_i XOR b_i XOR c_i: s0 = 1 XOR 1 XOR 0 = 0, s1 = 1 XOR 1 XOR 1 = 1, s2 = 1 XOR 0 XOR 1 = 0, s3 = 0 XOR 0 XOR 1 = 1. Result 1010 = 10. Correct, and every carry was found in parallel.

The cost and the compromise: The formula for c32 would need gates with 33 inputs and a huge number of terms; real gates cannot have that many inputs without becoming slow. So designers use groups: 4-bit carry lookahead blocks, each producing a group generate and group propagate signal, and a second level of lookahead across the blocks. This hierarchical carry lookahead keeps delay growing roughly with the logarithm of the width instead of linearly. Other fast adders, such as carry-select and parallel-prefix adders, follow the same spirit: spend more gates to save time.

Status flags: Besides the result, the ALU outputs condition bits that many ISAs store in a flags or status register. Zero (Z): result is all zeros, detected by a NOR over all result bits. Negative (N): the top bit of the result. Carry (C): carry-out of the top bit, meaning unsigned overflow on addition. Overflow (V): signed overflow, which can be computed as the carry into the top bit XOR the carry out of the top bit. Branch instructions such as 'branch if equal' or 'branch if less than' use these flags. Some ISAs like MIPS do not keep a flags register and compare directly in the branch instruction, which is a design choice, not a law.

Flag example: 8-bit add 0111 1111 + 0000 0001 (127 + 1). Result 1000 0000. Z = 0, N = 1, C = 0 (no carry out of bit 7), V = 1 (carry into bit 7 is 1, carry out is 0, XOR = 1). As unsigned, 127 + 1 = 128 is fine (C = 0). As signed, 127 + 1 cannot be +128, so V = 1. The same bits, two meanings, two different flags.

Shifters: Shifting moves bits left or right. A logical left shift by 1 multiplies an unsigned number by 2: 0000 0101 (5) becomes 0000 1010 (10). A logical right shift fills with 0 and divides unsigned numbers by 2. An arithmetic right shift fills with copies of the sign bit, so 1111 1000 (-8) becomes 1111 1100 (-4), dividing signed numbers by 2 (rounding towards minus infinity). A rotate moves bits out of one end and back in at the other. Compilers turn 'x * 8' into 'x shifted left by 3' because a shift is cheaper than a multiply.

The barrel shifter: Shifting one place per clock would make a 31-place shift take 31 cycles. A barrel shifter does any shift amount in one pass. For 32 bits it uses 5 stages of multiplexers: stage 1 shifts by 1 or 0, stage 2 by 2 or 0, stage 3 by 4 or 0, stage 4 by 8 or 0, stage 5 by 16 or 0. A shift by 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 turns on stages 1, 3 and 4. The cost is about n x log2(n) multiplexers, a classic trade of area for speed.

When to use what: For a tiny, cheap microcontroller, a ripple-carry adder and a one-bit-per-cycle shifter may be enough, since they use the fewest gates. For a high-speed processor, carry lookahead or prefix adders and a barrel shifter are worth their extra area because they shorten the clock cycle. When not to use a fancy adder: when the adder is not on the critical path, the extra gates and power give no benefit.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz price filter: When you filter phones between 10,000 and 20,000 taka, the server runs comparisons for every product: price - 10,000 and 20,000 - price, checking the sign of each result. Millions of such ALU subtractions happen in milliseconds. A fast adder is directly why the filter feels instant.

Real-life example 2, a digital weighing scale at a Kawran Bazar shop: Its small microcontroller adds sensor readings and shifts the sum right to divide by 8 for an average of 8 readings. Since the chip is cheap and slow, its designer chose a simple adder. Speed is not needed there; low cost is. Same ALU ideas, different trade-off.

Common mistakes: Confusing the carry flag (unsigned overflow) with the overflow flag (signed overflow). Thinking carry lookahead removes all delay; it reduces it from linear to roughly logarithmic, but gates still take time. Using logical right shift on negative numbers and expecting division. Forgetting that the subtractor needs both the inverted B and carry-in = 1.

What exams ask: Draw a 1-bit ALU and extend it to n bits. Explain the delay of a ripple-carry adder. Derive c1 to c4 of a carry lookahead adder using G and P. Compute flags for a given addition. Explain logical vs arithmetic shift and the barrel shifter.

Recap: The ALU is a combinational block where a MUX selects among AND, OR, ADD and others. Subtraction comes from inverting B and setting carry-in to 1. Ripple carry is simple but slow; carry lookahead uses generate and propagate to compute carries in parallel. Flags Z, N, C and V report facts about the result. Shifters, especially barrel shifters, move bits quickly. Next lesson we make the ALU multiply and divide.
key_points: The ALU is a combinational circuit that performs arithmetic and logic operations chosen by control bits through a MUX.
Subtraction uses the adder with B inverted (XOR with Binvert) and carry-in set to 1.
A ripple-carry adder chains full adders; its delay grows linearly with the number of bits.
Carry lookahead: Gi = ai.bi, Pi = ai + bi, c(i+1) = Gi + Pi.ci, expanded so all carries are computed in parallel.
Large adders use hierarchical lookahead blocks so delay grows roughly logarithmically.
Flags: Z (zero), N (negative), C (carry, unsigned overflow), V (signed overflow = carry in XOR carry out of top bit).
Logical shifts fill with 0; arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit; rotate wraps bits around.
A barrel shifter does any shift in one pass using log2(n) stages of multiplexers.
lessons.tip: Do the carry lookahead equations by hand for c1 to c4 until you can write them without looking. Then test them on two or three 4-bit additions; if the carries match ordinary addition, you truly understand G and P.
lessons.task: Pick four pairs of 4-bit numbers, for example 0111 + 0011 and 1111 + 0001. For each pair compute G, P, the carries c1 to c4, the sum, and the Z, N, C, V flags. Check the sum by ordinary decimal addition.

quiz.q: Why is a ripple-carry adder slow for wide numbers?
options: Each bit's carry must wait for the carry from the previous bit
It needs a clock for each bit
quiz.explain: The carry passes through every full adder in turn, so delay grows with the number of bits.

quiz.q: In carry lookahead, the generate signal Gi is:
quiz.explain: Gi = ai AND bi: when both bits are 1, this position produces a carry regardless of the carry-in.

quiz.q: How does the ALU compute A - B using its adder?
options: Invert A and set carry-in to 0
Invert B and set carry-in to 1
quiz.explain: A - B = A + NOT(B) + 1, the two's complement method.

quiz.q: 8-bit: 0111 1111 + 0000 0001. Which flags are set?
quiz.explain: Result 1000 0000: top bit is 1 (N), and two positives gave a negative (V). No carry out, not zero.

quiz.q: An arithmetic right shift of 1111 1000 (-8) by 1 gives:
quiz.explain: Arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit, giving 1111 1100 = -4.

lessons.title: Multiplication and Division in Hardware: Shift-and-Add, Booth, Restoring and Non-Restoring
lessons.content:
In class four you learned long multiplication: write one number under the other, multiply by each digit, shift each line one place left, then add all the lines. You also learned long division: try how many times the divisor fits, subtract, bring down the next digit. Surprise: the processor in your phone does almost exactly the same thing, only in binary, where it becomes even easier. In this lesson we build multiplication and division out of the adder and shifter from the last lesson, and see the smart tricks that make them faster.

What the problem is: The ALU from lesson 5 can add, subtract and shift, but many programs need multiply and divide: computing a price times quantity, scaling an image, averaging marks. Early and very small processors had no multiply instruction at all; programmers wrote loops of additions. That works but is slow. So designers asked: can we build multiplication and division from adders and shifters in a clean, regular way? Yes, and the method comes straight from school arithmetic.

Binary long multiplication: In binary each multiplier digit is 0 or 1, so each partial product is either 0 or the multiplicand itself, shifted. Example: 1011 (11) x 1101 (13). Multiplier bits from the right: 1, 0, 1, 1. Partial products: 1011, 0000 shifted 1, 1011 shifted 2, 1011 shifted 3, i.e. 1011, 00000, 101100, 1011000. Add them: 1011 + 101100 + 1011000 = 10001111 = 143. And 11 x 13 = 143. Correct. Note: multiplying two n-bit numbers can give up to 2n bits, so the product needs a double-width register.

The shift-and-add multiplier, the hardware: We need three registers: the multiplicand M (n bits), the multiplier Q (n bits), and an accumulator A (n bits) which, together with Q, forms the 2n-bit product. A diagram in words: M -> [n-bit adder] <- A, and A,Q shift right together. A control counter counts n steps.

The shift-and-add algorithm, step by step: Start with A = 0. Repeat n times: Step 1, look at the rightmost bit of Q. If it is 1, add M to A (keeping the carry). If it is 0, add nothing. Step 2, shift the combined C, A, Q one place right; the carry goes into the top of A and the bit leaving Q is thrown away because it has been used. After n steps, A and Q together hold the 2n-bit product. Clever detail: the product grows into Q's space exactly as the multiplier bits are used up, so no extra register is needed.

Worked trace, 0101 (5) x 0011 (3), 4 bits: Start A = 0000, Q = 0011. Step 1: Q0 = 1, A = 0000 + 0101 = 0101; shift right: A = 0010, Q = 1001. Step 2: Q0 = 1, A = 0010 + 0101 = 0111; shift: A = 0011, Q = 1100. Step 3: Q0 = 0, no add; shift: A = 0001, Q = 1110. Step 4: Q0 = 0; shift: A = 0000, Q = 1111. Product A,Q = 0000 1111 = 15. Correct.

The cost: This needs n cycles, each with an addition. For 32 bits that is 32 add-and-shift steps. Simple and small, but slow. Also, it works for unsigned numbers. For signed numbers you could convert to positive, multiply, and fix the sign, but there is a neater way.

Booth's algorithm, the problem it solves: Andrew Donald Booth published this method in 1951. It multiplies two's complement signed numbers directly, and it can skip work when the multiplier has long runs of 1s. The idea: a run of 1s like 0111 1000 equals 1000 0000 - 0000 1000. Instead of adding four times, subtract once at the start of the run and add once at the end.

Booth's rule: Keep an extra bit Q-1 to the right of Q, starting at 0. At each step look at the pair (Q0, Q-1). If it is 1,0, the start of a run of 1s: A = A - M. If it is 0,1, the end of a run: A = A + M. If it is 0,0 or 1,1: do nothing. Then do an arithmetic shift right of A, Q, Q-1 together (copy the sign bit of A). Repeat n times. The product is in A,Q.

Booth worked example, 7 x 3 in 4 bits: M = 0111, -M = 1001, Q = 0011, A = 0000, Q-1 = 0. Step 1: pair 1,0, A = 0000 + 1001 = 1001; shift: A = 1100, Q = 1001, Q-1 = 1. Step 2: pair 1,1, nothing; shift: A = 1110, Q = 0100, Q-1 = 1. Step 3: pair 0,1, A = 1110 + 0111 = 0101 (ignore carry); shift: A = 0010, Q = 1010, Q-1 = 0. Step 4: pair 0,0; shift: A = 0001, Q = 0101, Q-1 = 0. Product 0001 0101 = 21. Correct, and the same steps work when M or Q is negative.

When Booth helps and when not: Booth helps when the multiplier has long blocks of 1s or 0s, and it handles signed numbers without extra sign fixing. It does not help for patterns like 0101 0101, where every pair changes and you do an add or subtract almost every step, which can be no better than plain shift-and-add. Modern designs use a variant called radix-4 (modified) Booth encoding, which looks at 3 bits at a time to halve the number of partial products.

Fast multipliers: High-performance processors cannot wait 32 or 64 cycles. They generate all the partial products at once with AND gates, then add them in parallel using a tree of adders (for example a Wallace tree, which uses carry-save adders to reduce many numbers to two), and finish with one fast adder. This costs a lot of silicon but gives a result in a few cycles. Again: area traded for speed.

Binary long division: Division is repeated subtraction with shifting. Divide 7 (0111) by 2 (0010). Like school: bring down bits one at a time; whenever the partial remainder is at least the divisor, subtract and write 1 in the quotient, otherwise write 0. Result: quotient 0011 (3), remainder 1. Division produces two answers, quotient and remainder, and dividing by zero must be detected separately.

Restoring division, the hardware algorithm: Registers: A (remainder, one bit wider than n), Q (dividend, which becomes the quotient), M (divisor). Start A = 0. Repeat n times: Step 1, shift A,Q left by one. Step 2, A = A - M. Step 3, if A is negative, set Q0 = 0 and restore A = A + M. Otherwise set Q0 = 1. At the end Q holds the quotient and A the remainder.

Restoring trace, 7 / 2: A = 00000, Q = 0111, M = 00010. Step 1: shift, A = 00000, Q = 1110; A - M = 11110, negative, Q0 = 0, restore A = 00000. Step 2: shift, A = 00001, Q = 1100; A - M negative, Q0 = 0, restore A = 00001. Step 3: shift, A = 00011, Q = 1000; A - M = 00001, positive, Q0 = 1, Q = 1001. Step 4: shift, A = 00011, Q = 0010; A - M = 00001, Q0 = 1, Q = 0011. Quotient 3, remainder 1.

Non-restoring division, removing the wasted step: In restoring division, a failed subtraction costs an extra addition to undo it. Non-restoring division notices that 'restore then shift then subtract' equals 'shift then add'. Rule: if A is not negative, shift A,Q left and subtract M; if A is negative, shift A,Q left and add M. Then set Q0 = 1 if the new A is not negative, else 0. After the last step, if A is negative, add M once to correct the remainder. Each step now has exactly one add or subtract, which saves time and makes control simpler.

An analogy: Sharing 7 shingaras among plates of 2. Restoring is like taking 2 shingaras out, seeing there were not enough, and putting them back before trying again. Non-restoring is the smarter friend who remembers the shortfall and fixes it in the next move instead of putting things back. Where it breaks: hardware works on bits and signs, not on shingaras, and the 'fix' is an exact algebraic identity, not a guess.

Division in real chips: Division is usually the slowest basic integer operation. Modern processors use faster methods such as SRT division, which produces more than one quotient bit per step using a lookup table. A famous lesson: in 1994 the Intel Pentium had the FDIV bug, where a few missing entries in such a lookup table made some floating-point divisions slightly wrong. Intel replaced affected chips. Testing arithmetic hardware thoroughly matters.

When to choose which: For a tiny, low-cost controller in a toy or a remote control, a shift-and-add multiplier or even a software loop is fine, because area and price matter more than speed and multiplications are rare. For a general processor that runs graphics, audio or machine learning, a fast parallel multiplier is worth the silicon because multiplications are everywhere. For division, most designs accept a slower, iterative unit, because divisions are much rarer than additions and multiplications in typical programs. When not to add a hardware divider at all: in very small chips where the few divisions can be done in software. Measure the instruction mix first, as lesson 3 taught, then spend silicon where the program spends its time.

Real-life example 1, a shop billing app in Sylhet: The app computes price x quantity for every item. On a phone CPU with a fast hardware multiplier this takes a few cycles each. On a very cheap microcontroller without a multiplier, the compiler inserts a software shift-and-add loop, and a big bill visibly takes longer.

Real-life example 2, compilers avoiding division: Because division is slow, compilers replace 'x / 8' for unsigned x with a right shift by 3, and replace division by a constant like 10 with a multiplication by a precomputed 'magic number' followed by a shift. Programs that compute averages of exam marks or split bills run faster without the programmer doing anything.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the product needs 2n bits. In Booth's, using a logical instead of arithmetic shift, or forgetting Q-1. Mixing up which pair means add and which means subtract (1,0 subtract; 0,1 add). In restoring division, forgetting to restore after a negative result. In non-restoring, forgetting the final correction of the remainder.

What exams ask: Draw the shift-and-add multiplier hardware and trace a 4-bit example. Multiply two signed numbers using Booth's algorithm with a step table. Divide using restoring and non-restoring methods with a step table. Compare restoring and non-restoring. Explain why Booth's algorithm can be faster.

Recap: Binary multiplication adds shifted copies of the multiplicand wherever the multiplier has a 1. The shift-and-add hardware uses A, Q and M and needs n steps. Booth's algorithm handles signed numbers and skips runs of 1s by looking at Q0 and Q-1. Division is shift and subtract; restoring undoes failed subtractions, non-restoring avoids that waste. Fast chips spend more gates on trees and lookup tables. Next lesson we extend arithmetic to floating-point numbers.
key_points: Binary multiplication adds shifted copies of the multiplicand for every 1 in the multiplier; an n x n product needs 2n bits.
Shift-and-add hardware uses registers A, Q, M: if Q0 = 1 add M to A, then shift A,Q right; repeat n times.
Booth's algorithm looks at (Q0, Q-1): 1,0 subtract M; 0,1 add M; 0,0 or 1,1 do nothing; then arithmetic shift right.
Booth multiplies two's complement numbers directly and saves work on long runs of 1s, but not on alternating bits.
Fast multipliers generate all partial products at once and add them with adder trees such as a Wallace tree.
Restoring division: shift left, subtract M, and if negative set Q0 = 0 and add M back; else Q0 = 1.
Non-restoring division adds or subtracts M depending on the sign of A, avoiding restore steps, with one final remainder correction.
Division is the slowest basic integer operation; compilers replace division by constants with shifts or multiplications.
lessons.tip: Always draw a step table with columns Step, Action, A, Q (and Q-1 for Booth). Exams give marks for each correct row, and the table stops you from losing track of which bit to look at.
lessons.task: Using a 4-bit step table, multiply 6 x 5 with shift-and-add, then multiply -3 x 5 with Booth's algorithm, then divide 13 by 4 with restoring division. Check each answer with ordinary decimal arithmetic.

quiz.q: Multiplying two 8-bit unsigned numbers can need how many bits for the product?
quiz.explain: An n-bit by n-bit product can be up to 2n bits, so 16 bits.

quiz.q: In Booth's algorithm, the pair (Q0, Q-1) = (1, 0) means:
quiz.explain: 1,0 marks the start of a run of 1s, so M is subtracted.

quiz.q: Which multiplier pattern gives Booth's algorithm little or no benefit?
quiz.explain: Alternating bits change at every pair, so an add or subtract happens almost every step.

quiz.q: In restoring division, what happens when A - M is negative?
options: Q0 = 0 and add M back to A
The algorithm stops with an error
quiz.explain: The subtraction failed, so the quotient bit is 0 and A is restored by adding M.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of non-restoring over restoring division?
options: It avoids the extra restore addition in each failed step
It works only for positive numbers
quiz.explain: Non-restoring folds the restore into the next step, so each step has exactly one add or subtract.

lessons.title: Floating-Point Arithmetic: Adding, Multiplying and Rounding
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to add 1.5 crore taka and 25 paisa using scientific notation. In decimal you would write 1.5 x 10^7 and 2.5 x 10^-1. You cannot just add 1.5 and 2.5, because the powers of ten are different. First you line them up, then add, then tidy the result, then round to the number of digits you can keep.
