lessons.title: Hardwired Control: Turning Opcodes into Signals
lessons.content:
Imagine a traffic police officer at the Farmgate intersection. Cars, buses and rickshaws are the data, and the roads are the datapath. But without the officer's hand signals, everyone would crash. The officer looks at the situation and gives exact signals: this lane go, that lane stop, buses turn left. A CPU's control unit is that officer. In lesson 12 we built the roads, the datapath, and we listed signals like RegDst, ALUSrc and MemWrite. Today we answer: who sets these signals, and how? The first and fastest answer is hardwired control.

What a control unit does: The control unit reads the instruction (mainly its opcode, and sometimes other fields), and produces control signals that drive the multiplexers, the ALU, the register file and the memories. In a multi-step design it also keeps track of which step of the instruction we are in. Its outputs decide what the datapath does in every clock cycle. Without correct control signals, even a perfect datapath does nothing useful.

What hardwired means: In hardwired control the signals are produced by fixed logic circuits made of gates, decoders and flip-flops. The rules are literally wired into the hardware. The other approach, microprogrammed control, stores the signals as words in a small memory inside the CPU (lesson 14). Hardwired is like an officer who has memorised every rule and reacts instantly; microprogrammed is like an officer who looks up each situation in a rule book.

The problem it solves: The datapath has many switches, and each instruction needs a different combination. Writing every combination by hand for every clock is impossible to manage in your head. The control unit is the systematic answer: list each instruction, list the signals it needs, write a truth table, simplify it into logic, and you get a circuit that does the right thing every time, at the speed of gates.

The main control unit for single-cycle MIPS: In our single-cycle datapath, the main control unit takes the 6-bit opcode as input and produces nine outputs: RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch, and the 2-bit ALUOp. Since every instruction finishes in one cycle, the control is purely combinational: no memory of past steps is needed. It is just a truth table.

The truth table, row by row: R-type (opcode 0): RegDst = 1 (write rd), ALUSrc = 0 (second ALU input is a register), MemtoReg = 0 (write the ALU result), RegWrite = 1, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 10. lw (opcode 35): RegDst = 0 (write rt), ALUSrc = 1 (use the immediate), MemtoReg = 1 (write memory data), RegWrite = 1, MemRead = 1, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 00. sw (opcode 43): RegDst = X, ALUSrc = 1, MemtoReg = X, RegWrite = 0, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 1, Branch = 0, ALUOp = 00. beq (opcode 4): RegDst = X, ALUSrc = 0, MemtoReg = X, RegWrite = 0, MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 0, Branch = 1, ALUOp = 01.

Why each value makes sense: Do not memorise the table; derive it. lw writes a register, so RegWrite = 1; it writes the value from memory, so MemtoReg = 1; it computes an address with the immediate, so ALUSrc = 1; its destination is rt, so RegDst = 0. sw writes memory, not a register, so RegWrite = 0 and MemWrite = 1. beq compares two registers, so ALUSrc = 0, and it writes nothing. If you understand the datapath, the table writes itself.

What X (don't care) means: For sw and beq, nothing is written to the register file, so it does not matter which register RegDst picks or what MemtoReg chooses. We write X, meaning the signal can be 0 or 1. Don't cares let the logic designer choose whichever value makes the circuit smaller, just like don't cares in Karnaugh maps from Digital Logic Design. But be careful: RegWrite and MemWrite must never be X, because a wrong 1 would destroy data.

Two-level control, the ALU control: The main control does not decide the exact ALU operation for R-type instructions, because all R-type instructions share opcode 0. Instead it sends ALUOp, and a small second unit, the ALU control, looks at ALUOp plus the 6-bit funct field. ALUOp = 00 means add (for lw and sw address). ALUOp = 01 means subtract (for beq comparison). ALUOp = 10 means look at funct: funct 32 (add) gives add, 34 (sub) gives subtract, 36 (and) gives AND, 37 (or) gives OR, 42 (slt) gives set-on-less-than. Splitting control into two levels keeps each piece small and fast.

The ALU's 4-bit control inputs: In the classic textbook ALU, the ALU control produces a 4-bit code: 0000 for AND, 0001 for OR, 0010 for add, 0110 for subtract, 0111 for set-on-less-than. So add $t0, $s1, $s2 goes like this: opcode 0 -> ALUOp 10 -> funct 32 -> ALU control 0010 -> the ALU adds. And lw goes: opcode 35 -> ALUOp 00 -> ALU control 0010 -> add, regardless of funct.

From truth table to gates: Each output is a Boolean function of the opcode bits. For example, RegDst is 1 only for R-type, so RegDst = 1 exactly when all six opcode bits are 0, which is a 6-input AND of the inverted bits. MemWrite is 1 only for opcode 43 (binary 101011), so it is an AND gate that matches that pattern. In practice, designers first decode the opcode into one line per instruction type (R-type, lw, sw, beq), and then each control signal is an OR of the relevant lines: RegWrite = R-type OR lw. ALUSrc = lw OR sw. This decoder-plus-OR structure is a programmable logic array style circuit, simple and very fast.

A mental simulation, beq: The instruction beq $t0, $t1, loop arrives with opcode 4. The decoder line for beq goes to 1. So Branch = 1, ALUOp = 01, ALUSrc = 0, and RegWrite, MemRead and MemWrite are 0. The ALU control sees 01 and sets the ALU to subtract. Say $t0 = 7 and $t1 = 7: the ALU outputs 0, Zero = 1, Branch AND Zero = 1, so the PC takes the branch target. If $t1 were 9, Zero = 0 and the PC simply moves to PC + 4. Notice how one opcode sets up the whole datapath, and the data itself decides only the final choice.

What if a control signal is wrong: Failure thinking helps here. Suppose a manufacturing fault keeps RegWrite stuck at 0. Then add and lw still compute the right values, but nothing is ever saved into registers, so every program silently produces garbage. If MemWrite were stuck at 1, every instruction would overwrite some memory word, destroying data. This is why chip makers test every control line after manufacturing, and why designers treat write signals with extra care.

Hardwired control with steps: In multi-step machines, such as Mano's basic computer or the multi-cycle MIPS of lesson 15, an instruction takes several clocks, so the control unit must know which step it is in. Mano's basic computer uses a 4-bit sequence counter (SC) feeding a 4-to-16 decoder that produces timing signals T0, T1, ..., T15. Exactly one timing signal is 1 at a time. The opcode bits feed a 3-to-8 decoder that produces D0 to D7, one per instruction type. Control logic gates combine these: for example, the add instruction's step 'T4: DR <- M[AR]' happens when D1 AND T4 is 1. After the last step, SC is cleared to 0 and the next fetch begins at T0.

The state machine view: Another way to see hardwired control for multi-step machines is as a finite state machine, exactly like the sequential circuits from Digital Logic Design. Each state is one step; the outputs in each state are the control signals; the next state depends on the current state and the opcode. The state is held in a register, and combinational logic computes the outputs and the next state. Lesson 15 draws this machine for multi-cycle MIPS.

Advantages of hardwired control: It is fast, because signals come straight out of gates with no memory lookup. It uses little hardware for a small, regular instruction set. That is why RISC processors, with simple and uniform instructions, almost always use hardwired control.

Disadvantages: It is hard to change. Adding a new instruction or fixing a bug means redesigning the logic and making a new chip. For a large, complex instruction set with many multi-step instructions, the logic becomes huge and messy, and it is hard to verify. This is exactly why complex CISC machines historically chose microprogramming.

When to use hardwired control: For RISC cores, for small embedded processors, for any simple instruction set where speed matters and the design is stable. When not: when the instruction set is large and irregular, or when you expect to fix or extend the instruction behaviour after manufacturing. In those cases microprogrammed control, or a mix, is safer. Modern x86 chips actually use a mix: common simple instructions are decoded by fast hardwired logic, and rare complex ones use a microcode ROM.

Real-life example 1, the traffic signal at a junction: A simple fixed-time traffic light at a junction in Rajshahi cycles green, yellow, red with a timer. Its controller is a tiny hardwired state machine: a counter and some gates decide which light is on. It is cheap and never needs changing. That is hardwired control in daily life. If the city wanted to change the pattern every week, a programmable controller would be easier, which is the idea behind microprogramming.

Real-life example 2, a washing machine: A basic automatic washing machine runs fill, wash, rinse, spin. Each step turns specific things on: the water valve, the motor in slow mode, the drain pump, the motor in fast mode. A controller looks at the current step and the selected program and turns signals on and off, just like a control unit looks at the timing step and the opcode. Same pattern: state plus input gives control signals.

Common mistakes: Putting X for RegWrite or MemWrite; these must be definite, or data can be corrupted. Forgetting that RegDst = 0 for lw because the destination is rt. Thinking the main control decides add versus subtract for R-type; that is the ALU control's job using funct. Mixing up ALUOp values: 00 add, 01 subtract, 10 use funct. Forgetting to clear the sequence counter at the end of an instruction in a step-based design, which would make the machine run garbage steps.

What exams usually ask: Fill in the control truth table for R-type, lw, sw and beq and justify each entry. Explain why some entries are don't cares. Explain two-level control with ALUOp and funct. Write logic equations for RegWrite, ALUSrc or MemtoReg. Draw the hardwired control unit of the basic computer with sequence counter and decoders. Compare hardwired and microprogrammed control.

Quick recap: The control unit turns the opcode (and step) into control signals. Hardwired control does it with fixed gates and decoders: fast but hard to change. For single-cycle MIPS it is a combinational truth table with nine outputs, plus a small ALU control using ALUOp and funct. For multi-step machines, a sequence counter or state register adds timing. RISC designs prefer hardwired control. Next lesson, the other way: storing control in memory as microprograms.
key_points: The control unit reads the opcode (and current step) and produces signals that drive multiplexers, ALU, registers and memory.
Hardwired control builds this with fixed logic: gates, decoders and flip-flops.
Single-cycle MIPS main control is combinational: opcode in, RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch, ALUOp out.
R-type: RegDst 1, ALUSrc 0, MemtoReg 0, RegWrite 1, ALUOp 10. lw: RegDst 0, ALUSrc 1, MemtoReg 1, RegWrite 1, MemRead 1, ALUOp 00.
sw: ALUSrc 1, MemWrite 1, RegWrite 0. beq: ALUSrc 0, Branch 1, ALUOp 01. RegWrite and MemWrite are never don't care.
ALU control combines ALUOp and funct: 00 add, 01 subtract, 10 use funct (add, sub, and, or, slt).
Step-based hardwired control uses a sequence counter and decoder (T0, T1, ...) or a finite state machine.
Hardwired is fast but hard to change; RISC prefers it, complex CISC historically used microprogramming.
lessons.tip: Never memorise the control table. Instead, for each instruction, trace its path through the datapath drawing from lesson 12 and ask which multiplexer must pick which input and which writes must happen. You will rebuild the table in under a minute.
lessons.task: Extend the control truth table with addi (opcode 8: rt = rs + immediate). Decide each signal: RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch and ALUOp, and justify each one in one sentence.

lessons.title: Microprogrammed Control
lessons.content:
Imagine two cooks. The first cook has memorised every recipe so deeply that his hands move automatically: he never looks at a book, and he is very fast. But if the owner wants to add a new dish, the cook needs months of retraining. The second cook keeps a recipe book on the shelf. For each dish he opens the right page and follows the lines one by one. He is a little slower, because he has to read each line, but adding a new dish is easy: just write a new page. In lesson 13 we built the first kind of control unit, the hardwired one. In this lesson we build the second kind, the recipe-book kind. It is called microprogrammed control.

A quick reminder of the job: The control unit's job is to produce control signals. These are the on/off wires that tell the datapath what to do in each clock cycle: which register to load, which value the ALU should compute, whether memory should read or write, whether the PC should increment. For every machine instruction, the control unit must produce the right pattern of signals, in the right order, cycle by cycle. The question is only how we generate that pattern.

The problem with hardwired control: A hardwired control unit produces the signals using fixed logic gates, flip-flops and a sequence counter. For a small, regular instruction set this is perfect: it is fast and compact. But imagine an instruction set with hundreds of instructions, some needing 20 or 30 steps, with many special cases. The logic equations become huge and tangled. Designing them is slow, finding a mistake is painful, and fixing a mistake after the chip is made is impossible, because the fix means changing the wiring. Early computer designers faced exactly this.

Where the idea came from: In 1951 Maurice Wilkes at Cambridge University suggested a cleaner way. He noticed that the control signals for one clock cycle are just a pattern of 1s and 0s. A pattern of bits can be stored in memory. So why not store the signal patterns for every step of every instruction in a small special memory, and simply read them out one after another? Wilkes called each stored step a microinstruction, and a sequence of them a microprogram. Later, IBM used microprogramming in most models of the System/360 family (1964), which is one reason cheap and expensive models could all implement the same instruction set.

The key words: A control word is one row of bits where each bit (or group of bits) drives control signals. A microinstruction is a control word plus some bits that say what to do next. A microprogram is a sequence of microinstructions; the one that carries out a single machine instruction is often called its microroutine. Micro-operations are the tiny register-transfer actions from lesson 11, like AR <- PC. The control memory, also called the control store, holds all the microinstructions. It is usually a ROM inside the processor, because the microprogram does not change while the computer runs.

The parts of a microprogrammed control unit: Picture this one-line diagram: IR opcode -> mapping logic -> CAR -> control memory -> microinstruction -> (control signals to datapath) and (next-address bits -> sequencer -> CAR). The control address register, CAR, holds the address of the next microinstruction, just like the PC holds the address of the next machine instruction. The control memory is read at that address. The output is the current microinstruction, often held in a control data register or microinstruction buffer. The sequencer, also called the next-address generator, decides the next value of CAR.

How it works, step by step: Step 1, when the computer starts, CAR points to the fetch microroutine. Step 2, the fetch microinstructions run: copy PC into the memory address register, read memory, increment PC, place the instruction into IR. Step 3, the opcode bits in IR go through the mapping logic, which turns each opcode into the starting address of that instruction's microroutine in control memory. Step 4, CAR jumps there, and the microroutine runs one microinstruction per clock, each one turning on the right control signals. Step 5, the last microinstruction of the routine sends CAR back to the fetch routine. Then the whole cycle repeats for the next machine instruction.

How the sequencer chooses the next address: Each microinstruction has bits that tell the sequencer one of a few choices. Increment: CAR <- CAR + 1, go to the next row, the most common case. Unconditional branch: CAR <- the address field written inside the microinstruction. Conditional branch: jump only if a status bit is true, for example if the accumulator is zero, otherwise increment. Map: CAR <- the address produced from the opcode, used once after fetch. Some designs also allow call and return, so that common pieces, such as fetching an operand, can be written once and reused like a subroutine, with a small register saving the return address.

A microinstruction format: A typical format looks like this: [ micro-operation fields | condition select | branch type | address field ]. In M. Morris Mano's well known textbook design, the control memory has 128 words of 20 bits each. Each microinstruction has three 3-bit micro-operation fields (F1, F2, F3), a 2-bit condition field (CD), a 2-bit branch field (BR) and a 7-bit address field (AD). 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 7 = 20 bits. Seven address bits make sense because 2^7 = 128 words.

A tiny worked microroutine: Let us run the fetch and an ADD that adds a memory word to the accumulator. Fetch, microinstruction 1: AR <- PC. Microinstruction 2: DR <- M[AR], PC <- PC + 1. Microinstruction 3: IR <- DR, then map the opcode. Say ADD maps to address 8. Microinstruction at 8: AR <- address part of IR. At 9: DR <- M[AR]. At 10: AC <- AC + DR, then branch back to fetch. So one machine instruction ADD took 3 + 3 = 6 microinstructions, which means 6 clock cycles. Notice how each line is just a list of which signals are on. Writing a new instruction means writing a few new lines in control memory.

Worked size calculation: Suppose a control unit needs 200 microinstructions in total, and each microinstruction is 32 bits wide. The CAR must address 200 rows, and 2^7 = 128 is too few while 2^8 = 256 is enough, so CAR needs 8 bits. The control memory is 256 words x 32 bits = 8,192 bits, which is 1 KB. Exams love this kind of question: count the rows, find the address bits with powers of two, then multiply rows by width.

Horizontal microprogramming: In horizontal format, every control signal gets its own bit. If the datapath has 60 control signals, the control field has 60 bits. Advantage: any combination of signals can be on together, so many micro-operations can happen in the same cycle, and no decoding is needed, so it is fast. Disadvantage: the microinstructions are very wide, so the control memory is big and costly, and most bits are 0 most of the time.

Vertical microprogramming: In vertical format, signals that can never be on together are grouped and encoded. Example: the ALU can do only one of 8 operations at a time. Horizontal needs 8 bits, one per operation. Vertical encodes the choice in 3 bits, because 2^3 = 8, and a 3-to-8 decoder turns those 3 bits back into 8 signals. Mano's F1, F2, F3 fields are exactly this: each 3-bit field selects one of 7 micro-operations or none. Advantage: narrow words, smaller control memory. Disadvantage: decoders add delay, and fewer things can happen in parallel, so a routine may need more microinstructions.

Horizontal versus vertical in one picture: Horizontal: wide word -> signals directly -> fast, parallel, big memory. Vertical: narrow word -> decoders -> signals -> slower, less parallel, small memory. Real designs often mix both: some fields encoded, some bits direct.

Hardwired versus microprogrammed: Speed: hardwired is faster, because signals come straight from logic, while microprogrammed control must read control memory every cycle. Flexibility: microprogrammed wins; changing behaviour means changing memory contents, not wiring. Design effort: microprogrammed is easier and more systematic for big, complex instruction sets. Cost of a simple ISA: hardwired is smaller. Typical use: RISC processors such as MIPS and most ARM cores use hardwired control because their instructions are simple and regular. Classic CISC processors such as the IBM System/360 and early x86 chips relied heavily on microcode.

What modern x86 chips do: Today's Intel and AMD processors are a mix. Simple, common x86 instructions are decoded directly by hardware into internal micro-operations. A few long, complicated instructions are handled by a microcode ROM that produces a sequence of micro-operations. Many of these processors also support microcode updates: a patch loaded at boot by the BIOS/UEFI firmware or the operating system can change some behaviour to fix bugs. Some security fixes after the Spectre problems of 2018 were delivered partly this way.

When to choose microprogrammed control: when the instruction set is large or complex, when you expect to fix bugs or add instructions later, when you want one instruction set across many hardware models, or when design time matters more than the last bit of speed. When not to: when the instruction set is small and regular, when every nanosecond counts, such as a deep pipeline that must start a new instruction every cycle, or when the chip must be tiny and cheap.

Real-life example 1, a garment factory in Gazipur: A sewing line has many machines. A supervisor holds a stack of cards for each product: shirt, trouser, polo. Each card says which machines run in this step and which worker does what. For a shirt, card 1 says cut, card 2 says stitch body, card 3 says attach sleeves, and the last card says go back to the start for the next shirt. The stack of cards is the control memory, each card is a microinstruction, the card number being read is the CAR, and choosing the stack by product name is the mapping logic. When the buyer orders a new design, the factory writes new cards instead of rebuilding machines. Where the analogy breaks: workers can think and adjust; the control memory is followed exactly, with no judgment.

Real-life example 2, Windows Update on a laptop: If you look at the update history on a Windows laptop with an Intel chip, you may sometimes see an entry for an Intel microcode update. This is the microprogramming idea still alive: the chip in your laptop was already sold, but part of its behaviour could be corrected by loading new microcode, something that would be impossible with a purely hardwired design.

Common mistakes: Students often confuse a microinstruction with a machine instruction. A machine instruction, like ADD, is what the programmer writes and lives in main memory. A microinstruction is one internal step stored in control memory inside the CPU, invisible to the programmer. Another mistake is saying the microprogram lives in RAM; normally it is in a ROM or a special fast memory in the processor. A third mistake is thinking vertical format is always better because it is smaller; it costs decoding time and parallelism. Also remember CAR is to microinstructions what PC is to machine instructions.

What exams ask: Draw the block diagram of a microprogrammed control unit and explain CAR, control memory, sequencer and mapping. Compare hardwired and microprogrammed control in a table. Compare horizontal and vertical microinstructions. Given the number of microinstructions and the width, compute CAR bits and control memory size. Write a fetch microroutine in register transfer language.

Recap: Microprogrammed control stores the control signals for each step as microinstructions in a control memory. CAR points to the current microinstruction, a mapping turns the opcode into a starting address, and a sequencer picks the next address by increment, branch, condition or map. Horizontal format is wide and fast; vertical is narrow and needs decoders. Hardwired control is faster and suits RISC; microprogrammed control is flexible and suits complex instruction sets. Next lesson we look at the full instruction cycle and multi-cycle execution.
key_points: Microprogrammed control stores the control signals of each step as microinstructions in a control memory (control store), usually a ROM inside the CPU.
Maurice Wilkes proposed microprogramming in 1951; most IBM System/360 models used it.
CAR (control address register) holds the address of the next microinstruction, like the PC for machine instructions.
Mapping logic converts the opcode into the start address of its microroutine; the sequencer chooses increment, branch, conditional branch or map.
Control memory size = number of words x word width; CAR bits = ceiling of log2(number of words).
Horizontal format: one bit per signal, wide, fast, parallel. Vertical format: encoded fields with decoders, narrow, slower.
Hardwired control is faster and suits simple RISC ISAs; microprogrammed control is flexible and suits large CISC ISAs.
Modern x86 chips still use microcode for complex instructions and can receive microcode updates.
lessons.tip: Always draw the two loops side by side: PC fetches machine instructions from main memory, CAR fetches microinstructions from control memory. Most confusion disappears once you see that it is a computer inside the computer.
lessons.task: On paper, design a tiny control memory: write the 3 fetch microinstructions and a 3-line microroutine for a LOAD instruction (AC <- M[address]). Then count how many bits you would need if you had 12 control signals in horizontal format, and how many if 8 of them were mutually exclusive ALU signals encoded vertically.

quiz.q: What does the control address register (CAR) hold?
options: The address of the next machine instruction
The address of the next microinstruction in control memory
The opcode of the current instruction
quiz.explain: CAR plays the role of a program counter for the microprogram: it points into control memory.

quiz.q: A control unit has 300 microinstructions, each 24 bits wide. How many bits does CAR need?
quiz.explain: 2^8 = 256 is too few, 2^9 = 512 is enough, so CAR needs 9 bits.

quiz.q: Which statement about horizontal microinstructions is true?
options: Each control signal has its own bit, so they are wide but need no decoding
They are narrower than vertical microinstructions
They always need a decoder for every field
They allow only one micro-operation per cycle
quiz.explain: Horizontal format gives every signal a direct bit: wide words, no decoders, much parallelism.

quiz.q: Why do most RISC processors use hardwired control?
options: Hardwired control is easier to change after manufacture
RISC processors have no control unit
Their simple, regular instructions make fast fixed logic practical
Microprogramming cannot handle load and store instructions
quiz.explain: With a small regular ISA, hardwired logic stays manageable and gives the speed a pipeline needs.

quiz.q: An ALU can perform 16 different operations, only one at a time. In vertical format, how many bits encode the ALU choice?
quiz.explain: 2^4 = 16, so 4 encoded bits plus a 4-to-16 decoder replace 16 separate bits.

lessons.title: Multi-Cycle Execution and the Instruction Cycle
lessons.content:
Imagine a doctor's chamber in Dhanmondi with a strange rule: every patient gets exactly 30 minutes, because the most complicated patient once needed 30 minutes. A child with a small cold, who needs 5 minutes, still blocks the room for 30. The waiting room fills up, and the doctor spends most of the time doing nothing. A smarter rule is to give appointments in 5-minute slots, and let each patient take as many slots as they actually need. The simple patient leaves after one slot, the complex one stays for six. This lesson is about the same idea inside a processor: moving from a single-cycle design, where every instruction gets one long clock cycle, to a multi-cycle design, where each instruction takes as many short cycles as it needs. Then we look at the complete instruction cycle, including two extra phases: indirect and interrupt.

Recap of the single-cycle processor: In lesson 12 we built a datapath where every instruction finishes in exactly one clock cycle. During that one cycle the instruction is fetched, the registers are read, the ALU works, memory may be accessed, and the result is written back. Its CPI is 1, which sounds perfect. But there is a hidden cost: the clock period must be long enough for the slowest instruction.

The problem, with numbers: Suppose memory access takes 200 ps (picoseconds), the ALU takes 100 ps, and reading or writing the register file takes 50 ps. These are the classic textbook example numbers. A load word (lw) needs instruction fetch 200 + register read 50 + ALU 100 + data memory 200 + register write 50 = 600 ps. An R-type add needs 200 + 50 + 100 + 50 = 400 ps. A branch (beq) needs 200 + 50 + 100 = 350 ps. In a single-cycle design the clock must be 600 ps for everyone, so the add wastes 200 ps and the branch wastes 250 ps every time. Worse, if the ISA had a slow instruction, such as a multiply that needed 2,000 ps, then every instruction, even the simplest, would have to take 2,000 ps.

A second problem, wasted hardware: In a single cycle, each hardware unit can be used only once. If an instruction needs memory twice, once to fetch the instruction and once to read data, the single-cycle design needs two separate memories (instruction memory and data memory). If it needs to add twice, once for PC + 4 and once in the ALU, it needs separate adders. Hardware is duplicated just because everything must happen at the same time.

The solution, multi-cycle execution: Break each instruction into steps. Each step does about one major job: one memory access, or one ALU operation, or one register file access. The clock period only needs to fit the longest step, not the longest instruction. Each instruction then uses as many cycles as it has steps. Values that must survive from one step to the next are kept in extra internal registers, such as the instruction register (IR), a memory data register (MDR), registers A and B for values read from the register file, and ALUOut for the ALU result. Because work is spread over time, one memory and one ALU can be shared by different steps.

The five steps of a classic multi-cycle MIPS: Step 1, instruction fetch: IR <- Memory[PC]; PC <- PC + 4. Step 2, instruction decode and register fetch: A <- Reg[rs]; B <- Reg[rt]; and, just in case this is a branch, ALUOut <- PC + (sign-extended offset shifted left by 2). Step 3, execution: for R-type, ALUOut <- A op B; for load/store, ALUOut <- A + offset (the memory address); for a branch, compare A and B and, if equal, PC <- ALUOut, and the branch is finished. Step 4, memory access or R-type completion: a load reads MDR <- Memory[ALUOut]; a store writes Memory[ALUOut] <- B and finishes; an R-type writes Reg[rd] <- ALUOut and finishes. Step 5, write-back for loads only: Reg[rt] <- MDR.

Counting cycles per instruction: From those steps, a load takes 5 cycles, a store 4, an R-type 4, a branch 3, and a jump 3. Picture it as a timeline: lw: F D E M W; add: F D E W; beq: F D E. Short instructions leave early, just like the child with the cold.

Worked CPI example: Suppose a program mix is 25% loads, 10% stores, 45% R-type, 15% branches and 5% jumps. Average CPI = 0.25 x 5 + 0.10 x 4 + 0.45 x 4 + 0.15 x 3 + 0.05 x 3 = 1.25 + 0.40 + 1.80 + 0.45 + 0.15 = 4.05. With a 200 ps clock (the slowest step is a memory access), the average time per instruction is 4.05 x 200 = 810 ps.

An honest surprise: 810 ps is slower than the single-cycle 600 ps! With these particular numbers, where the steps are not balanced and almost every instruction needs four or more steps, multi-cycle does not win on speed. Its real wins are elsewhere. First, hardware sharing: one memory and one ALU instead of two memories and three adders. Second, it handles variable-length work well. Go back to the 2,000 ps multiply: in single-cycle every instruction pays 2,000 ps, but in multi-cycle the multiply can take ten 200 ps steps while an add still takes four. Third, it is the natural way to build processors whose instructions vary a lot in complexity, which is why it fits CISC designs. And it is the stepping stone to pipelining (lesson 16), which overlaps these steps to get both a short clock and a CPI close to 1.

How the control works in multi-cycle: The control unit is now a finite state machine. Each state corresponds to one step and turns on the signals for that step. State 0 is fetch, state 1 is decode, and from state 1 the machine branches to a different state depending on the opcode. Each path ends by going back to state 0. You can build this state machine with hardwired logic (lesson 13), using a state register and next-state logic, or with a microprogram (lesson 14), where each state becomes one microinstruction and the opcode-based branch becomes the mapping step.

The instruction cycle in general: Every processor, simple or complex, repeats the instruction cycle. Its basic phases are: fetch the instruction, decode it, find the operands, execute, store the result, and then check whether anything urgent has happened. In one line: Fetch -> Decode -> (Indirect?) -> Execute -> (Interrupt?) -> Fetch again. The two question-marked phases happen only when needed. Let us look at each.

The indirect cycle: Some instructions do not contain the address of their data directly. Instead they contain the address of a memory word that holds the real address. This is indirect addressing from lesson 9. In M. Morris Mano's basic computer, a mode bit called I in the instruction says which kind it is. If I = 1, the processor runs an extra indirect phase: it reads memory once more to fetch the real address, called the effective address, and only then executes. Example: the instruction says ADD indirect 300. Memory word 300 contains 750, and word 750 contains 9. The indirect cycle reads 300 and gets 750; the execute cycle reads 750 and adds 9 to the accumulator. One extra memory access, one extra phase.

What an interrupt is: An interrupt is a signal from outside the current program, saying 'stop what you are doing for a moment, something needs attention'. A key was pressed, a network packet arrived, a timer expired, a disk finished reading. Without interrupts, the CPU would have to keep checking every device again and again, which wastes time. The details of devices and interrupt controllers come in lesson 24 and in the Microprocessors course; here we care about where interrupts fit in the instruction cycle.

The interrupt cycle, step by step: The processor does not stop in the middle of an instruction. It finishes the current instruction completely, then checks: is an interrupt request pending, and are interrupts enabled? If not, it goes to fetch the next instruction as usual. If yes, it enters the interrupt cycle. Step 1, save the return address: the current PC, which already points to the next instruction, is saved, either in a fixed memory location or on a stack. Step 2, disable further interrupts so the processor is not interrupted again while switching. Step 3, load the PC with the address of the interrupt service routine. Then normal fetching continues, but now from the service routine. When the routine finishes, a return instruction restores the saved PC and the original program continues as if nothing happened. In Mano's basic computer, the return address is stored at memory location 0 and the PC is set so that the service code starts from location 1.

Why check only between instructions: If the CPU could stop halfway through an instruction, the half-done state, such as a register partly updated, would be very hard to save and resume correctly. Checking only at instruction boundaries keeps things clean: every instruction either has fully happened or has not started. This is called a precise interrupt, and it becomes much harder to guarantee once instructions overlap in a pipeline.

When multi-cycle is the right choice: when hardware must be small and cheap, when instructions vary a lot in length or complexity, when there are slow operations like multiply, divide or floating point, and when you are learning, because it shows the steps clearly. When it is not: for high performance, where pipelining overlaps the steps and beats both single-cycle and plain multi-cycle designs. Almost every modern processor, from your phone to a server, is pipelined, but each pipeline stage is basically one of these multi-cycle steps.

Real-life example 1, the NID card office: At an election office in Bangladesh, imagine every visitor is forced through every counter: photo, fingerprint, signature, payment, document check, even if they only came to correct a spelling. That is single-cycle thinking: everyone pays the cost of the longest job. A sensible office lets each visitor go only through the counters they need, one counter at a time, and the same fingerprint machine serves many visitors at different times. That is multi-cycle: short steps, shared equipment, and each job takes only the steps it needs. Where the analogy breaks: real visitors can choose counters in any order; a processor's steps follow a fixed order set by the control state machine.

Real-life example 2, interrupts while studying: You are solving a maths problem for your SSC exam. Your mother calls you to bring the shopping bag from the rickshaw. You do not drop the pencil mid-digit; you finish the line you are writing (finish the current instruction). You note the problem number (save the PC). You do not answer the phone while carrying the bag (disable other interrupts). You go and help (run the service routine). You come back, look at your note, and continue from the next line (restore PC and resume). That is exactly the interrupt cycle.

Common mistakes: Thinking multi-cycle is always faster than single-cycle; it depends on the step times and the instruction mix, as our 810 ps versus 600 ps example showed. Forgetting that multi-cycle needs extra internal registers (IR, MDR, A, B, ALUOut) to hold values between steps. Believing an interrupt stops the CPU in the middle of an instruction; it is checked after the instruction completes. Forgetting to disable interrupts during the interrupt cycle. Mixing up the indirect cycle, which fetches an address, with the execute cycle, which fetches or uses data.

What exams ask: Explain why single-cycle implementation is inefficient. List the steps of a multi-cycle implementation and how many cycles each instruction type takes. Compute average CPI and execution time for a given mix and compare with single-cycle. Draw the instruction cycle state diagram with indirect and interrupt phases. Explain what happens during the interrupt cycle, in register transfer language.

Recap: Single-cycle design makes every instruction as slow as the slowest one and duplicates hardware. Multi-cycle design splits instructions into short steps, shares one memory and one ALU, and lets each instruction take only the cycles it needs; control becomes a finite state machine. Whether it is faster depends on the numbers. The full instruction cycle is fetch, decode, optional indirect, execute, and an interrupt check after each instruction, where the PC is saved, interrupts are disabled and the service routine is started. Next lesson: pipelining, which overlaps these steps like a factory assembly line.
key_points: Single-cycle design forces the clock period to fit the slowest instruction, wasting time on simple ones.
Multi-cycle design splits each instruction into steps of one major operation each; the clock fits the longest step.
Classic multi-cycle MIPS: load 5 cycles, store 4, R-type 4, branch 3, jump 3; extra registers IR, MDR, A, B, ALUOut hold values between steps.
Average CPI = sum of (fraction x cycles); time per instruction = CPI x clock period. Multi-cycle is not automatically faster.
Multi-cycle shares one memory and one ALU and handles slow, variable-length instructions well; its control is a finite state machine.
Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, optional indirect (fetch effective address), execute, then interrupt check.
Interrupts are checked only after an instruction completes; the interrupt cycle saves PC, disables interrupts and jumps to the service routine.
lessons.tip: Whenever you compare single-cycle and multi-cycle, always compute both numbers: time per instruction = CPI x clock period. Never judge from CPI alone or from clock period alone.
lessons.task: Using memory 200 ps, ALU 100 ps and register file 50 ps, compute the single-cycle clock period. Then take your own instruction mix (for example 30% loads, 50% R-type, 20% branches) and compute the multi-cycle average CPI and time per instruction. Which design wins for your mix?

quiz.q: In a single-cycle processor, what decides the clock period?
quiz.explain: Every instruction must finish in one cycle, so the cycle must be long enough for the slowest one.

quiz.q: In the classic multi-cycle MIPS, how many cycles does a load word take?
quiz.explain: Fetch, decode, address calculation, memory read, and write-back: 5 cycles.

quiz.q: A mix is 50% R-type (4 cycles) and 50% branch (3 cycles), clock 200 ps. What is the average time per instruction?
When does a processor normally check for an interrupt?
options: In the middle of the ALU operation
Only when the program asks for it
After the current instruction has completed
quiz.explain: Checking at instruction boundaries means no half-finished instruction state has to be saved.

quiz.q: What does the indirect cycle do?
options: Fetches the effective address from memory
Saves the PC for an interrupt
Writes the result to the register file
quiz.explain: With indirect addressing the instruction holds the address of the address; the indirect cycle reads memory to get the real (effective) address.

lessons.title: Pipelining Basics
lessons.content:
Imagine your family has four big bags of dirty clothes after Eid. Doing laundry has four steps: wash in the machine, dry, fold, and put away in the almirah. Say each step takes 30 minutes. The slow way: do bag 1 completely (wash, dry, fold, put away), then start bag 2. Four bags times four steps times 30 minutes is 8 hours. The smart way: as soon as bag 1 moves from the washer to the dryer, put bag 2 in the washer. When bag 1 goes to folding, bag 2 goes to the dryer and bag 3 goes into the washer. Now all four machines and people are busy at the same time. The last bag finishes after only 3.5 hours. Nobody washed faster; you just overlapped the work. That overlapping is called pipelining, and it is the single most important speed trick inside every modern processor.

What pipelining is: Pipelining is a technique where the execution of an instruction is split into stages, and different instructions are in different stages at the same time. While one instruction is being executed, the next one is being decoded, and the one after that is being fetched. Each instruction still goes through every stage, but a new instruction can start every clock cycle.

The problem it solves: In lesson 15 we saw two designs. Single-cycle has CPI = 1 but a very long clock, set by the slowest instruction. Multi-cycle has a short clock, but CPI of around 4 or 5, because each instruction uses one step at a time while the rest of the hardware sits idle. In multi-cycle, when the ALU is working on instruction 1, the instruction memory is doing nothing. That is wasted hardware time. Pipelining asks: why not let the idle units work on other instructions? The goal is the best of both: a short clock like multi-cycle and a CPI close to 1 like single-cycle.

Where the idea came from: Assembly lines in factories used this idea long before computers. In computers, overlapping of instruction fetch and execution appeared in large machines in the late 1950s and 1960s, such as IBM's Stretch project and the CDC 6600. In the 1980s, the RISC processors (MIPS, SPARC) were designed with a simple five-stage pipeline in mind from day one. Today almost every processor, from a cheap microcontroller to a server chip, is pipelined.

The classic five stages: Stage 1, IF (instruction fetch): read the instruction from instruction memory at address PC, and compute PC + 4. Stage 2, ID (instruction decode and register read): figure out what the instruction is and read its source registers. Stage 3, EX (execute): the ALU does the operation, or calculates a memory address, or compares for a branch. Stage 4, MEM (memory access): a load reads data memory, a store writes it; other instructions just pass through. Stage 5, WB (write back): the result is written into the destination register. One line: IF -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB.

A timing diagram: Let us watch four instructions, I1 to I4, with one stage per clock cycle. Cycle 1: I1 in IF. Cycle 2: I1 in ID, I2 in IF. Cycle 3: I1 in EX, I2 in ID, I3 in IF. Cycle 4: I1 in MEM, I2 in EX, I3 in ID, I4 in IF. Cycle 5: I1 in WB (finished), I2 in MEM, I3 in EX, I4 in ID. Cycle 6: I2 finishes. Cycle 7: I3 finishes. Cycle 8: I4 finishes. Draw it as a staircase: each row shifted one column to the right. From cycle 5 onwards, one instruction finishes every cycle.

Pipeline registers, the internal secret: How can five instructions share one datapath without mixing up their data? Between every two stages sits a pipeline register: IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB. At the end of each clock cycle, every stage writes its results into the register on its right, and at the start of the next cycle, the next stage reads them. These registers carry everything an instruction will need later: its register values, its immediate value, its destination register number, and its control signals. You can think of each pipeline register as the tray that moves an instruction's 'file' from one desk to the next. Without them, the next instruction would overwrite the values the previous one still needs.

The basic formula: Suppose a pipeline has k stages, each taking one cycle, and we run n instructions with no interruptions. The first instruction needs k cycles to come out. After that, one more instruction finishes every cycle, so the remaining n - 1 instructions need n - 1 more cycles. Total = k + (n - 1) cycles. Without pipelining, each instruction takes k cycles, so the total is n x k cycles. Speedup = (n x k) / (k + n - 1). When n is very large, this approaches k. So an ideal k-stage pipeline is up to k times faster.

Worked example 1, the laundry: k = 4 stages, n = 4 loads, 30 minutes per stage. Without pipelining: 4 x 4 = 16 stage-times = 8 hours. With pipelining: 4 + 3 = 7 stage-times = 3.5 hours. Speedup = 16 / 7, about 2.3, not 4. Why? With only 4 loads, a lot of time is spent filling and draining the pipeline. With 100 loads, the speedup would be 400 / 103, about 3.9, very close to 4.

Worked example 2, unequal stages: Real stages are not all the same length. Say IF takes 200 ps, register read 100 ps, ALU 200 ps, memory 200 ps and register write 100 ps. A single-cycle processor needs 800 ps for a load (200 + 100 + 200 + 200 + 100). In the pipeline every stage must fit into one clock, so the clock is set by the slowest stage: 200 ps. For a long program, one instruction finishes every 200 ps, so the speedup is 800 / 200 = 4, not 5. Lesson: unbalanced stages waste part of the speedup, so designers try hard to make stages equal.

Worked example 3, many instructions: Run 1,000 instructions on that 5-stage, 200 ps pipeline. Time = (5 + 999) x 200 ps = 200,800 ps, about 200.8 ns. On the single-cycle machine: 1,000 x 800 ps = 800 ns. Speedup is about 3.98.

Latency versus throughput: This is the most important idea in the lesson. Latency is how long one instruction takes from start to finish. Throughput is how many instructions finish per unit of time. Pipelining does not make any single instruction faster. In example 2, one load takes 5 x 200 = 1,000 ps in the pipeline, which is actually longer than 800 ps in single-cycle, because the short stages are stretched to 200 ps. What pipelining improves is throughput: one instruction completes every cycle. In the laundry, each bag still takes 2 hours from washer to almirah; you simply finish more bags per hour.

The hidden overhead: Pipeline registers are not free. Each one adds a small delay, perhaps tens of picoseconds, for the data to be latched. If each stage is 200 ps and the register adds 20 ps, the real clock is 220 ps. So splitting a pipeline into more and more stages gives smaller and smaller gains: the stage work shrinks, but the register overhead stays the same.

Why an instruction set can help: Some instruction sets are much easier to pipeline. MIPS was designed for it. All instructions are 32 bits long, so fetching is always the same and the next address is always PC + 4. There are only a few formats, and the source register fields are in the same place in each, so registers can be read while decoding. Memory is touched only by load and store, so the MEM stage is simple. x86, with variable-length instructions from 1 to 15 bytes and memory operands in many instructions, is much harder to pipeline directly; modern x86 chips first translate instructions into simpler internal micro-operations and pipeline those.

Ideal versus real: In an ideal pipeline CPI = 1. Real pipelines run into hazards: situations where the next instruction cannot go ahead in the next cycle. An instruction may need a result that is not ready yet, two instructions may want the same hardware, or a branch may change which instruction should come next. Then the pipeline must wait, called a stall or bubble. Real CPI = 1 + average stall cycles per instruction. Lesson 17 is all about hazards and how to reduce stalls.

Deeper pipelines, when and when not: More stages mean less work per stage and a faster clock. Some Intel Pentium 4 processors used pipelines of more than 20 stages to reach high clock rates. But deeper pipelines have costs: more pipeline register overhead, a bigger penalty when a branch is guessed wrong (more half-done instructions to throw away), and more power. Later designs went back to more moderate depths. Pipelining is great for long streams of simple, independent instructions. It helps less for code full of unpredictable branches or instructions that depend on the result immediately before them.

Real-life example 1, packing biryani for a wedding: At a big wedding in Chattogram, the caterer packs 500 boxes of biryani. If one person fills one box completely, with rice, then meat, then egg and salad, then closes and stacks it, every box takes about two minutes. Instead the caterer makes a line of four people: the first puts rice, the second meat, the third egg and salad, the fourth closes and stacks. Each person takes about 30 seconds. Once the line is full, a finished box comes out every 30 seconds. The four people are the stages, the hand-over spot on the table between them is the pipeline register, and the slowest person decides the speed of the whole line, exactly like the slowest stage decides the clock. Where the analogy breaks: in a processor, the items in the line can depend on each other (one instruction needs another's result), while biryani boxes never depend on each other.

Real-life example 2, checking exam scripts: In a board exam in Bangladesh, a team of teachers checks scripts. Instead of one teacher checking all 10 questions of a script, teacher A checks questions 1 to 2, teacher B checks 3 to 4, and so on, and the script moves along. Each script still needs the same total checking time (latency is not reduced), but the team finishes far more scripts per day (throughput goes up). If teacher C is slow, scripts pile up in front of her and everyone else waits: an unbalanced stage.

Common mistakes: Saying pipelining makes each instruction faster; it improves throughput, not latency. Forgetting the fill time: the formula is k + n - 1, not n. Assuming the speedup always equals the number of stages; unequal stages, register overhead and hazards reduce it. Forgetting pipeline registers in diagrams. Mixing up 'number of stages' with 'number of instructions in the pipeline'; in a full 5-stage pipeline, there are up to 5 instructions in flight.

What exams ask: Explain pipelining with an analogy. Draw a space-time (timing) diagram for n instructions in a k-stage pipeline. Derive and use the formula for total time and speedup. Given stage delays, find the clock period, the pipelined time and the speedup over a non-pipelined design. Explain the difference between latency and throughput. Explain why MIPS is easy to pipeline.

Recap: Pipelining overlaps instructions so that each stage works on a different instruction at the same time. The classic five stages are IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB, separated by pipeline registers. For n instructions in k stages, time = k + n - 1 cycles and speedup approaches k. The clock is set by the slowest stage plus register overhead. Pipelining improves throughput, not latency, and real pipelines lose time to hazards. Next lesson: those hazards, and the clever tricks that fix them.
key_points: Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages and overlaps different instructions in different stages.
Classic 5 stages: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB, separated by pipeline registers IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB.
Pipeline registers carry each instruction's data and control signals from stage to stage.
For n instructions in a k-stage pipeline: time = k + n - 1 cycles; speedup = nk / (k + n - 1), approaching k.
The clock period is set by the slowest stage plus pipeline register overhead; unbalanced stages reduce speedup.
Pipelining improves throughput, not the latency of a single instruction.
Uniform instruction length and simple formats (as in MIPS) make pipelining easier.
Real CPI = 1 + stall cycles per instruction because of hazards.
lessons.tip: Draw the staircase timing diagram for every pipeline question, even when not asked. Counting boxes on paper prevents the most common mistake, forgetting the k - 1 fill cycles.
lessons.task: Write five one-step jobs you do every morning (for example: brush, bathe, dress, eat, pack bag) and imagine three family members doing them with one bathroom, one wardrobe, one table. Draw a timing diagram on paper where each person moves to the next step as soon as it is free. How long does it take sequentially versus overlapped?

quiz.q: A 5-stage pipeline runs 10 instructions with no stalls. How many cycles does it take?
Stage delays are 150, 200, 120, 200 and 100 ps. Ignoring register overhead, what is the pipeline clock period?
quiz.explain: Every stage must fit in one cycle, so the slowest stage (200 ps) decides the clock.

quiz.q: What does pipelining mainly improve?
options: Throughput, instructions completed per unit time
quiz.explain: Each instruction still passes every stage; more instructions just finish per unit of time.

quiz.q: What is the job of a pipeline register such as ID/EX?
options: To store the program in memory
To hold an instruction's values and control signals between two stages
quiz.explain: Pipeline registers separate stages and carry each instruction's data and control forward, so instructions do not mix.

quiz.q: Why is the real speedup of a 5-stage pipeline often less than 5?
options: Because pipelining makes each stage slower on purpose
Because only one instruction can be in the pipeline
Because of unbalanced stages, register overhead, fill time and hazards
quiz.explain: Speedup approaches k only with equal stages, no overhead, many instructions and no stalls.

lessons.title: Pipeline Hazards
lessons.content:
Go back to the biryani packing line from lesson 16. It works beautifully as long as every box is independent. Now imagine three kinds of trouble. First, the rice person and the closing person both need the only big spoon at the same moment. Second, the meat person is told 'put the same amount of meat as the previous box got rice', so she must wait until the previous box has its rice measured. Third, the manager shouts 'stop, the next 50 boxes are vegetarian!', but three boxes already have meat in them and must be thrown out. In a processor pipeline, these three troubles have names: structural hazards, data hazards and control hazards. This lesson is about what they are, why they happen inside the 5-stage pipeline, and the clever tricks used to fix them.

What a hazard is: A hazard is any situation that stops the next instruction from entering or moving through the pipeline in the next clock cycle as planned. When a hazard happens, the pipeline must wait. A wasted cycle where no useful instruction moves forward is called a stall or a bubble. Every stall raises the CPI above the ideal value of 1: real CPI = 1 + average stall cycles per instruction. The whole art of pipeline design is to keep stalls rare.

A quick reminder of the stages: IF fetches the instruction, ID decodes it and reads registers, EX uses the ALU, MEM reads or writes data memory, WB writes the result into a register. Keep this line in mind: IF -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB. The key fact for hazards is timing: a result is normally written to the register file only in WB, the fifth stage, but the next instructions want to read registers in ID, their second stage.

Structural hazards, the shared spoon: A structural hazard happens when two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle. Classic example: if there is only one memory for both instructions and data, then in cycle 4 a load in its MEM stage wants to read data while a new instruction in its IF stage wants to be fetched. Both cannot happen. The fixes are about adding or splitting hardware. Pipelined processors use separate instruction and data memories, which in real chips means a separate L1 instruction cache and L1 data cache. The register file is another possible conflict, since WB writes and ID reads in the same cycle; the usual trick is to write in the first half of the clock cycle and read in the second half, so both fit in one cycle. MIPS was designed so that, with these choices, the basic pipeline has no structural hazards.

Data hazards, the waiting for a value: A data hazard happens when an instruction depends on the result of an earlier instruction that has not finished yet. Example: add $s0, $t0, $t1 followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3. The sub needs $s0, which add computes. But add writes $s0 only in WB, in cycle 5, while sub wants to read $s0 in its ID stage in cycle 3. If nothing is done, sub reads the old, wrong value of $s0. This is the most common hazard in real programs, because programs constantly use values they just computed.

Three types of data dependence: Using names that describe the order of reads (R) and writes (W). RAW, read after write: the later instruction reads what the earlier one writes. This is a true dependence; the add/sub example is RAW. WAR, write after read: the later instruction writes a register that the earlier one still needs to read. WAW, write after write: both write the same register, and the final value must be the later one. In the simple in-order 5-stage pipeline, every instruction reads registers in ID and writes in WB, always in order, so only RAW can cause trouble. WAR and WAW become real problems in processors that execute instructions out of order or have stages of different lengths, which we meet in lesson 18.

Fix 1, stalling: The simplest fix is to make sub wait. Hardware called the hazard detection unit notices the dependence and freezes the dependent instruction in ID, while the earlier one moves ahead. With the write-first-half/read-second-half register file, sub can read the correct $s0 in cycle 5, the same cycle add writes it. So sub must wait 2 extra cycles. Timeline: add: IF ID EX MEM WB; sub: IF stall stall ID EX MEM WB. Correct, but slow. If this happened after many instructions, the CPI would rise badly.

Fix 2, forwarding (bypassing): Here is the clever observation. The value of $s0 already exists at the end of add's EX stage, in cycle 3, sitting in the EX/MEM pipeline register. It is only written to the register file later. Sub needs it at the start of its own EX stage, in cycle 4. So why not take it straight from the EX/MEM register and feed it into the ALU input? That is forwarding, also called bypassing. Extra wires and multiplexers at the ALU inputs choose between the register file value, the value in EX/MEM (from the previous instruction), and the value in MEM/WB (from two instructions ago). With forwarding, the add/sub pair needs zero stalls.

How the forwarding unit decides: The forwarding unit compares register numbers. In words: if the instruction in EX/MEM will write a register, and that register is not $zero, and its number equals the source register of the instruction now in EX, then forward from EX/MEM. A similar check is done for MEM/WB. If both match, the more recent value, from EX/MEM, wins. The check against register $zero matters because $zero is always 0 in MIPS and must never be replaced by a forwarded value.

The load-use hazard, where forwarding is not enough: Now try lw $s0, 20($t1) followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3. The loaded value arrives only at the end of the load's MEM stage, in cycle 4. But sub wants it at the start of its EX stage, also in cycle 4. You cannot send a value backward in time. So even with forwarding, one stall is needed: the hazard detection unit holds sub in ID for one cycle, inserts a bubble (an empty instruction with all control signals 0) into EX, and then forwards the value from MEM/WB. In words, the check is: if the instruction in EX is a load, and its destination register matches a source register of the instruction in ID, stall for one cycle.

Fix 3, compiler scheduling: Software can help too. The compiler can reorder independent instructions to fill the gap after a load. Example, computing a = b + e and c = b + f: lw $t1, 0($t0); lw $t2, 4($t0); add $t3, $t1, $t2; sw $t3, 12($t0); lw $t4, 8($t0); add $t5, $t1, $t4; sw $t5, 16($t0). Both adds come right after the load they need, so there are two load-use stalls. Seven instructions in a 5-stage pipeline need 7 + 4 = 11 cycles without stalls, so this takes 13. Move the third load (lw $t4) up to right after the second load. Now no add follows its own load directly, and the code finishes in 11 cycles. Same result, two cycles saved, no extra hardware.

Control hazards, the changed plan: A control hazard happens because of branches and jumps. The pipeline fetches a new instruction every cycle, but for a branch like beq, it does not know whether the branch is taken, or where it goes, until the comparison is done. Meanwhile, which instructions should it be fetching? If it waits, cycles are lost. If it guesses and guesses wrong, the wrongly fetched instructions must be thrown away, which is called flushing. In the original 5-stage design the branch outcome was known in MEM, costing 3 cycles. A common improvement moves the comparison and target calculation into ID, so a wrong path costs only 1 cycle.

Fixes for control hazards: Stall on every branch: simple but slow. Predict not taken: keep fetching the next sequential instructions; if the branch turns out not taken, nothing is lost; if taken, flush the wrong instructions. Delayed branch: the original MIPS defined one branch delay slot, meaning the instruction right after a branch always executes, and the compiler tries to put a useful instruction there. Dynamic branch prediction: hardware remembers the past behaviour of each branch and guesses accordingly, which is the topic of lesson 18.

Worked CPI example: Suppose 25% of instructions are loads, and 40% of those are immediately followed by an instruction that uses the loaded value. Each such case costs 1 stall. Also, 15% of instructions are branches, with a 1-cycle penalty whenever a branch is taken, and 60% of branches are taken. Stalls per instruction = 0.25 x 0.40 x 1 + 0.15 x 0.60 x 1 = 0.10 + 0.09 = 0.19. CPI = 1 + 0.19 = 1.19. The processor runs at 1 / 1.19, about 84% of its ideal speed. This is how architects decide which hazard is worth attacking first: here both matter about equally.

When to use which fix: Forwarding is almost always worth it; it is cheap hardware and removes most data stalls. Stalling is the safety net for the cases forwarding cannot solve, like load-use. Compiler scheduling is free at run time but depends on finding independent instructions. For branches, simple prediction is fine in short pipelines; deep pipelines need strong dynamic prediction because each misprediction throws away many cycles of work. When not to bother: in a tiny non-pipelined microcontroller, there are no pipeline hazards at all, and all this hardware would only add cost.

Real-life example 1, Ammu's cooking: Ammu is cooking bhuna khichuri with a helper. Frying the onions must finish before the masala goes in: that is a RAW dependence. The slow way: the helper fries onions, puts them in a bowl in the fridge (the register file), and Ammu later takes them out (reading the register). Forwarding is the helper passing the hot onions directly from his pan into Ammu's pot the moment they are ready, skipping the fridge. The load-use hazard is when the onions are still at the shop: the helper must first go and bring them, and Ammu has no choice but to wait one step. Where the analogy breaks: in the CPU the forwarded value is an exact copy, and the register file still gets written later as well.

Real-life example 2, the bus at Farmgate: A Dhaka bus driver approaching Farmgate does not know yet whether the traffic police will send him straight or make him turn. If he keeps driving straight (predict not taken) and the police signal straight, no time is lost. If the police signal a turn, he must reverse and go another way: the time spent going straight is wasted, like flushing fetched instructions. An experienced driver who remembers that at this hour the police usually send buses left will guess better, which is exactly what dynamic branch prediction does.

Common mistakes: Saying forwarding removes all data stalls; the load-use case still needs one stall. Forgetting the register $zero check in forwarding conditions. Counting stalls without the write-first-half/read-second-half rule and getting 3 instead of 2. Calling WAR and WAW problems in the simple 5-stage in-order pipeline; there, only RAW hazards occur. Forgetting that a bubble is inserted by setting control signals to zero, not by deleting an instruction.

What exams ask: Define and classify hazards with examples. Identify all RAW dependences in a code sequence. Draw the pipeline diagram with and without forwarding and count cycles. Explain the load-use hazard and why it needs a stall. Reorder code to remove stalls. Compute CPI given hazard frequencies and penalties. Explain branch penalty, predict-not-taken and delayed branch.

Recap: Hazards stop the pipeline from starting an instruction every cycle. Structural hazards come from shared hardware and are fixed by separate memories and clever register file timing. Data hazards come from dependences, mostly RAW in a simple pipeline, and are fixed by forwarding, stalls (needed for load-use) and compiler reordering. Control hazards come from branches and are reduced by early branch resolution, prediction and delay slots. Real CPI = 1 + stalls per instruction. Next lesson goes deeper into branch prediction and into processors that run several instructions per cycle.
key_points: A hazard prevents the next instruction from proceeding in the next cycle; each stall adds to CPI (CPI = 1 + stalls per instruction).
Structural hazards: two instructions need the same hardware; fixed by separate instruction/data memories and writing the register file in the first half-cycle, reading in the second.
Data hazards: RAW (true dependence), WAR and WAW; the simple in-order 5-stage pipeline only suffers RAW.
Forwarding (bypassing) sends results from EX/MEM or MEM/WB directly to the ALU inputs, removing most data stalls.
A load followed immediately by a use of its result (load-use hazard) needs 1 stall even with forwarding.
Compilers can reorder independent instructions to fill load-use gaps without extra hardware.
Control hazards come from branches; fixes are stalling, predict not taken with flushing, delayed branch, and dynamic prediction.
Moving branch resolution to ID reduces the branch penalty from 3 cycles to 1 in the classic MIPS pipeline.
lessons.tip: For every pair of instructions, ask two questions: does the second read a register the first writes, and is the first a load? Yes-yes means one stall even with forwarding; yes-no means forwarding fixes it.
lessons.task: Write this code on paper: lw $t1, 0($t0); add $t2, $t1, $t1; lw $t3, 4($t0); sub $t4, $t3, $t2. Mark every RAW dependence, draw the 5-stage pipeline diagram with forwarding, and count the cycles. Then reorder the instructions to remove all stalls and count again.

quiz.q: In the simple in-order 5-stage MIPS pipeline, which data hazard type causes problems?
quiz.explain: Registers are read in ID and written in WB, in program order, so only read-after-write dependences can read a stale value.

quiz.q: add $s0, $t0, $t1 is followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3. With full forwarding, how many stall cycles are needed?
quiz.explain: The add result is ready at the end of EX and is forwarded from EX/MEM to sub's EX stage in the next cycle.

quiz.q: Why does a load followed immediately by a dependent instruction still need a stall with forwarding?
options: Because loads never use the ALU
Because the register file cannot be read
Because forwarding only works for branches
Because the loaded data is ready only at the end of MEM, when the next instruction already needs it in EX
quiz.explain: The data cannot be sent backward in time, so the dependent instruction waits one cycle and then gets it from MEM/WB.

quiz.q: 25% loads, 40% of them followed by a dependent use (1 stall each), no other stalls. What is the CPI?
quiz.explain: Stalls per instruction = 0.25 x 0.40 x 1 = 0.10, so CPI = 1.10.

quiz.q: What does 'predict not taken' do when the branch turns out to be taken?
options: Nothing, the result is correct anyway
It flushes the wrongly fetched instructions and fetches from the branch target
It executes both paths and keeps both results
quiz.explain: Instructions fetched after the branch were from the wrong path, so they are turned into bubbles and fetching restarts at the target.

lessons.title: Branch Prediction and Instruction-Level Parallelism
lessons.content:
Think about the tea stall owner near your school. Every morning, the same office worker comes and says 'one milk tea, less sugar'. After a week, the owner starts making that tea the moment he sees the man turning the corner. Most days, the tea is ready when he arrives and both save time. On the rare day the man wants lemon tea instead, the owner throws away the milk tea and starts again; a small loss. That is branch prediction: guessing what will happen next, working ahead on the guess, and throwing work away only when the guess is wrong. In this lesson we see how processors guess branches, and then how they go further, finding and running several independent instructions at the same time. That second idea is called instruction-level parallelism, or ILP.

The problem, again: In lesson 17 we saw that a branch creates a control hazard. The pipeline must fetch a new instruction every cycle, but it does not know which instruction comes after a branch until the branch is resolved. Branches are common: in typical programs a noticeable fraction of all instructions, often somewhere around one in every five to ten, are branches. Every loop, every if-else, every function return involves one. In a short 5-stage pipeline the penalty for a wrong guess is small, but in a deep modern pipeline, a wrong path may mean throwing away 15 or more cycles of work. So guessing well is worth a lot of hardware.

The cost in numbers: Suppose 20% of instructions are branches, the predictor is wrong 10% of the time, and each misprediction costs 15 cycles. Extra CPI = 0.20 x 0.10 x 15 = 0.30. If the ideal CPI is 1, the real CPI becomes 1.30, a 30% slowdown just from wrong guesses. If the predictor improves to only 5% wrong, the extra CPI drops to 0.15. Small improvements in accuracy give big gains.

Static prediction: Static means the guess is fixed before the program runs and does not change. Option 1, always predict not taken: just keep fetching the next instructions. Option 2, always predict taken. Option 3, backward taken, forward not taken: a branch that jumps backward to an earlier address is usually the bottom of a loop, which is taken many times, so guess taken; a forward branch often skips an unusual case, so guess not taken. The compiler can also give hints based on profiling, meaning it runs the program on sample data and records which way each branch usually goes. Static prediction is cheap but cannot adapt when a branch's behaviour changes.

Dynamic prediction with 1 bit: Dynamic means the hardware learns while the program runs. The simplest version is a branch history table, also called a branch prediction buffer: a small memory indexed by the lower bits of the branch instruction's address. Each entry holds one bit: 1 means 'last time this branch was taken', 0 means 'last time it was not taken'. The prediction is simply 'it will do what it did last time'. After the branch resolves, the bit is updated.

The weakness of 1 bit, worked: Consider a loop that runs 10 iterations, and the whole loop is executed many times by an outer loop. The loop branch is taken 9 times and not taken once (at exit). With 1 bit: on the last iteration the predictor says taken but the branch falls through, a miss, and the bit flips to 0. Next time the loop starts, the first iteration's branch is predicted not taken but is taken, a second miss, and the bit flips back to 1. So there are 2 misses per 10 branches: 80% accuracy, even though the branch is taken 90% of the time.

The 2-bit saturating counter: The fix is to require two wrong guesses in a row before changing the prediction. Each entry is a 2-bit counter with four states: 11 strongly taken, 10 weakly taken, 01 weakly not taken, 00 strongly not taken. States 11 and 10 predict taken; 01 and 00 predict not taken. A taken branch adds 1 (stopping at 11), a not-taken branch subtracts 1 (stopping at 00). One line: 00 <-> 01 <-> 10 <-> 11. For our loop: the counter sits at 11 during the loop. At exit, it drops to 10, still predicting taken. When the loop restarts, the first branch is taken and correctly predicted, and the counter climbs back to 11. Only 1 miss per 10 branches: 90% accuracy. One odd outcome does not change the prediction.

The branch target buffer: Knowing taken or not taken is half the problem; you also need the target address, and you need it in the IF stage, before the instruction is even decoded. A branch target buffer, BTB, is a small cache indexed by the PC of the instruction being fetched. If the PC matches an entry, the BTB says 'this is a branch I have seen, and last time it went to address X'. Combined with the direction predictor, the processor can fetch from X in the very next cycle, with no bubble at all when the guess is right.

More advanced predictors, briefly: Branches often depend on other branches. If one if-statement checks x > 0 and a later one checks x > 0 again, the second outcome follows the first. Correlating or two-level predictors use the recent history of outcomes, recorded as a pattern of bits, to choose which counter to use. Tournament predictors keep two different predictors and a third one that learns which of the two is more reliable for each branch. Modern processors use sophisticated predictors whose accuracy on typical programs is often well above 90%. The exact designs in commercial chips are mostly not published in full detail.

From guessing to parallelism: Branch prediction keeps the pipeline full. But even a perfect 5-stage pipeline finishes at most one instruction per cycle, so CPI cannot go below 1. To go faster, processors must start more than one instruction per cycle. Look at this code: a = b + c; d = e + f; g = a + d. The first two lines do not depend on each other, so they could run at the same time. The third needs both. Independence between nearby instructions is called instruction-level parallelism. Hardware and compilers try to find and use it.

Superscalar processors: A superscalar processor has multiple pipelines, or at least multiple execution units, and can issue several instructions in the same cycle. A 2-way superscalar can start two instructions per cycle, a 4-way can start four. Ideal CPI becomes 0.5 or 0.25, so designers usually speak of IPC, instructions per cycle, which ideally is 2 or 4. In practice dependences and stalls keep IPC lower than the ideal. Modern desktop and phone processors are superscalar.

VLIW, the compiler's way: Instead of hardware finding parallel instructions, a VLIW (very long instruction word) design lets the compiler pack several independent operations into one long instruction. The hardware is simpler, but the compiler must know a lot about timing, and code compiled for one model may not suit another. Intel's Itanium followed this style, and it is common in some digital signal processors.

Out-of-order execution: In-order pipelines stop everything when one instruction waits, for example for a slow memory load. Out-of-order processors let later independent instructions go ahead. Instructions are fetched and decoded in order, then placed in waiting areas called reservation stations. Each instruction starts executing as soon as its operands are ready, even if older instructions are still waiting. This idea goes back to Robert Tomasulo's algorithm, used in the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 in the 1960s.

Register renaming, removing false dependences: Out of order, WAR and WAW hazards become real. Example: I1: add r1, r2, r3. I2: sub r4, r1, r5. I3: add r1, r6, r7. I2 truly needs I1's r1 (RAW). But I3 also writes r1. If I3 finishes first, I2 could read the wrong r1 (WAR), and the final r1 could end up wrong (WAW). Yet I3 does not actually need anything from I1 or I2; they only clash because they happen to reuse the name r1. Hardware fixes this by renaming: it has many more physical registers than the ISA shows, and gives I3's result a fresh physical register, say p10. Now I3 can run in parallel safely, and later instructions that read r1 are pointed to p10. WAR and WAW are called false or name dependences; only RAW is a true dependence.

In-order commit and speculation: If instructions finish out of order, what happens when one of them causes an error, or a branch was mispredicted? A reorder buffer keeps the instructions in program order and lets each one commit, meaning update the official registers and memory, only when all older instructions have committed. Work done on a wrongly predicted path is simply discarded before commit. Running instructions on a predicted path before knowing it is right is called speculative execution. A real warning: in 2018 the Spectre and Meltdown attacks showed that speculative execution can leave traces in the cache that leak secret data, and processors and operating systems had to add protections.
