Trade-offs, when and when not: Branch prediction, superscalar issue and out-of-order execution make single-thread programs much faster, which is why phone and laptop processors use them. But they cost a lot of chip area and power: large predictor tables, many physical registers, reservation stations and reorder buffers. Small embedded controllers, such as the chip in a washing machine, skip most of this to stay cheap and low-power. Also, ILP is limited by true dependences in the program itself; beyond a point, extra hardware finds little extra parallelism. That is one reason the industry moved to multiple cores, covered in lesson 25.

Real-life example 1, the tea stall with 2-bit memory: Our tea stall owner is clever. If the office worker asks for lemon tea once, he does not immediately switch; he thinks 'maybe just today', and still prepares milk tea next morning. Only after two lemon tea days in a row does he switch his guess. That is the 2-bit counter: a single unusual day does not undo a long habit. The prepared tea ready at the counter as the man arrives is like the BTB providing the target in time. Where the analogy breaks: the owner can use extra clues like weather; a simple hardware predictor only sees past outcomes of branches.

Real-life example 2, the exam hall: In an HSC exam, you read the question paper and answer the easy questions first, while thinking about the hard one in the back of your mind. That is out-of-order execution: do whatever is ready. But when you hand in the script, every answer is labelled with its correct question number, so the examiner sees them in proper order. That is in-order commit through the reorder buffer. If you started answering a question you misread, you cross it out before submission, like discarding wrong speculative work.

Common mistakes: Thinking a 1-bit predictor gets a 10-iteration loop 90% right; it gets 80% because it misses twice per loop run. Forgetting that the 2-bit counter needs two consecutive wrong outcomes to change its prediction. Confusing the BTB, which gives the target address, with the direction predictor, which gives taken or not taken. Believing out-of-order processors also commit out of order. Calling WAR and WAW true dependences; they are name dependences removed by renaming.

What exams ask: Compare static and dynamic branch prediction. Draw the state diagram of a 2-bit predictor. Trace a 1-bit and a 2-bit predictor over a given sequence of outcomes and count mispredictions. Compute the CPI impact of branch mispredictions. Define superscalar, VLIW, out-of-order execution and register renaming. Identify RAW, WAR and WAW in a code sequence and show how renaming removes the false ones.

Recap: Branches are frequent, and wrong guesses cost more in deeper pipelines. Static prediction uses fixed rules; dynamic prediction learns, with 2-bit counters beating 1-bit ones on loops, and a BTB supplying targets during fetch. Beyond prediction, superscalar processors issue several instructions per cycle, out-of-order execution runs ready instructions early, register renaming removes false dependences, and a reorder buffer commits results in order. All of this costs area and power. Next we leave the processor core and enter the memory hierarchy.
key_points: Branch mispredictions add CPI = branch fraction x misprediction rate x penalty; deeper pipelines have bigger penalties.
Static prediction uses fixed rules such as always not taken, always taken, or backward taken forward not taken.
A 1-bit predictor mispredicts twice per run of a loop; a 2-bit saturating counter mispredicts only once.
A 2-bit counter needs two consecutive wrong outcomes to change its prediction (states 00, 01, 10, 11).
A branch target buffer (BTB) supplies the predicted target address during the IF stage.
Superscalar processors issue several instructions per cycle (IPC above 1); VLIW lets the compiler bundle operations.
Out-of-order execution runs instructions when operands are ready; register renaming removes WAR and WAW (name dependences).
A reorder buffer commits results in program order, so wrong speculative work can be discarded.
lessons.tip: Always trace predictors in a small table with columns: actual outcome, prediction, hit or miss, new state. Exam questions on predictors are easy marks once you trace step by step instead of guessing.
lessons.task: Take the branch outcome sequence T T T N T T T N (T = taken, N = not taken). Start a 1-bit predictor at T and a 2-bit counter at 11. Trace both on paper and count the mispredictions. Which predictor wins, and why?

quiz.q: A loop branch is taken 9 times and then not taken once, and the loop runs many times. What is the accuracy of a 1-bit predictor?
quiz.explain: It misses at loop exit and again at the first iteration of the next run: 2 misses per 10 branches.

quiz.q: A 2-bit counter is in state 11 (strongly taken). The branch is not taken once. What does it predict next?
quiz.explain: It moves from 11 to 10, weakly taken, which still predicts taken.

quiz.q: 20% branches, 5% misprediction rate, 20-cycle penalty. How much CPI do mispredictions add?
What does register renaming remove?
quiz.explain: Renaming gives each new result a fresh physical register, so instructions that only reuse a register name no longer conflict.

quiz.q: Why do out-of-order processors use a reorder buffer?
options: To commit results in program order and discard wrong speculative work
quiz.explain: Execution can be out of order, but the official state is updated in order, which keeps exceptions precise and allows wrong-path work to be thrown away.

lessons.title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
lessons.content:
Picture a mudi dokan, a small grocery shop in your para. The shopkeeper sits on a stool. Right next to his hand are the things people ask for most: salt, matches, biscuits, a few packets of tea. On the shelves behind him are more items, a short walk away. In the godown at the back are full sacks of rice and boxes of soap. And when even the godown runs out, he takes a CNG to Kawran Bazar to buy wholesale, which takes hours. He does not keep everything next to his hand, because that space is tiny. He does not keep everything at Kawran Bazar, because then every customer would wait for hours. He keeps a little near, more a bit further, and a lot far away. A computer stores data exactly this way. It is called the memory hierarchy, and it works because of a simple fact about programs called locality.

The problem, the speed gap: A modern processor can do an operation in well under a nanosecond. Main memory, built from DRAM, takes roughly 50 to 100 nanoseconds to deliver a piece of data, which is the time for well over a hundred processor cycles. Over the decades, processor speed improved much faster than DRAM speed, so this gap, often called the processor-memory gap or memory wall, kept growing. If the processor had to wait for main memory on every load, all the pipelining tricks of the last lessons would be wasted: a 3 GHz processor would spend almost all its time waiting.

Why not just build one big fast memory? Because of physics and money. Fast memory technologies use more transistors per bit, take more chip area, cost more per byte and use more power. Big, cheap memory technologies are slower. On top of that, a bigger memory is physically larger, so signals take longer to travel across it. You cannot have one memory that is huge, fast and cheap at the same time. This is the basic trade-off the hierarchy is built around.

What the memory hierarchy is: The memory hierarchy is an arrangement of several levels of memory, from small, fast and expensive near the processor, to large, slow and cheap far from it. A typical picture from top to bottom: Registers -> L1 cache -> L2 cache -> L3 cache -> Main memory (DRAM) -> Secondary storage (SSD or hard disk). Going down, each level is bigger, slower, and cheaper per byte. The goal is that the whole system feels almost as fast as the top level while having almost the size and low cost of the bottom level.

The levels with rough numbers: These are typical orders of magnitude for a modern laptop, not exact values for any one chip. Registers: a few hundred bytes to a few KB, accessed within a cycle. L1 cache: tens of KB per core, about a nanosecond. L2 cache: hundreds of KB to a few MB, a few nanoseconds. L3 cache: several MB to tens of MB shared by cores, around ten to a few tens of nanoseconds. Main memory: several GB, roughly 50 to 100 ns. SSD: hundreds of GB to a few TB, tens to hundreds of microseconds. Hard disk: up to many TB, several milliseconds, because a mechanical arm must move and the platter must rotate. From L1 to a hard disk, the access time grows by roughly a million times.

The memory technologies: SRAM (static RAM) stores each bit in a small circuit of usually six transistors that holds its value as long as power is on. It is fast and needs no refreshing, but it is large per bit, so it is used for caches and registers. DRAM (dynamic RAM) stores each bit as charge in a tiny capacitor with one transistor. It is much denser and cheaper, but the charge leaks away, so every row must be refreshed many times a second, and reading is slower. It is used for main memory. Flash memory, used in SSDs, phones and pen drives, keeps data without power (non-volatile) and has no moving parts, but each block can be erased only a limited number of times. Magnetic hard disks are cheapest per byte and non-volatile, but slow because of mechanical movement. SRAM and DRAM are volatile: their contents vanish when power is lost.

Locality, the secret that makes it work: A hierarchy only helps if the data the processor needs is usually already in the fast upper level. Luckily, real programs are not random. They show locality of reference, meaning they tend to use a small part of their data and code at any moment. There are two kinds.

Temporal locality: If a piece of data or an instruction is used now, it is likely to be used again soon. Loop counters, running totals, and the instructions inside a loop are used again and again. So it makes sense to keep recently used items in the fast level.

Spatial locality: If an address is used now, nearby addresses are likely to be used soon. Instructions are executed one after another, and arrays are usually walked element by element. So when we bring one item from a slow level, it makes sense to bring its neighbours too. That is why data moves between cache and memory in blocks, also called lines, typically 64 bytes in modern processors, not one byte at a time.

Locality in a real loop: Look at: sum = 0; for i = 0 to 999: sum = sum + a[i]. The variables sum and i are used in every iteration: temporal locality. The array elements a[0], a[1], a[2] are next to each other in memory: spatial locality. The few instructions of the loop body run 1,000 times: temporal locality for code, and they sit in consecutive addresses: spatial locality for code. When a[0] is loaded, the whole block containing a[0] to a[15] (if elements are 4 bytes and the block is 64 bytes) comes into the cache, so the next 15 accesses are fast.

Hits, misses and the key terms: When the processor looks for data in a level and finds it, that is a hit. If not, it is a miss, and the data must be fetched from the next lower level. Hit rate (hit ratio) is the fraction of accesses that hit; miss rate = 1 - hit rate. Hit time is the time to access the upper level, including checking whether it is a hit. Miss penalty is the extra time to fetch the block from the lower level and deliver it. The unit moved between cache and main memory is a block or line; between main memory and disk it is a page, which we will meet in lesson 23.

Average memory access time: The most important formula in this part of the course is AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty. Example: hit time 1 ns, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 100 ns. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 ns. Without a cache, every access would take about 100 ns, so the cache makes memory look about 16 times faster. Now improve the miss rate to 2%: AMAT = 1 + 0.02 x 100 = 3 ns. A small drop in miss rate halved the average time. This shows why architects fight for every percent of hit rate.

A second formula you will see in exams: Some textbooks write effective access time with hit ratio h, cache time Tc and memory time Tm. If the cache is checked first and memory is accessed only after a miss: T = h x Tc + (1 - h) x (Tc + Tm), which simplifies to Tc + (1 - h) x Tm, the same as AMAT. If cache and memory are accessed at the same time: T = h x Tc + (1 - h) x Tm. Example with h = 0.9, Tc = 10 ns, Tm = 100 ns: the first gives 10 + 0.1 x 100 = 20 ns; the second gives 9 + 10 = 19 ns. Always read which assumption the question makes.

Multi-level example: A processor has L1 with hit time 1 ns and miss rate 5%. Misses go to L2, which has hit time 10 ns and a local miss rate of 20%. L2 misses go to memory at 100 ns. First, L2's own average time = 10 + 0.20 x 100 = 30 ns. That is L1's miss penalty. So AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 30 = 2.5 ns. Without L2, it would be 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 ns. The second level more than halves the average.

Who manages each level: Registers are managed by the compiler, which decides which variables live in them. Caches are managed entirely by hardware; the programmer does not move data in or out directly. Main memory and disk are managed by the operating system together with hardware, through virtual memory. Each pair of adjacent levels works on the same principle: keep what is likely to be needed soon in the faster level.

When the hierarchy works well, and when it does not: It works well for programs with good locality: walking arrays in order, tight loops, reusing small working sets. It works badly for programs that jump randomly across huge amounts of data, such as following pointers through a giant linked structure, or for data used only once, like streaming a large video file, where caching gives little benefit. Programmers can help: in C, a 2-D array is stored row by row, so looping over rows in the outer loop and columns in the inner loop uses spatial locality, while the opposite order jumps across memory and can be several times slower for large arrays.

Real-life example 1, studying for an exam: On your table you keep the one book and notebook you are using now: that is like a register and L1 cache. On the bookshelf in your room are the other textbooks for this term: like main memory. The Nilkhet book market is like the hard disk: it has almost everything, but going there takes hours. You do not bring every book to the table, and you do not go to Nilkhet for every page. Because you keep reading the same chapter for a while (temporal locality) and read pages in order (spatial locality), the table serves you most of the time. Where the analogy breaks: when the computer fetches a block, it copies it; the data still exists in the lower level. When you take a book from the shelf, the shelf has one less book.

Real-life example 2, bKash servers and your phone: When you open the bKash app, your recent transactions appear quickly because the app keeps recent data on the phone, and the phone's processor keeps the app's active code and data in its caches. Data that is used often stays close; rarely used data stays far away, on the company's servers or storage. The same idea, keep hot data near and cold data far, repeats from the processor's L1 cache all the way to big data centers.

Common mistakes: Thinking cache is part of main memory or of the hard disk; it is a separate, faster memory between the CPU and main memory. Mixing up temporal locality (same item again, soon) and spatial locality (nearby items, soon). Forgetting that the miss penalty is added only for the fraction of accesses that miss, not all accesses. Using the wrong effective access time formula without checking whether access is sequential or simultaneous. Saying SRAM is used for main memory; it is used for caches, while DRAM is main memory.

What exams ask: Draw the memory hierarchy pyramid and explain the trends in speed, size and cost. Define temporal and spatial locality with code examples. Define hit, miss, hit ratio, hit time and miss penalty. Compute AMAT or effective access time for one and two cache levels. Compare SRAM and DRAM. Explain why a hierarchy gives the illusion of a large, fast memory.

Recap: Processors are far faster than main memory, and no single technology is big, fast and cheap. The memory hierarchy stacks registers, caches, main memory and storage, getting bigger, slower and cheaper going down. It works because programs show temporal and spatial locality, so most accesses hit in the fast levels. AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty tells how well it works. Next lesson opens the cache itself: how an address is split into tag, index and offset, and where a block is allowed to go.
key_points: The processor-memory gap: processors are far faster than DRAM main memory, so waiting on memory would waste most cycles.
Memory hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3 cache, main memory, SSD/disk; going down, levels get bigger, slower and cheaper per byte.
SRAM (about 6 transistors per bit, no refresh, fast) is used for caches; DRAM (1 transistor + 1 capacitor, needs refresh, dense) for main memory.
Temporal locality: recently used items are likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality: nearby addresses are likely to be used soon.
Data moves between cache and memory in blocks (lines), typically 64 bytes, to exploit spatial locality.
AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty; a small drop in miss rate can greatly reduce average access time.
With two levels, L1's miss penalty is L2's own average access time.
Compiler manages registers, hardware manages caches, the OS and hardware manage main memory and disk.
lessons.tip: In every AMAT problem, first write the formula, then fill numbers level by level from the bottom up (memory, then L2, then L1). Working bottom up avoids the most common mistake of mixing local and global miss rates.
lessons.task: Write a small table in your notebook of five storage places in your home or school (pocket, bag, desk drawer, shelf, school library) with how long it takes to get something from each and how much each can hold. Then note which things you keep in the closest places and why. Match each place to a level of the memory hierarchy.

quiz.q: Going down the memory hierarchy from registers to disk, what happens?
options: Faster, smaller, more expensive per byte
quiz.explain: Lower levels trade speed for capacity and low cost per byte.

quiz.q: A loop adds a[0], a[1], a[2] and so on. Accessing the array elements one after another is an example of what?
quiz.explain: Neighbouring addresses are used one after another, which is spatial locality.

quiz.q: Hit time 2 ns, miss rate 10%, miss penalty 50 ns. What is the AMAT?
Which memory technology is normally used for CPU caches?
quiz.explain: SRAM is fast and needs no refresh, so it suits small caches; DRAM is denser and used for main memory.

quiz.q: L1: hit time 1 ns, miss rate 10%. L2: hit time 8 ns, local miss rate 25%. Memory: 80 ns. What is the AMAT?
quiz.explain: L2 average = 8 + 0.25 x 80 = 28 ns, so AMAT = 1 + 0.10 x 28 = 3.8 ns.

lessons.title: Cache Memory I: Mapping
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother keeps a small basket of spices right next to the stove: salt, turmeric, chilli, cumin. The big stock of spices sits in a cupboard in another room. When she cooks, she grabs from the basket in one second. Only when something is missing does she walk to the cupboard, which takes much longer. Sooner or later the basket is full, and she has to decide two things: where in the basket does each spice go, and which old jar comes out to make room? The CPU cache works exactly like that basket, and this lesson is about the first question: where does each piece of memory go inside the cache.

What a cache is: A cache is a small, very fast memory, built from SRAM and placed on the processor chip, that keeps copies of the parts of main memory that the CPU used recently. Main memory (DRAM) might take around 50 to 100 nanoseconds to answer, while a level 1 cache answers in around one nanosecond or less, just a few clock cycles. When the CPU wants a byte, it checks the cache first. If the data is there, that is a hit. If not, that is a miss, and the data must be brought from the slower memory.

The problem it solves: In lesson 19 you saw the gap: processors got fast much quicker than DRAM did. A modern core can finish several instructions per nanosecond, but one trip to DRAM costs dozens of nanoseconds. Without a cache, the CPU would sit idle most of the time, waiting for memory, like a fast cook waiting for someone to bring each spice from the far cupboard. Thanks to locality (programs reuse the same data and touch nearby data), a small cache can catch most accesses, often well over 90 percent in typical programs.

Before caches: Early computers of the 1950s and 1960s had memory that was roughly as fast as the processor, so no cache was needed. As processors sped up, designers added caches. The IBM System/360 Model 85 in 1968 was one of the first commercial machines with a cache. Today every phone and laptop processor has several levels of cache on the chip.

Blocks, not bytes: The cache does not store single bytes. It stores fixed-size chunks called blocks (or lines), for example 64 bytes in most modern x86 and ARM processors. When you miss on one byte, the whole block containing it is copied in. Why? Spatial locality: if you just read array element a[0], you will very likely read a[1], a[2] next, and they arrive in the same block for free. Main memory is thought of as a long row of blocks numbered 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. Block number = byte address divided by block size (ignoring the remainder).

The central question: The cache has far fewer slots (lines) than memory has blocks. So many memory blocks must share the same cache slots. A mapping function decides which line or lines a memory block is allowed to sit in. There are three classic answers: direct mapped, fully associative and set associative. Each one trades speed and hardware cost against how often useful data gets kicked out.

How the cache knows what it holds: Each cache line stores three things: the data block itself, a tag, and a valid bit. The tag is the part of the address that tells which memory block is sitting in this line right now, because many blocks could have been put there. The valid bit says whether the line holds real data at all; at power-on all valid bits are 0. A hit means: the line is valid and its tag matches the tag of the address the CPU asked for.

Direct mapped cache: Each memory block can go into exactly one line. The rule is simple: line = block number mod number of lines. With 8 lines, block 3 goes to line 3, block 11 goes to line 11 mod 8 = 3, block 19 also goes to line 3. Think of a school with 8 lockers where your locker is your roll number mod 8. Very easy to find, but roll 3, 11 and 19 fight over the same locker.

Splitting the address: Because the number of lines and the block size are powers of 2, the hardware does not actually divide. It simply cuts the address bits into three fields: Tag | Index | Offset. The offset (lowest bits) picks the byte inside the block; with block size B bytes it needs log2(B) bits. The index (middle bits) picks the line; with L lines it needs log2(L) bits. The tag is everything left over at the top.

Worked example, tiny cache: Take an 8-bit address, a direct mapped cache with 8 lines and 4-byte blocks. Offset = log2(4) = 2 bits. Index = log2(8) = 3 bits. Tag = 8 - 3 - 2 = 3 bits. Now the CPU asks for address 45. In binary 45 = 00101101. Cut it: tag 001, index 011, offset 01. So the cache looks at line 3, checks if it is valid and if its stored tag is 001. If yes, hit, and it returns byte 1 of that block. Check with arithmetic: block number = 45 / 4 = 11, line = 11 mod 8 = 3, tag = 11 / 8 = 1. Same answer, the bit-cutting is just fast division.

Worked example, real size: A 32-bit address, a 64 KB direct mapped cache, 16-byte blocks. Offset = log2(16) = 4 bits. Number of lines = 65536 / 16 = 4096, so index = 12 bits. Tag = 32 - 12 - 4 = 16 bits. Exam questions love exactly this calculation. Always check that tag + index + offset equals the full address width.

The lookup step by step: Step 1, take the index bits and use them to select one line directly, like a decoder choosing a row. Step 2, read that line's valid bit and tag. Step 3, compare the stored tag with the address tag using one comparator. Step 4, if valid and equal, hit: use the offset to pick the byte and send it to the CPU. Step 5, if not, miss: fetch the whole block from memory, write it into this line, store the new tag, set valid to 1, then give the byte to the CPU. Picture: address -> [index picks line] -> [compare tag] -> hit? data : go to memory.

The weakness, conflict misses: Suppose a program keeps switching between address 0 and address 32 in our tiny cache. Address 0 is block 0, line 0. Address 32 is block 8, and 8 mod 8 = 0, line 0 again. Each access throws out the other block, so every single access misses, even though the other 7 lines sit empty. This is called thrashing. Direct mapping is cheap and fast, but it can waste space this way.

Fully associative cache: The opposite extreme. A block can go into any line. Now there is no index field at all; the address is just Tag | Offset. In our tiny example the tag becomes 8 - 2 = 6 bits. To find data, the hardware must compare the address tag with the tags of all lines at the same time, which needs one comparator per line. Think of a parking lot with no numbered spots: you can park anywhere, so the lot fills well, but to find your car you must check every spot. No conflict misses, best use of space, but expensive and slower, so fully associative designs are only used for small structures such as a TLB (lesson 23).

Set associative cache, the middle road: Group the lines into sets. A block maps to exactly one set (like direct mapping) but can sit in any line within that set (like associative). A cache with k lines per set is called k-way set associative. Set = block number mod number of sets. The address becomes Tag | Set index | Offset.

Worked example, 2-way: Take the same 8-line cache with 4-byte blocks, but make it 2-way. Then there are 8 / 2 = 4 sets, so set index = 2 bits, offset = 2 bits, tag = 8 - 2 - 2 = 4 bits. Address 45 = 0010 11 01: tag 0010, set 11 (set 3), offset 01. Check: block 11, set = 11 mod 4 = 3, tag = 11 / 4 = 2. The hardware compares the tag against the 2 lines of set 3 in parallel, needing just 2 comparators. Now addresses 0 and 32 (blocks 0 and 8) both go to set 0, but set 0 has two lines, so both fit and the thrashing stops.

One family, three members: Direct mapped is simply 1-way set associative. Fully associative is a single set containing all lines. So you can think of everything as set associative with a different number of ways. More ways means fewer conflict misses but more comparators, more power and a slightly slower hit. Real L1 caches are commonly 4-way to 12-way, chosen by measurement, not by rule.

Comparison in words: Direct mapped: 1 comparator, fastest and cheapest hit, most conflict misses. Set associative (k-way): k comparators, a good balance, the most common choice. Fully associative: one comparator per line, no conflict misses, costly, only for small caches. When a new block arrives in an associative or set associative cache, someone must choose which old line to replace; that is the replacement policy, the topic of lesson 21.

Real-life example 1, Dhaka University hall rooms: Imagine a hall where every student is given exactly one room by roll number mod number of rooms. That is direct mapping: the guard finds you instantly, but two friends with clashing rolls keep evicting each other. Now say each room has 2 beds and your roll decides only the room. That is 2-way set associative: still easy to find (go to one room, check two beds), and two clashing students can share. Fully associative would be: sleep in any bed anywhere, and the guard must search the whole hall at once to find you.

Real-life example 2, a program you write: Suppose you write a C program that adds two arrays a and b element by element, and by bad luck a and b start at addresses that are exactly a multiple of the cache size apart. In a direct mapped cache, a[i] and b[i] map to the same line, so reading a[i] kicks out b[i] and the other way round. The loop can run several times slower than expected. On a 2-way or 4-way cache the problem mostly vanishes. Programmers in high performance computing sometimes add a little padding between arrays to dodge exactly this.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the valid bit, which is needed because at start-up the tags contain garbage. Mixing up the number of lines and the number of sets when computing the index for a set associative cache; the index counts sets, not lines. Using bits instead of bytes for the block size. Forgetting that the offset counts bytes inside a block, so a 64-byte block needs 6 offset bits. Thinking that the cache is visible to the programmer; it is organization, not architecture, and a correct program gives the same answer with or without it, only slower.

What exams ask: Given address size, cache size, block size and associativity, find the number of tag, index and offset bits. Show which line or set an address maps to. Trace a sequence of addresses through a small cache and mark each hit or miss. Compare the three mappings with a diagram. Explain why set associative is a compromise. Also compute the total bits stored: each line holds data bits + tag bits + 1 valid bit (+ a dirty bit in write-back caches, lesson 21).

Quick recap: A cache keeps copies of recently used memory blocks close to the CPU. Each line holds a block, a tag and a valid bit. The address is cut into tag, index and offset. Direct mapped: one place per block, cheap but conflict-prone. Fully associative: anywhere, no conflicts, expensive. Set associative: one set, any way inside it, the practical winner. Next lesson: what to throw out, how to handle writes, and how to measure cache performance.
key_points: A cache is a small fast SRAM memory that keeps copies of recently used memory blocks near the CPU.
Data moves between memory and cache in blocks (lines), commonly 64 bytes, to exploit spatial locality.
Each cache line stores data, a tag and a valid bit; a hit means valid and tag match.
The address is split into tag, index and offset: offset = log2(block size), index = log2(number of lines or sets).
Direct mapped: line = block mod lines; cheap and fast but suffers conflict misses (thrashing).
Fully associative: block can go anywhere, needs one comparator per line, no conflict misses, used for small structures.
k-way set associative: set = block mod sets, block can use any of k lines in the set; the common practical choice.
Direct mapped is 1-way set associative; fully associative is one set holding all lines.
lessons.tip: For every cache question, first write three numbers: offset bits, index bits, tag bits, and check they add up to the address width. Most marks are lost by skipping this one line.
lessons.task: On paper, draw an 8-line direct mapped cache with 4-byte blocks and 8-bit addresses. Trace this address sequence and mark hit or miss: 0, 4, 32, 0, 45, 47, 32. Then redo it for a 2-way set associative cache with 4 sets and see which misses disappear.

quiz.q: A direct mapped cache has 4096 lines and 16-byte blocks, with 32-bit addresses. How many tag bits?
quiz.explain: Offset = 4 bits, index = 12 bits, tag = 32 - 12 - 4 = 16 bits.

quiz.q: Why does the cache store a tag in each line?
options: To identify which memory block is currently in that line
To count how many times the line was used
To mark the line as empty
quiz.explain: Many blocks map to the same line or set, so the tag records which one is there now. The valid bit marks empty lines.

quiz.q: In a direct mapped cache with 8 lines, addresses 0 and 32 (4-byte blocks) are accessed alternately. What happens?
options: The cache uses LRU to keep both
Every access misses because both map to line 0
quiz.explain: Block 0 and block 8 both give line 0 (8 mod 8 = 0), so they keep evicting each other: thrashing.

quiz.q: Which statement about a fully associative cache is true?
options: It has the largest index field
A block can be placed in any line, so the tag is compared with all lines
It is the most common design for large L3 caches
quiz.explain: There is no index; every line's tag is checked in parallel, needing one comparator per line, which is why it is used for small structures.

quiz.q: An 8-line, 2-way set associative cache has how many sets?
quiz.explain: Sets = lines / ways = 8 / 2 = 4, so the set index needs 2 bits.

lessons.title: Cache Memory II: Policies and Performance
lessons.content:
Go back to your mother's spice basket from last lesson. We decided where each spice is allowed to sit. Now three new questions show up. When the basket is full and a new spice must come in, which old jar goes back to the cupboard? If she adds more salt to the jar in the basket, does she also run and update the big jar in the cupboard right away, or later? And how do we measure whether the basket is actually saving her time? These are the three questions of this lesson: replacement, writing, and performance.

What a cache policy is: A policy is a fixed rule the cache hardware follows automatically, with no help from the program. The replacement policy chooses which line to throw out on a miss. The write policy decides when a changed value is copied back to main memory. The allocation policy decides whether a write miss brings the block into the cache. Together with mapping (lesson 20), these rules decide how well a cache performs.

When replacement is needed: In a direct mapped cache there is no choice at all; the block has exactly one possible line, so whatever is there goes out. In a set associative or fully associative cache, the new block could go into any of several lines of its set. If one of them is invalid (empty), use it. If all are full, the replacement policy picks a victim.

The ideal but impossible policy: The best victim is the block that will not be needed for the longest time in the future. This is called the optimal (or Belady's) policy. A real cache cannot see the future, so it cannot use it, but it is useful in exams and research as a benchmark: no real policy can beat it.

LRU, least recently used: Throw out the block that has gone unused for the longest time. The idea comes from temporal locality: if you have not touched something for a while, you probably will not touch it soon. For a 2-way set, LRU needs just one bit per set saying which way was used last. For more ways it gets expensive to track exact order, so many real caches use pseudo-LRU, a cheaper approximation.

FIFO and random: FIFO (first in, first out) throws out the block that entered the set earliest, no matter how often it was used since. It is simple, like a queue. Random picks any line. It sounds silly, but it needs almost no hardware, and for caches with many ways its miss rate is often not much worse than LRU. Some real processors have used random or pseudo-random replacement for exactly that reason.

Worked trace, LRU vs FIFO: Take one 2-way set and this block sequence: A, B, A, C, B. With LRU: A miss, B miss, A hit (now B is least recent), C miss and evicts B, B miss and evicts A (A is now least recent). Total 4 misses. With FIFO: A miss, B miss, A hit (order of entry is still A then B), C miss and evicts A (it came in first), B hit. Total 3 misses. So FIFO won this short sequence. Lesson: no practical policy is best for every pattern; LRU usually wins on real programs, but not always.

The write problem: Reading is easy because the cache copy and the memory copy are the same. But when the CPU writes, say x = x + 1, the cache copy changes. Now memory holds an old value. If nobody fixes this, a DMA device or another core reading memory would see a stale value. Two main strategies handle this.

Write-through: Every write updates both the cache and main memory at the same time. Memory is always up to date, which is simple and safe. The cost: every store goes to slow memory. If a loop increments a counter 1,000 times, memory is written 1,000 times. To hide this, processors add a write buffer: a small queue where stores wait while the CPU continues. The CPU stalls only if the buffer is full.

Write-back: Writes update only the cache. Each line gets an extra dirty bit, set to 1 when the line is modified. Memory is updated only when a dirty line is evicted. In the counter example, memory is written only once, when that line finally leaves the cache. This saves a lot of memory traffic, which is why most modern L1, L2 and L3 caches are write-back. The cost: more complex hardware, and a miss that evicts a dirty line needs two memory transfers (write the old block out, read the new one in).

Write miss policies: What if the CPU writes to an address that is not in the cache? Write allocate: first bring the block into the cache, then write it there, hoping more writes nearby will follow. No-write-allocate (write around): write straight to memory and do not load the block. The usual pairing is write-back with write allocate, and write-through with no-write-allocate.

Why misses happen, the 3 Cs: Compulsory (cold) misses: the very first access to a block always misses, because it was never loaded. Bigger blocks reduce these. Capacity misses: the program's working data is simply bigger than the cache, so blocks get thrown out and needed again. Only a bigger cache helps. Conflict misses: in direct mapped or set associative caches, too many blocks fight over the same set even though other sets have room. More associativity helps. In multicore systems a fourth C appears, coherence misses, covered in lesson 25.

Measuring performance, hit rate and miss rate: Hit rate = hits / total accesses. Miss rate = 1 - hit rate. If a program makes 1,000 memory accesses and 950 hit, the hit rate is 95 percent and the miss rate is 5 percent. Hit time is how long a hit takes. Miss penalty is the extra time to fetch the block from the next level.

AMAT, the key formula: Average Memory Access Time = Hit time + Miss rate x Miss penalty. Example: hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 5 percent, miss penalty 100 cycles. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 cycles. Notice the shock: a 5 percent miss rate made memory six times slower on average than a perfect cache. That is why designers fight for every percent.

Multilevel caches: One cache cannot be both tiny-fast and huge. So processors stack levels: a small L1 (tens of KB, a few cycles), a bigger L2 (hundreds of KB to a few MB), and often a large shared L3 (several MB to tens of MB). A miss in L1 goes to L2, then L3, then DRAM. Picture: CPU -> L1 -> L2 -> L3 -> DRAM, each step bigger and slower.

Worked example, two levels: L1 hit time 1 cycle, L1 miss rate 5 percent. L2 hit time 10 cycles, L2 local miss rate 20 percent (of the accesses that reach it). Memory penalty 100 cycles. L1 miss penalty = 10 + 0.2 x 100 = 30 cycles. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 30 = 2.5 cycles. Without L2 it would be 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 cycles. The L2 more than halved the average time. The global miss rate of L2 is 0.05 x 0.2 = 1 percent: only 1 in 100 accesses goes all the way to DRAM.

Effect on CPI: Memory stalls add to the cycles per instruction. Stall cycles per instruction = memory accesses per instruction x miss rate x miss penalty. Say the base CPI is 1, each instruction makes 1.3 memory accesses on average (1 instruction fetch plus 0.3 data accesses), the miss rate is 2 percent and the penalty is 100 cycles. Stalls = 1.3 x 0.02 x 100 = 2.6. Real CPI = 1 + 2.6 = 3.6. The processor runs at less than a third of its ideal speed because of memory. This links directly to the CPU time equation from lesson 3.

Trade-offs to remember: Bigger cache: fewer capacity misses, but slower hit time, more area and power. Bigger block: fewer compulsory misses thanks to spatial locality, but a larger miss penalty, and if too big, fewer blocks fit, so conflict misses can rise. More associativity: fewer conflict misses, but slower and costlier lookup. There is no free lunch; real designs are tuned by running benchmarks.

Real-life example 1, the bKash agent's cash drawer: A bKash agent in a Mohammadpur shop keeps some cash in a drawer and the rest in a bank. Each cash-in or cash-out is a write to the drawer. Write-through would be walking to the bank after every single transaction to update the bank balance: always correct, but painfully slow. Write-back is keeping a notebook of drawer changes and settling with the bank only at closing time, or when the drawer must be swapped: much faster, but if the shop catches fire before settlement, the bank's record is out of date. That is the exact risk write-back hardware must manage with dirty bits.

Real-life example 2, why loop order matters: In C, a 2D array is stored row by row. Summing a 1000 x 1000 int array with for i, for j, a[i][j] walks memory in order: with 64-byte blocks, one miss loads 16 ints, so roughly 1 miss per 16 accesses. Swapping the loops to a[j][i] jumps 4,000 bytes each step, so almost every access touches a new block, and if the rows do not fit in the cache, nearly every access misses. The same answer, often several times slower. This is compulsory and capacity behaviour you can see with a stopwatch.

Common mistakes: Using the global miss rate where the formula needs the local one, or the other way round. Forgetting that write-back needs a dirty bit and that evicting a dirty line costs an extra write. Thinking LRU is always optimal; it is not, the optimal policy needs the future. Saying a bigger block always helps; past a point it hurts. Forgetting to multiply by memory accesses per instruction when finding CPI.

What exams ask: Compute AMAT for one or two levels. Compute effective CPI with cache stalls. Trace LRU and FIFO on a sequence and count misses. Compare write-through and write-back in a table. Classify misses into the 3 Cs and say which design change reduces each. Explain the role of the dirty bit and the write buffer.

Quick recap: On a miss in an associative set, a replacement policy (LRU, FIFO, random) picks the victim. Write-through keeps memory current at the cost of traffic; write-back saves traffic with a dirty bit. Misses come from the 3 Cs. AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty, and multilevel caches cut the penalty. Next lesson we go below the cache to main memory itself: how DRAM chips are built and organized.
key_points: Replacement policies choose the victim in a full set: LRU, FIFO, random; the optimal (Belady) policy needs the future.
No practical policy is best for every access pattern; LRU usually does well on real programs.
Write-through updates memory on every write (often with a write buffer); write-back updates memory only when a dirty line is evicted.
Write allocate loads the block on a write miss; no-write-allocate writes straight to memory.
The 3 Cs of misses: compulsory, capacity and conflict (plus coherence in multicores).
AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty; e.g. 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 cycles.
Multilevel caches (L1, L2, L3) reduce the miss penalty seen by L1.
Memory stall cycles per instruction = accesses per instruction x miss rate x miss penalty, added to base CPI.
lessons.tip: Write the AMAT formula at the top of your page before any cache numerical, and for two levels plug L2's AMAT in as L1's miss penalty. That one substitution solves most multilevel questions.
lessons.task: Trace LRU and FIFO for a single 3-way set with the sequence A, B, C, A, D, B, A, E and count misses for each. Then compute AMAT for hit time 2 cycles, miss rate 4 percent and miss penalty 80 cycles.

quiz.q: Hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 10 percent, miss penalty 50 cycles. What is AMAT?
quiz.explain: AMAT = 1 + 0.1 x 50 = 6 cycles.

quiz.q: What is the dirty bit used for?
options: Marking a line modified so it is written back to memory on eviction
quiz.explain: In a write-back cache only dirty lines need to be copied to memory when they are evicted.

quiz.q: A program's data is larger than the whole cache, so blocks are evicted and needed again. What kind of miss is this?
quiz.explain: Capacity misses happen because the cache is simply too small for the working set; only a bigger cache helps.

quiz.q: Which pairing of policies is the usual one?
quiz.explain: Write-back usually pairs with write allocate, and write-through usually pairs with no-write-allocate.

quiz.q: Base CPI 1, 1.5 memory accesses per instruction, miss rate 2 percent, penalty 100 cycles. Real CPI?

lessons.title: Main Memory Organisation
lessons.content:
Think of the exam hall at your school during SSC. Hundreds of students sit in neat rows and columns, and every seat has a number like row 12, column 7. When the invigilator needs a particular student, he does not search the whole hall. He walks to row 12, then looks along that row to column 7. Main memory, the RAM in your phone or laptop, is organised in almost exactly this way: billions of tiny storage cells arranged in rows and columns, and an address that tells the hardware which row and which column to open. This lesson opens the RAM chip and shows how it is built, why it needs constant refreshing, and how many small chips are joined into one big memory.

What main memory is: Main memory is the large working memory that holds the programs and data currently in use. The CPU can read or write any byte of it directly by giving an address, which is why it is called random access memory: any location takes about the same time, unlike a tape where you must wind to the spot. In almost every computer today, main memory is built from DRAM, dynamic RAM. It sits below the caches in the hierarchy: much bigger than cache (gigabytes instead of megabytes) but much slower (tens of nanoseconds instead of about one).

The problem: A computer needs a lot of memory, and it must be cheap per bit, otherwise a laptop with 16 GB would cost a fortune. The fast memory used in caches, SRAM, needs six transistors for every single bit. That makes it big and expensive. Designers needed a memory cell that is tiny, so that billions of them fit on one chip. DRAM is the answer, and its smallness comes with a strange side effect that we will meet soon: it forgets.

Before DRAM: In the 1950s and 1960s, main memory was magnetic core memory: tiny rings of magnetic material threaded on wires by hand, each ring storing one bit by its direction of magnetisation. It kept data without power but was bulky and costly. In 1970 Intel released the 1103, one of the first commercially successful DRAM chips, and within a few years semiconductor DRAM replaced core memory almost everywhere.

The DRAM cell: One DRAM bit is just one transistor and one tiny capacitor (1T1C). The capacitor is a little bucket of electric charge: charged means 1, empty means 0. The transistor is a gate that connects the capacitor to a wire called the bit line when the row's word line is switched on. Because the cell is so simple, DRAM packs far more bits into the same area than SRAM. Picture: word line -> [transistor gate] -> capacitor stores charge, bit line carries it out.

Why it is called dynamic, refresh: The capacitor is not perfect; its charge slowly leaks away, in milliseconds. If nothing is done, a 1 would fade into a 0. So the memory controller must refresh every row regularly: read it and write it back at full strength. The common standard requires every row to be refreshed within 64 milliseconds. During refresh that part of the memory cannot serve normal requests, which costs a small slice of time. SRAM, by contrast, is static: as long as power is on, its cross-coupled transistors hold the bit firmly and need no refresh.

Reading destroys the data: When a DRAM row is read, the tiny charges of the whole row flow onto the bit lines, where sense amplifiers detect whether each one was a 1 or a 0 and amplify it. Taking the charge out drains the capacitors, so the sense amplifiers immediately write the values back. This row of sense amplifiers holding the whole open row is called the row buffer.

Rows and columns inside the chip: The cells form a big two-dimensional array. To read a bit, the chip first activates one row (the whole row goes into the row buffer), then picks one column from the row buffer. The address is split into a row address and a column address. To save pins on the chip package, the same address pins are used twice: first the row address is sent with a signal called RAS (row address strobe), then the column address with CAS (column address strobe). This is called address multiplexing. A chip with 2^20 cells arranged as 1024 x 1024 needs 20 address bits, but only 10 address pins.

Row buffer hits: Opening a row is slow; reading another column from an already open row is fast. So if a program reads addresses that lie in the same row one after another, the memory answers quicker. That is one more reason why sequential access, like walking an array in order, beats jumping around. Memory controllers even reorder requests to group ones that hit the open row.

SRAM vs DRAM side by side: SRAM: about six transistors per bit, no refresh, very fast, expensive, low density, used for caches and registers. DRAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit, needs refresh, slower, cheap, high density, used for main memory. Both are volatile: they lose everything when power goes. That is why your unsaved Word file disappears during a load-shedding power cut if the laptop battery is dead.

Chip size notation: A memory chip is described as words x bits per word. A 1K x 8 chip holds 1024 words of 8 bits each, so it needs 10 address lines (2^10 = 1024) and 8 data lines. A 64K x 1 chip holds 65,536 single bits, needing 16 address lines and 1 data line. Total bits = words x width.

Building wider memory: Suppose you need 1K x 16 but only have 1K x 8 chips. Put two chips side by side. Both receive the same 10 address lines and the same chip select. One chip supplies data bits 0 to 7, the other bits 8 to 15. Together they behave like one 16-bit-wide memory. This is width (word size) expansion.

Building deeper memory: Now suppose you need 4K x 8 from 1K x 8 chips. You need 4 chips stacked, each covering 1K addresses. 4K needs 12 address lines. The lower 10 lines (A0 to A9) go to every chip to pick a word inside it. The upper 2 lines (A10, A11) go into a 2-to-4 decoder, whose four outputs drive the chip select of the four chips. So addresses 0 to 1023 hit chip 0, 1024 to 2047 hit chip 1, and so on. Only the selected chip responds; the others keep their data outputs disconnected (high impedance). This is depth (address) expansion, and it uses the decoder from Digital Logic Design.

Worked example, both together: Build 8K x 16 from 2K x 8 chips. Number of chips = (8K / 2K) x (16 / 8) = 4 x 2 = 8 chips, arranged as 4 rows of 2. Total address lines = 13 (2^13 = 8192). Each chip needs 11 (2^11 = 2048), so A0 to A10 go to all chips. The remaining 2 lines, A11 and A12, feed a 2-to-4 decoder that selects one row of two chips. This exact pattern is a favourite exam question.

Interleaving: One DRAM bank is busy for a while after each access. If consecutive addresses all live in the same bank, the CPU waits each time. Interleaving spreads consecutive addresses across several banks. With 4-way low-order interleaving, the lowest 2 bits of the word address choose the bank: address 0 goes to bank 0, 1 to bank 1, 2 to bank 2, 3 to bank 3, 4 back to bank 0. Now four sequential accesses can overlap in time, like four bank counters serving four customers at once. High-order interleaving instead gives each bank a big contiguous range; it is simpler to expand but does not speed up sequential access.

Synchronous DRAM and DDR: Older DRAM worked asynchronously, responding whenever signals changed. SDRAM is synchronised to a clock, so the controller can pipeline requests. DDR SDRAM (double data rate) transfers data on both the rising and the falling edge of the clock, giving two transfers per clock cycle. Later generations (DDR2, DDR3, DDR4, DDR5) raised speeds further. Bandwidth example: DDR4-3200 performs 3200 million transfers per second; on a standard 64-bit (8-byte) channel that is 3200 x 8 = 25,600 MB/s, about 25.6 GB/s.

Latency vs bandwidth: Latency is how long the first byte takes to arrive. Bandwidth is how many bytes per second flow once data starts coming. A wide motorway (bandwidth) does not make Gabtoli to Motijheel shorter (latency). DRAM bandwidth has grown a lot over the years, but latency in nanoseconds has improved slowly, which is why caches remain so important.

ROM types in brief: Not all main memory is RAM. ROM (read-only memory) keeps data without power and holds things like boot firmware. Mask ROM is written at the factory. PROM can be programmed once by the user. EPROM can be erased with ultraviolet light and reprogrammed. EEPROM can be erased electrically, byte by byte. Flash memory is a kind of EEPROM erased in large blocks; it is what your phone's storage and USB pen drives use.

Real-life example 1, a laptop RAM upgrade at Elephant Road: A shopkeeper tells you your laptop has one 8 GB DDR4 stick and one empty slot, and suggests adding another identical stick. Two sticks in two channels let the memory controller use both channels at once, roughly doubling peak bandwidth (dual channel), on top of doubling capacity. Matching type and speed matters: a DDR5 stick physically will not fit a DDR4 slot, and mixing speeds usually makes both run at the slower one.

Real-life example 2, Kamalapur ticket counters: Imagine only one ticket counter at Kamalapur railway station, where after each ticket the clerk needs a moment to file papers. A long queue forms. Open four counters and send passenger 1 to counter A, passenger 2 to B, passenger 3 to C, passenger 4 to D, then 5 back to A. While A files papers, B, C and D are already serving. That is low-order interleaving: the work of each bank overlaps with the others. Where the analogy breaks: real banks share one data bus, so their results still leave one after another, just with no waiting between them.

Common mistakes: Saying DRAM needs refresh because reading destroys data; the main reason is leakage, and reading is restored at once by the sense amplifiers. Forgetting that ROM is also random access. Confusing chip count formulas: chips = (total words / chip words) x (total width / chip width). Forgetting the decoder inputs are the high address bits, not the low ones. Thinking DDR doubles the clock frequency; it uses both clock edges.

What exams ask: Compare SRAM and DRAM. Explain refresh and why DRAM is called dynamic. Design an M x N memory from smaller chips, giving number of chips, address lines and a decoder diagram. Explain interleaving with a table of addresses and banks. Calculate DDR bandwidth. List ROM types with how they are erased.

Quick recap: Main memory is DRAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit, cheap and dense, but leaky, so it needs refresh. Cells sit in rows and columns, addressed with RAS then CAS, with a row buffer that makes same-row reads fast. Bigger memories are built from chips by width and depth expansion with a decoder. Interleaving overlaps bank accesses, and DDR moves data on both clock edges. Next lesson: how the operating system and hardware together pretend every program has its own huge memory, virtual memory.
key_points: Main memory is built from DRAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit, cheap and dense.
DRAM charge leaks, so every row must be refreshed regularly (commonly within 64 ms); SRAM needs no refresh.
DRAM cells form rows and columns; the row address (RAS) and column address (CAS) share pins via address multiplexing.
Reading a row is destructive and is restored by the sense amplifiers in the row buffer; same-row accesses are faster.
Chip notation words x width; chips needed = (total words / chip words) x (total width / chip width).
Depth expansion uses the high address bits into a decoder to drive chip select; width expansion places chips side by side.
Low-order interleaving spreads consecutive addresses across banks so accesses overlap.
DDR SDRAM transfers on both clock edges; DDR4-3200 on a 64-bit channel gives about 25.6 GB/s.
lessons.tip: For memory design questions, always write three lines first: chips needed, total address lines, address lines per chip. The difference between the last two is the number of decoder inputs.
lessons.task: On paper, design a 16K x 8 memory using 4K x 4 chips. Find the number of chips, total address lines, which lines go to every chip, and the size of the decoder. Draw the chips in a grid with the decoder on the left.

quiz.q: Why does DRAM need refresh?
options: Its transistors wear out after each read
The CPU clock is too fast
quiz.explain: The stored charge leaks away in milliseconds, so rows must be read and rewritten regularly.

quiz.q: How many 2K x 8 chips are needed to build an 8K x 16 memory?
Building 4K x 8 from 1K x 8 chips, what drives the 2-to-4 decoder?
quiz.explain: The lower 10 lines select a word inside each chip; the top 2 lines select which chip.

quiz.q: In 4-way low-order interleaving, which bank holds word address 6?
quiz.explain: Bank = address mod 4 = 6 mod 4 = 2.

quiz.q: What does DDR (double data rate) mean?
options: Data is transferred on both the rising and falling clock edges
quiz.explain: DDR transfers data twice per clock cycle, once on each edge.

lessons.title: Virtual Memory
lessons.content:
Imagine a big apartment building in Dhanmondi where every flat owner is told, 'Your flat number is 1A.' Every single family believes they live in flat 1A. Their letters say 1A, their guests ask for 1A. But the guard at the gate holds a secret notebook: the Rahman family's 1A is really the third floor east side, the Chowdhury family's 1A is really the seventh floor west side. Nobody gets confused, nobody enters another family's flat, and the guard can even move a family's furniture to the storeroom while they are away. That notebook trick is virtual memory, and it is how your phone runs dozens of apps at once, each one believing it owns the whole memory.

What virtual memory is: Virtual memory is a technique where each program uses its own set of addresses, called virtual addresses, and the hardware together with the operating system translates them into real physical addresses in RAM. The program never sees physical addresses. Some of its data may not even be in RAM at the moment; it may be waiting on the disk or flash storage, and it is brought in only when needed.

The problems it solves: First, size. Programs together often want more memory than the RAM has. Second, sharing. Many programs run at the same time, and each one was compiled as if it starts at address 0; they cannot all really live at address 0. Third, safety. One buggy or malicious program must not be able to read or overwrite another program's memory, such as your banking app's data. Virtual memory solves all three at once.

Before virtual memory: Programmers had to fit programs into physical memory themselves. When a program was too big, they used overlays: they split the program into pieces by hand and wrote code to load one piece over another when needed. It was tedious and error-prone. The Atlas computer at the University of Manchester, around 1962, was the first to do this automatically with paging, letting programmers treat a small fast memory plus a drum store as one big memory.

Pages and frames: Virtual memory divides the virtual address space into fixed-size chunks called pages, and physical memory into chunks of the same size called frames. A common page size is 4 KB (4096 bytes). Any page can be placed in any free frame. Because all pieces are the same size, there are no awkward gaps, just like a parking lot where every car is the same size and fits any slot.

Splitting the virtual address: Since the page size is a power of two, a virtual address splits cleanly into two fields: Virtual Page Number (VPN) | Page Offset. With 4 KB pages the offset is log2(4096) = 12 bits. With a 32-bit virtual address the VPN is 32 - 12 = 20 bits, so there are 2^20, about one million, virtual pages. The offset never changes during translation; only the page number gets replaced by a frame number.

The page table: For each process, the operating system keeps a page table in memory: one entry per virtual page. A page table entry (PTE) holds a valid (present) bit saying whether the page is in RAM, the physical frame number if it is, and extra bits: a dirty bit (the page was modified), a reference bit (it was used recently), and protection bits (readable, writable, executable, user or kernel only). A special CPU register, the page table base register, points to the current process's table. Switching processes means just switching this register.

Translation step by step: Step 1, the CPU produces a virtual address, say 0x00003ABC. Step 2, split it: VPN = 0x00003, offset = 0xABC. Step 3, look up entry 3 in the page table. Step 4, if valid, read the frame number, say 7. Step 5, glue frame number and offset together: physical address = 0x7ABC. Step 6, check the protection bits; if the program tries to write a read-only page, raise an exception. Picture: virtual address -> [VPN | offset] -> page table[VPN] -> [frame | offset] -> physical memory. The hardware that does this is the memory management unit, the MMU.

Page faults: If the valid bit is 0, the page is not in RAM. The MMU raises a page fault, an exception that hands control to the operating system. The OS finds the page on disk, picks a free frame (or frees one by evicting another page, writing it back first if it is dirty), loads the page, updates the page table entry, and restarts the instruction that faulted. The program never knows anything happened, except that it was slow. And slow it is: a disk or flash access takes microseconds to milliseconds, compared with tens of nanoseconds for RAM, which is why page faults must be rare.

Which page to evict: The ideas are the same as cache replacement in lesson 21: optimal (needs the future), FIFO, LRU. Because exact LRU is costly, operating systems use approximations based on the reference bit, such as the clock algorithm, which sweeps around the frames like a clock hand giving each recently used page a second chance. A curious fact: with FIFO, giving a program more frames can sometimes cause more faults, which is called Belady's anomaly. LRU never shows this anomaly. The Operating Systems course studies these algorithms in depth.

The size problem of page tables: In our 32-bit example, one million entries of 4 bytes each make a 4 MB page table for every process. Most of it is empty, because a program uses only a small part of its address space. The usual fix is a multilevel (hierarchical) page table: split the VPN into two parts, say 10 bits + 10 bits. The first part indexes a small top-level table whose entries point to second-level tables, and second-level tables are created only for regions actually in use. 64-bit processors use four or more levels.

The speed problem and the TLB: Look carefully: every memory access now needs a page table lookup, which itself is a memory access. With multilevel tables, it is several. That could make every load several times slower. The fix is the translation lookaside buffer, TLB: a small, fast cache that stores recent VPN-to-frame translations. It is usually highly associative and holds tens to a few thousand entries. Thanks to locality, most accesses hit in the TLB, often well over 99 percent, and then no page table walk is needed at all.

TLB worked example: Suppose a memory access takes 100 ns, a single-level page table is used, the TLB lookup time is small enough to ignore, and the TLB hit rate is 98 percent. TLB hit: 100 ns (just the data access). TLB miss: 100 ns to read the page table + 100 ns for the data = 200 ns. Effective access time = 0.98 x 100 + 0.02 x 200 = 98 + 4 = 102 ns. Without a TLB every access would cost 200 ns. The TLB hides almost the entire translation cost.

Protection and sharing: Since each process has its own page table, process A simply has no entry that points to process B's frames, so it cannot touch them. When a program uses a bad pointer to an unmapped page, the result is the familiar segmentation fault or access violation, which kills that program but keeps the rest of the system safe. The reverse is also useful: two processes can map the same physical frame on purpose, for example to share the code of a common library, saving RAM.

When virtual memory helps most: Running many programs safely at once, running a program larger than free RAM, loading programs quickly (pages come in only when touched, called demand paging), and sharing libraries. When it hurts or is avoided: in tiny microcontrollers, like the one in a washing machine, there is often no MMU at all because the hardware cost and unpredictable timing are not worth it. Hard real-time systems also avoid page faults because a sudden millisecond delay can break deadlines.

Thrashing: If programs together actively use more pages than fit in RAM, the system spends most of its time moving pages between RAM and disk and very little time doing useful work. This is thrashing. You have seen it on an old laptop with 4 GB RAM and twenty Chrome tabs: the disk light stays on and everything freezes. The cure is more RAM or fewer running programs, not a faster CPU.

Paging compared with caching: Both ideas keep a small fast copy of a big slow store and both rely on locality, but the details differ. A cache block is tens of bytes; a page is kilobytes. A cache miss costs tens to hundreds of cycles and is handled fully by hardware; a page fault costs millions of cycles and is handled by operating system software. Caches usually have limited associativity; a page can go into any free frame, so paging is fully associative, which is affordable because the OS has plenty of time to choose a victim. Caches are invisible to the OS; paging is a joint job of the MMU hardware and the OS.

Real-life example 1, a cheap Android phone: A 3 GB RAM phone keeps WhatsApp, Facebook, Daraz and the camera open. Each app has its own virtual address space and page table. When memory runs low, Android does not keep all of them in RAM; it reclaims pages and may kill background apps. That is why when you switch back to Facebook it sometimes reloads from the start. Code pages can always be re-read from storage, which is what makes this cheap.

Real-life example 2, the hall seat plan: During a university admission test at Dhaka University, thousands of candidates have a roll number (virtual address). The seat plan on the notice board (page table) maps each roll range to a real building and room (frame). Candidates never need to know the building layout, and two candidates can never be given the same seat. If a room is under repair, the board just maps that roll range to another room. Where the analogy breaks: the seat plan is printed once, while a page table changes all the time as pages come and go.

Common mistakes: Mixing up pages (virtual) and frames (physical). Thinking the offset is translated; it is copied unchanged. Thinking a page fault is an error; it is a normal event handled by the OS, and only an access to an invalid address becomes a crash. Confusing the TLB with the data cache: the TLB caches translations, the data cache caches data. Forgetting that the page table itself lives in main memory.

What exams ask: Given address size and page size, find offset bits, number of pages, and page table size. Translate a virtual address to a physical one using a given page table. Explain the steps of handling a page fault. Compute effective access time with a TLB. Compare paging with caching. Explain why multilevel page tables save memory. Define thrashing and demand paging.

Quick recap: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, translated page by page into physical frames by the MMU using a page table. Missing pages cause page faults that the OS fixes by loading from storage. Multilevel tables save space, and the TLB makes translation fast. Protection bits keep processes apart. Next lesson we leave memory and look at how the CPU talks to the outside world: input and output.
key_points: Virtual memory gives each process its own virtual addresses, translated to physical addresses by the MMU and OS.
Virtual space is split into pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, commonly 4 KB.
A virtual address is VPN + offset; only the VPN is translated to a frame number, the offset is copied.
Page table entries hold a valid bit, frame number, dirty, reference and protection bits.
A page fault occurs when the page is not in RAM; the OS loads it from storage and restarts the instruction.
Multilevel page tables avoid huge tables by creating lower levels only for used regions.
The TLB caches recent translations; e.g. 0.98 x 100 + 0.02 x 200 = 102 ns effective access time.
Thrashing happens when active pages do not fit in RAM; the fix is more RAM or fewer programs.
lessons.tip: In every virtual memory numerical, first write the address as two boxes, VPN and offset, with their bit widths. Translation is then just replacing the left box.
lessons.task: With 16-bit virtual addresses and 1 KB pages, find the offset bits and number of pages. Then make a small page table on paper (VPN 0 -> frame 5, VPN 1 -> invalid, VPN 2 -> frame 1) and translate 0x0412 and 0x0820 to physical addresses, saying which one causes a page fault.

quiz.q: With 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages, how many bits is the VPN?
quiz.explain: Offset = 12 bits, so VPN = 32 - 12 = 20 bits.

quiz.q: Which part of the virtual address is copied unchanged into the physical address?
quiz.explain: Translation replaces only the page number with a frame number; the offset stays the same.

quiz.q: What does the TLB store?
quiz.explain: The TLB is a small cache of translations, so most accesses skip the page table walk.

quiz.q: Memory access 100 ns, TLB hit rate 90 percent, single-level page table, TLB time ignored. Effective access time?
What happens on a page fault for a valid page that is on disk?
options: The OS loads the page into a frame, updates the page table and restarts the instruction
quiz.explain: A page fault is a normal OS-handled event; only invalid addresses lead to a crash.

lessons.title: Input/Output Organisation
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy head teacher in her office. Students knock with problems, the peon brings files, parents call on the phone, the printer next door finishes printing exam papers. If she walked out every ten seconds to check every door, phone and printer, she would never finish her own work. If she never checked at all, she would miss urgent things. And for a big job, like moving 500 answer scripts from one room to another, she should not carry them herself; she should tell a helper to do it and just inform her when done. These three choices, check repeatedly, get interrupted, or hand the job to a helper, are exactly the three ways a CPU handles input and output.

What I/O is: Input/output (I/O) is everything that moves data between the computer's CPU and memory on one side and the outside world on the other: keyboards, touch screens, displays, storage drives, network cards, cameras, sensors and so on. I/O organisation studies how these devices are connected, how the CPU addresses them, and how data transfers are controlled so that the CPU is not wasted.

The problem: Devices are wildly different. A keyboard produces maybe ten bytes per second when you type fast. A modern SSD can move billions of bytes per second. Some devices are electrical, some mechanical, they use different voltages, signals and timing, and almost all of them are far slower than the CPU. The CPU cannot be redesigned for each one. So designers need a standard way to connect devices, a standard way to talk to them, and methods that do not make a nanosecond-fast CPU wait for a millisecond-slow device.

Buses, the shared roads: A bus is a set of shared wires that connects components. A system bus has three groups of lines. Address lines carry the address of the memory location or device register being accessed. Data lines carry the actual data, in either direction. Control lines carry commands and status, such as read, write, clock, interrupt request and acknowledge. Picture: CPU <-> [address | data | control] <-> Memory and I/O interfaces. The number of data lines (the width) decides how many bits move at once; the number of address lines decides how many locations can be addressed: 32 address lines give 2^32 addresses.

Synchronous vs asynchronous buses: A synchronous bus has a clock line, and every action happens at fixed clock edges, like a train timetable. It is simple and fast, but every device must keep up with that clock, and long wires make clock skew a problem. An asynchronous bus has no shared clock; it uses a handshake. The sender puts data on the bus and raises a request line; the receiver takes the data and raises an acknowledge line; then both lower their lines. Slow and fast devices can share it, at the cost of extra signalling. Picture: Req up -> data read -> Ack up -> Req down -> Ack down.

Why one bus is not enough: Since everything shares the same wires, only one transfer can happen at a time, and the slowest device can limit everyone. So real computers use a hierarchy of connections: a very fast link between the CPU and memory, and separate I/O links for devices. Modern PCs connect devices with PCI Express, which is not a shared bus at all but fast serial point-to-point lanes, and USB for external devices.

The I/O interface (controller): A device is never wired straight to the CPU. Between them sits an I/O interface or device controller, a small circuit that translates. It usually offers a few registers to the CPU: a data register (the byte or word to send or receive), a status register (bits such as ready, busy, error) and a control register (commands like start, reset, mode). The CPU only reads and writes these registers; the controller handles the device's own signals, timing and format. This is why a new printer comes with a driver: the driver knows that controller's registers.

How the CPU addresses device registers: There are two approaches. Memory-mapped I/O: device registers are given ordinary memory addresses, so normal load and store instructions talk to devices. Most ARM and RISC systems do this. Isolated (port-mapped) I/O: devices have a separate address space accessed with special instructions like IN and OUT, as in the x86 family. Memory-mapped I/O needs no extra instructions but uses up part of the address space; isolated I/O keeps memory addresses free but needs special instructions.

Method 1, programmed I/O (polling): The CPU does everything itself. To print a character, it reads the status register again and again in a loop until the ready bit is 1, then writes the character to the data register, then repeats for the next character. Pseudo-code: while (status.ready == 0) { } ; data = ch. This is simple and fine for slow, rare events or tiny systems. The problem is the busy waiting: the CPU burns cycles doing nothing useful.

How costly polling can be, worked example: Suppose one poll costs 400 cycles on a 1 GHz CPU (10^9 cycles per second). A keyboard polled 100 times per second costs 100 x 400 = 40,000 cycles per second, just 0.004 percent of the CPU. Harmless. Now a disk sends data in 16-byte chunks at 16 MB per second; that is 1,000,000 chunks per second, so 1,000,000 polls x 400 = 400,000,000 cycles per second, a full 40 percent of the CPU. For fast devices polling is a waste.

Method 2, interrupt-driven I/O: Instead of the CPU asking again and again, the device tells the CPU when it is ready by raising an interrupt request line. The sequence: the CPU is running a program; the device raises an interrupt; the CPU finishes the current instruction; it saves the program counter and status (on the stack or in special registers); it jumps to an interrupt service routine (ISR) for that device; the ISR moves the data and clears the request; the CPU restores the saved state and continues the program as if nothing happened. The CPU does useful work between events. The cost is the overhead of saving and restoring state on each interrupt, which still adds up when a device interrupts for every single byte.

Who goes first, priority: Several devices may interrupt at once. With a daisy chain, devices are connected in series on the acknowledge line. When the CPU acknowledges, the signal passes through device 1; if device 1 requested, it keeps the acknowledge and puts its identity (vector) on the bus; if not, it passes the signal to device 2, and so on. So the device electrically closest to the CPU has the highest priority. It is cheap, but far devices can starve. With parallel priority, each device has its own request line into a priority encoder, which picks the highest-priority request quickly and can mask (ignore) chosen devices. Vectored interrupts let each device supply an address or number so the CPU jumps straight to the right ISR.

Method 3, direct memory access (DMA): For big transfers, even one interrupt per byte is too much. A DMA controller is a helper that moves a whole block between a device and memory without the CPU touching each byte. The CPU only sets it up: start memory address, number of bytes, direction (read or write). The DMA controller then requests the bus, transfers the data word by word, counting down, and raises one single interrupt when the whole block is done. Picture: CPU sets up -> DMA <-> Memory <-> Device -> one interrupt at the end.

Sharing the bus with DMA: The CPU and the DMA controller both want the memory bus. In burst mode, DMA takes the bus and moves the whole block at once; fast, but the CPU may be blocked from memory meanwhile. In cycle stealing, DMA takes the bus for one word at a time, stealing an occasional cycle, so the CPU slows slightly but keeps going. Since the CPU spends much time hitting in its caches, it often barely notices. Note that DMA writes memory directly, so the hardware or OS must keep caches consistent with it, the same stale-data issue we met with write-back caches.

I/O processors: Large systems take the idea further with I/O processors or channels, small processors dedicated to I/O that run their own simple programs of I/O commands. Mainframes used channels heavily. The main CPU just says 'run this I/O program' and gets an interrupt when it is done.

Comparing the three methods: Programmed I/O: simplest hardware, CPU fully busy, good for slow or simple devices. Interrupt-driven: CPU free between events, overhead per event, good for keyboards, mice, network packets arriving at random times. DMA: CPU free during the whole block, needs a DMA controller, best for disks, network cards, cameras and sound streaming.

Storage as an I/O device: A hard disk drive has spinning platters and a moving arm. Access time = seek time (moving the arm to the track) + rotational latency (waiting for the sector to come under the head) + transfer time. At 7200 RPM one rotation takes 60 / 7200 seconds = 8.33 ms, so the average rotational latency is half of that, about 4.17 ms. That is millions of CPU cycles.
