SSDs have no moving parts, so they avoid seek and rotation, which is why replacing an HDD with an SSD makes an old laptop feel new.

RAID in brief: RAID combines several disks. RAID 0 stripes data across disks for speed but has no redundancy, so one failed disk loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors the same data on two disks, so one can fail safely. RAID 5 stripes data with parity spread across all disks, so it survives one disk failure while wasting only one disk's worth of space. Banks and data centres in Bangladesh use such setups so a single dead disk does not take down a service.

Real-life example 1, downloading a video on your laptop: A Wi-Fi card receives packets of a video. It uses DMA to place packets directly into memory buffers, then raises an interrupt. The network driver's ISR processes the batch, and the file is later written to the SSD, again by DMA. Meanwhile the CPU plays music and runs your browser. If every byte needed the CPU to poll, your laptop would struggle at speeds a cheap phone handles easily.

Real-life example 2, the bus stop analogy: Programmed I/O is like standing at the Farmgate bus stop staring down the road every second, doing nothing else. Interrupt-driven I/O is like reading a book and lifting your head only when you hear the bus horn. DMA is like asking your friend to collect the parcel from the Sundarban Courier office and just text you when it is home. Where the analogy breaks: a real CPU must save its exact state before handling an interrupt, something you do not need to do when you close a book.

Common mistakes: Thinking DMA needs no CPU at all; the CPU sets it up and handles the final interrupt. Thinking interrupts are handled in the middle of an instruction; normally the current instruction completes first. Mixing up memory-mapped and isolated I/O. Saying the daisy chain gives priority to the farthest device; it is the nearest. Calling RAID 0 a backup; it has no redundancy.

What exams ask: Draw the system bus with address, data and control lines. Compare synchronous and asynchronous buses and draw a handshake. Compare programmed, interrupt-driven and DMA I/O in a table. List the steps when an interrupt occurs. Explain daisy-chain priority. Explain DMA set-up, burst mode and cycle stealing. Calculate the CPU fraction spent on polling, or disk access time.

Quick recap: Devices connect through buses and controllers with data, status and control registers, addressed by memory-mapped or isolated I/O. The CPU can poll (simple but wasteful), take interrupts (efficient for random events) or let DMA move whole blocks (best for bulk data). Priority schemes decide who is served first. Next and final lesson: what happens when we put many processors together, and a recap of the whole course.
key_points: A system bus has address, data and control lines; width and address lines set how much data moves and how much can be addressed.
Synchronous buses use a shared clock; asynchronous buses use request/acknowledge handshaking.
An I/O controller exposes data, status and control registers; the CPU talks only to these registers.
Memory-mapped I/O uses normal load/store; isolated I/O uses separate instructions like IN/OUT.
Programmed I/O polls and wastes CPU time on fast devices; interrupts let the device signal when ready.
On an interrupt the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves state, runs the ISR and restores state.
Daisy chain priority favours the device nearest the CPU; a priority encoder handles parallel requests.
DMA moves whole blocks between device and memory, interrupting the CPU only once at the end (burst or cycle stealing).
lessons.tip: Remember the three I/O methods with one question: who moves each byte? In programmed and interrupt I/O the CPU does; in DMA the DMA controller does. Most comparison questions are answered by that one line.
lessons.task: Calculate: a 2 GHz CPU spends 500 cycles per poll. What fraction of the CPU is used if a device is polled 1,000 times per second? And 4,000,000 times per second? Then compute the average rotational latency of a 5400 RPM hard disk.

quiz.q: Which bus lines carry signals like read, write and interrupt request?
quiz.explain: Control lines carry commands and status; address lines say where, data lines carry the values.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of programmed I/O (polling)?
options: It cannot read the status register
quiz.explain: The CPU repeatedly checks the status register and does no useful work while waiting.

quiz.q: In a daisy-chain interrupt scheme, which device has the highest priority?
options: The one with the largest address
The one electrically nearest to the CPU
quiz.explain: The acknowledge signal reaches the nearest device first, which can keep it.

quiz.q: In a DMA transfer, what does the CPU do?
options: Sets up address, count and direction, then handles one interrupt at the end
Polls the device after every byte
quiz.explain: The DMA controller moves the block; the CPU only sets it up and handles the completion interrupt.

quiz.q: A 7200 RPM disk has what average rotational latency?
quiz.explain: One rotation is 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms; on average you wait half a rotation, about 4.17 ms.

lessons.title: Parallel Processors and Course Recap
lessons.content:
Think about Eid shopping season at a big tailor shop in Bongobazar. One master tailor, no matter how skilled, can only sew so fast. To finish hundreds of orders before Eid, the shop hires ten tailors. Suddenly new problems appear: who cuts which cloth, how to share the one measuring tape, what if two tailors change the same customer's order at the same time, and why the shop is not exactly ten times faster. Modern processors face exactly these questions, because for the last two decades almost all speed-up has come not from one faster core, but from many cores working together.

What a parallel processor is: A parallel computer uses more than one processing unit at the same time to work on a problem. This includes multicore chips (several complete CPUs, called cores, on one chip), multiprocessor servers with several chips, vector and SIMD units that do the same operation on many numbers at once, GPUs with thousands of simple cores, and clusters of whole computers connected by a network.

The problem, the power wall: For many years designers made single cores faster by raising the clock rate and adding clever tricks like deeper pipelines and out-of-order execution (lessons 16 to 18). Around the mid-2000s this hit a wall. Dynamic power in CMOS chips grows roughly with capacitance x voltage squared x frequency. Voltage could no longer be lowered much, so higher clock rates meant far more heat than a chip and cooler could handle. Clock rates mostly stopped climbing at a few gigahertz. But transistor counts kept growing. The answer: use the extra transistors to put several cores on one chip.

Before multicore: Parallel machines existed long before, but they were expensive supercomputers or multi-chip servers used by universities, weather centres and banks. Ordinary programmers wrote sequential code and simply waited for next year's faster CPU to speed it up for free. After multicore became normal in laptops and then phones, that free lunch ended: a single-threaded program uses only one core no matter how many the chip has.

Flynn's taxonomy: In 1966 Michael Flynn classified computers by how many instruction streams and data streams they handle. SISD, single instruction single data: a classic single-core processor. SIMD, single instruction multiple data: one instruction operates on many data items at once, as in vector units and GPUs. MISD, multiple instruction single data: rare, mostly a theoretical category. MIMD, multiple instruction multiple data: several independent processors each running their own program on their own data; multicore chips and clusters are MIMD.

Shared memory multiprocessors: In a shared memory system all cores see one common address space; any core can load or store any address, and cores communicate by reading and writing shared variables. If every core reaches every memory location in about the same time, it is UMA (uniform memory access), also called SMP. In bigger servers memory is attached to different chips, so nearby memory is faster than far memory; this is NUMA (non-uniform memory access). Picture: Core0, Core1, Core2, Core3 each with private L1/L2 -> shared L3 -> memory controller -> DRAM.

Message passing systems: In a cluster, each computer has its own private memory, and processors cooperate by sending messages over a network. There is no shared address space, so there are no coherence problems between machines, but programmers must explicitly send and receive data. Large supercomputers and data centres, including the servers behind big web services, are built this way.

The cache coherence problem: Each core has its own private caches. Suppose X = 5 in memory. Core 1 reads X into its cache. Core 2 also reads X into its cache. Now core 1 writes X = 7 into its write-back cache. If nothing else happens, core 2 still reads 5 from its own cache: two cores disagree about the value of one variable. A system is cache coherent when every read returns the most recent write to that address, as if there were just one copy. Hardware must enforce this automatically.

Snooping and write-invalidate: In a snooping protocol all caches watch (snoop on) a shared bus or interconnect. The most common approach is write-invalidate: before a core writes a block, it broadcasts an invalidate message, and every other cache holding that block marks its copy invalid. The next time core 2 reads X, it misses, and gets the new value 7 from core 1's cache or from memory. Misses caused this way are the fourth C from lesson 21: coherence misses.

The MESI protocol: Many processors track each cache line with four states. Modified: only this cache has the line and it has been changed; memory is stale. Exclusive: only this cache has it, and it matches memory. Shared: several caches may have clean copies. Invalid: the copy is not usable. Worked trace: core 1 reads X (no one else has it) -> E in core 1. Core 2 reads X -> both become S. Core 1 writes X -> core 1 sends invalidate, core 2's copy becomes I, core 1 becomes M. Core 2 reads X -> core 1 supplies the data (and it is written back), both become S. Nice detail: a write in state E can become M silently, without any bus message, because nobody else has a copy.

Directories for many cores: Broadcasting every invalidate to every cache stops scaling when there are dozens or hundreds of cores. Directory-based coherence keeps, for each memory block, a record of which caches hold it, so invalidations go only to those caches. Large multicore and NUMA systems use directory schemes or mixtures.

False sharing, a real-world trap: Coherence works on whole cache lines, not single variables. If core 1 keeps updating counter a and core 2 keeps updating counter b, and a and b happen to sit in the same 64-byte line, the line bounces between the two caches on every write, even though the cores never share data. The program becomes much slower for no visible reason. The fix is to place such variables in different cache lines, for example by padding.

Synchronisation: When cores share data they need locks so that, say, two threads updating one bank balance do not lose an update. Ordinary loads and stores are not enough, because another core can sneak in between the read and the write. Processors therefore provide atomic instructions, such as test-and-set, compare-and-swap, or a load-linked/store-conditional pair, which read and modify a location as one indivisible step. Locks in programming languages are built on these.

SIMD and vector units: SIMD speeds up work where the same operation applies to many numbers, such as image filters, audio, and machine learning. Instead of adding two arrays one element at a time, a single SIMD instruction adds, for example, 4, 8 or 16 numbers in one go. x86 processors have SSE and AVX instructions; ARM processors have NEON. Your phone uses them when it applies a beauty filter on the camera.

GPUs: A graphics processing unit has thousands of small, simple cores organised to run the same program on many data items together. It hides memory latency not with huge caches but by switching between many waiting threads. GPUs began for drawing 3D graphics, where every pixel needs similar maths, and are now the main engine for training AI models. They are poor at branchy, sequential code, where a CPU core shines.

Hardware multithreading: A single core often sits idle waiting for memory. Simultaneous multithreading (SMT), which Intel markets as Hyper-Threading, lets one core keep the state of two (or more) threads and issue instructions from both, filling idle slots. It shows as twice the logical cores in Task Manager, but gives much less than double speed, because the threads share the same execution units and caches.

Amdahl's law again: If a fraction p of a program can run in parallel on n cores and the rest is sequential, speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n). Example: p = 0.9 on 8 cores: 1 / (0.1 + 0.9/8) = 1 / (0.1 + 0.1125) = 1 / 0.2125, about 4.7, not 8. Even with infinite cores the limit is 1 / 0.1 = 10. The sequential part rules. That is why the ten tailors are not ten times faster: the single cutting table is the bottleneck.

When to go parallel and when not: Parallelism pays when work splits into big independent chunks: image processing, video encoding, web servers handling many users, scientific simulations, AI training. It does not pay for small tasks where coordination costs more than the work, for code that is mostly sequential, or when shared data forces constant locking and coherence traffic. Sometimes a better algorithm or better cache use on one core beats eight cores.

Real-life example 1, a mobile financial service on Eid: On the day before Eid, a service like bKash sees a huge spike of transactions. No single core could handle it. Servers run many cores, each serving different requests in parallel (MIMD), across many machines (clusters with message passing). Inside each server, coherence hardware keeps shared caches consistent, and the hardest part of the design is keeping balance updates correct with locks and atomic operations while staying fast.

Real-life example 2, your phone's chip: Many phone chips use a big.LITTLE style design: a few large fast cores for heavy work like gaming, and several small efficient cores for background tasks like checking WhatsApp messages, to save battery. Next to them sits a GPU for graphics and often a neural processing unit for AI features. One chip, many kinds of parallel hardware, each used where it fits best.

Common mistakes: Believing n cores give n times speed; Amdahl's law says otherwise. Thinking coherence is the programmer's job on ordinary multicore CPUs; the hardware keeps caches coherent, but programmers still need locks for correct updates. Mixing up SIMD (one instruction, many data) with MIMD (many independent instruction streams). Forgetting false sharing. Thinking hyper-threads are full cores.

What exams ask: Explain Flynn's taxonomy with examples. Compare shared memory and message passing, UMA and NUMA. State the cache coherence problem with an example and explain snooping write-invalidate. Trace MESI states for a sequence of reads and writes. Compute Amdahl speedup. Explain why the industry moved to multicore.

Course recap, the whole journey: We started with the split between architecture (the ISA promise) and organization (how it is built), and learned to measure performance with CPU time = instructions x CPI x clock cycle time. We saw how numbers live in hardware, including IEEE 754, and how the ALU adds, multiplies and divides. We studied instruction sets, addressing modes, and RISC versus CISC. We built a datapath, controlled it with hardwired and microprogrammed control, and sped it up with multi-cycle design, pipelining, hazard handling and branch prediction. We climbed the memory hierarchy through caches, DRAM and virtual memory, connected the outside world with buses, interrupts and DMA, and finally put many processors together. One theme ran through everything: every design is a trade-off among speed, cost, power and correctness, guided by locality and by measurement.

What to learn next: Microprocessors and Assembly Language puts all of this onto a real chip and lets you program it instruction by instruction. Operating Systems builds on interrupts, virtual memory and multicore scheduling. Compiler Design turns high-level code into efficient instructions for an ISA. Embedded Systems and Computer Peripherals and Interfacing apply I/O organisation to real devices. If you love hardware, try a free Verilog simulator and build a tiny CPU yourself; if you love software, profile your own programs and watch the cache at work.
key_points: The power wall (power grows with voltage squared x frequency) stopped clock increases, so chips moved to multiple cores.
Flynn's taxonomy: SISD, SIMD, MISD (rare) and MIMD; multicore chips and clusters are MIMD.
Shared memory systems can be UMA (SMP) or NUMA; clusters use message passing with private memory.
Cache coherence ensures every read sees the latest write; snooping write-invalidate is the common method.
MESI states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid; directories replace broadcasting for many cores.
False sharing slows programs when independent variables share one cache line.
SIMD units (SSE/AVX, NEON) and GPUs apply one operation to many data items; SMT shares one core between threads.
Amdahl: speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n); p = 0.9 on 8 cores gives about 4.7, at most 10.
lessons.tip: To review the whole course, draw one big picture from memory: CPU pipeline in the middle, caches and DRAM below, virtual memory translation beside it, I/O on the right, and many cores around it. If you can explain every arrow, you know the course.
lessons.task: Open Task Manager (Windows) or a CPU info app on your phone and count physical cores and logical processors. Then compute Amdahl speedup for p = 0.75 on 2, 4 and 16 cores, and write one sentence on what limits the speedup.

quiz.q: Which Flynn category does a modern multicore laptop CPU belong to?
quiz.explain: Each core runs its own instruction stream on its own data, so it is MIMD.

quiz.q: Core 1 and core 2 both cache X = 5; core 1 writes 7 and core 2 still reads 5. What problem is this?
quiz.explain: Two private caches hold different values for the same address; coherence protocols prevent this.

quiz.q: In MESI, what state does core 2's copy take when core 1 writes a shared line?
quiz.explain: Write-invalidate makes all other copies Invalid, and the writer's copy becomes Modified.

quiz.q: A program is 90 percent parallel. What is the maximum speedup with unlimited cores?
quiz.explain: As n grows, speedup approaches 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 10.

quiz.q: Why did the industry move to multicore chips in the mid-2000s?
options: Software could no longer use one core
Memory became faster than the CPU
Raising clock rates produced too much power and heat
quiz.explain: The power wall stopped clock growth, so extra transistors were used for more cores instead.
